en: Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, Scroll One.
Compiled by Dharma Master Zhiyi of Zhang’an during the Sui Dynasty;
revised by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Zhìràn during the Tang Dynasty.

1. Introduction (1–2). Part One: The Upper Section of the Introduction. From ancient times, there have been those such as Xiao Shan-yao and Ping of Guannei who directly chanted the text to explain its meaning and divided it into chapters and sections; from this, a standard practice was established.
The textual passages of this sūtra vary in length, not being uniform; they consist of two, three, four, five, seven, or eight [sections].
Emperor Wu of Liang established only the "Middle Before" and "Middle After";
Kaishan included only the "Introduction" and "Main Body"; Guangzhai added the "Circulation."
Lingwei asked about the existence of *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination), and the answer was that there remains residual momentum.
Regarding the five gates of Hexi, the seven sections of Vasubandhu, and the eight gates of Xinghuang:
though each is as beautiful as orchids or chrysanthemums, the sūtras provide the prohibition while the śāstras offer the opening.
The cowherd girl adding water is "concealment" (chā);
the deepening of the stream and the splitting of the layers is "revelation" (vivaraṇa).
Now, [the text] is divided into five parts, and further into seven.

First, the enumeration of chapters; second, the indication of the location; third, the explanation of the name; fourth, the origination; fifth, the general and specific aspects; sixth, the citation of evidence; seventh, alternative interpretations. First, regarding the enumeration of chapters:

(1) the invocation of the assembly of *nirvāṇa*; (2) the exposition of the gift of *nirvāṇa*; (3) the manifestation of the practice of *nirvāṇa*; (4) the questions and answers on the meaning of *nirvāṇa*; (5) the application of the *nirvāṇa* through the methods of subduing and gathering, and so forth.

Second, regarding the indication of textual sections: from the beginning up to "blood flows and sprinkles the ground" is the section on Requesting; from Cunda up to the question of the Great Assembly is the section on Bestowing; from Manifesting Illness up to King Guṇarāja is the section on Practice; from the Lion’s Roar up to the end of the chapter is the section on Meaning; and from Kāśyapa to the end of the sutra is the section on Application.
Third, regarding the explanation of the name:
The Way does not operate in isolation; it awaits the proper time and relies on its companions.

Now that the time for Nirvana has arrived, the gateway of his countenance opens to illuminate all, and he emits sounds according to the capacities of beings, startling and awakening them as they gather here at Kuśinagara.
To "summon" (zhào) means to draw forth by means of conditions; to "invite" (qǐng) means to cause something to arrive.
Among the assemblies, there are both provisional and ultimate [teachings]: those that are ultimate may be summoned, while those that are provisional should be invited.
Since the fifty-two assemblies have gathered from the ten directions, all for the purpose of manifesting the Great Parinirvāṇa, they are called the "Summoned and Invited Assembly of Nirvāṇa."

Throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Buddha cultivated the Great Nirvāṇa-treasury, which is difficult to attain; fundamentally, he had no secretiveness or stinginess, yet [sentient beings] were not entirely capable of receiving it. Therefore, he first applied poison and later washed it away with water; the beginning was the same as the end, and he waited for the opportune moment.
Because Cunda presented an offering, he was granted eternal physical strength and vitality.
Because the bhikṣus requested him to remain, he rejected the false and discoursed on the true.
Through their earnest exhortation, Kāśyapa received his instructions.
Bestowing gifts in accordance with requests without delay or omission, the rain of Dharma overflowed and filled the city of Kuśinagara; therefore, this is called the "Expounding of the Nirvāṇa Gift.

Yet, the profound and serene secret treasury is not reached by mere practice; through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he manifested himself before others, reclining on his right side and remaining silent without speaking, thereby manifesting the conduct of illness.
At Kāśyapa’s invitation, he sat cross-legged with a serene and joyful countenance and spoke of the "Three Fingers and One.
The Bodhisattva practiced the five modes of conduct and the ten virtues; therefore, this is called the practice of manifesting nirvāṇa.

However, as the meaning of *nirvāṇa* is vast and inexhaustible, one who wishes to present a single point to encompass the whole is like pointing to the saltiness or sweetness of the ocean; thus, by specifically inquiring about Buddha-nature across six successive layers, the Buddha replies to each name as the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.

However, the essence of Buddha-nature is neither good nor evil; it employs both good and evil, pervading all without limit. Moreover, by encompassing the general outline, it briefly includes the vast: when employing goodness, Rāhula is thereby gathered in; when employing evil, Sunakṣatra is likewise included. Since this is the case for these two sons, all others may be treated accordingly.

Furthermore, its essence is neither heterodox nor orthodox, yet it employs both heterodoxy and orthodoxy in tandem: when employing orthodoxy, it initially gathers the five disciples headed by Aśvajit; when employing heterodoxy, it ultimately incorporates the ten externalists who follow heterodox paths.
Since it is so for the beginning and the end, the middle is likewise the same.
This is called the function of nirvāṇa.

Fourth, regarding its arising: it arises from the existence of giving; it is established through the practice of giving; through practice one perceives the meaning, and through realizing that meaning, its utility is manifested.
Furthermore, purpose arises from meaning; meaning arises from practice; practice arises from giving; and giving arises from the gathering of the assembly.
These factors arise from one another in both direct and reverse order; thus, they constitute a sequential progression.
Because it begins where there was no beginning, there is invocation; because it ends where there is no end, there is great function.

When evil is exhausted and the heterodox are eliminated, when goodness reaches its limit and the orthodox comes to rest, both subduing and gathering cease, and one ultimately enters nirvana in absolute stillness.
Fifth, regarding the common and specific [aspects]:
throughout the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching, there is nothing that is not addressed to the assembly.
If there were no assembly, would the teaching be in vain, and to whom would it be bestowed?
Therefore, this applies generally to the assembly.
To speak of it specifically, the gathering of the assembly is foremost at the beginning; one proclaims their names to summon and invite them.
Generally speaking, every single word and every single act is bestowed upon sentient beings.

When one bestows [gifts] after seeking them out through specific inquiries regarding causes and conditions, the text is extensive and the matter is clear; therefore, this is called the "Nirvana-bestowal of Explication.
Generally speaking, in instructing sentient beings, there is nothing that does not conform to the rules and standards, and all such practices are fully encompassed within this conduct.
Setting aside the separate discussion of the five elements and ten virtues, as the text is extensive and the matters therein are manifest, it is named the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

This scripture elucidates the Buddha-nature from beginning to end; while the Buddha-nature pervades all things such that there is nowhere it is not discerned, this particular section uses a single sequence of questions and answers to discuss the Buddha-nature exclusively.
When the manifestations of civilization become evident, it is termed the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.

Generally speaking, this entire treatise guides and benefits all sentient beings; just as the medicinal herbs of the great earth serve the needs of all living beings, so too does my Dharma. For this reason, it is called "Universal" (*pāramitā*).
The separate discussion on subsuming the evil and subsuming the heterodox is extensive in its text yet clear in its meaning; therefore, its application is explained separately.
Sixth, regarding the citation of evidence: first, many passages are cited, followed by a single location.

Regarding the initial extensive passages: for instance, the sound and light universally proclaiming that one should quickly go to the Buddha’s presence to pose the final question—is this not a summons?
Furthermore, the "Lion’s Roar" chapter states: "He summoned and invited the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions to assemble in the Śāla grove for the Great Lion’s Roar."
The "Cunda Chapter" states: "I now bestow upon you eternal life, physical form, and strength.
The "Chapter on King of Virtue" states: "If you now wish to exhaust the ocean of Great Nirvāṇa, you have encountered me, who possess abundant wisdom that can be bestowed as a gift."
The "Chapter on Noble Conduct" states: "A bodhisattva should single-mindedly cultivate five kinds of practices for the sake of Great Nirvāṇa.
It further states: "By cultivating Great Nirvāṇa, one attains ten merits."
In the "Lion’s Roar" chapter, six questions are posed regarding the Buddha-nature: for what reason is it called "Buddha-nature"?
The Tathāgata answers fully that the Buddha-nature is simply the meaning of Great Nirvāṇa.

The "Kāśyapa Chapter" states: "Wandering through the world with a compassionate heart. The world consists of nothing other than good and evil, heterodoxy and orthodoxy; by overturning the heterodoxy of the ten sages and subduing the evil of the "only son," this is the very function of *nirvāṇa*.

Next, to cite a passage from a single location, the *Siṃhanāda-parivarta* states: "Buddha-nature is also called the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, it is also called Prajñāpāramitā, it is also called Vajra-samādhi, it is also called Siṃhanāda-samādhi, and it is also called Buddha-nature."
"However, the Buddha-nature is not singular; why, then, are there five?
It is by means of these five names that they are designated, so as to lead one to understand that they are not actually five.

The assembly being summoned consists entirely of Tathāgatas who are fellow-practitioners and spiritual friends. From the perspective of their fundamental roots of virtue (*guṇamūla*), they all abide in the *Śūraṅgama*; from the perspective of their manifestations, they constitute the fifty-two assemblies. Therefore, the name *Śūraṅgama* is used to certify and summon this assembly."
I say: as for the fifty-two assemblies, the three assemblies of bhikṣus and so forth constitute one; the assembly of bodhisattvas constitutes another.

From two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* to a thousand billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, there are twenty-one assemblies with increasing numbers, eight assemblies with identical numbers, one assembly with no number, four intermediate assemblies, six for the six heavens, one for the Brahma assembly, one for the asuras, one for the Māra heaven, one for Maheśvara, and four for the four directions, totaling fifty-two.

The unsurpassed Tamer, with his knowledge of all modes, illuminates the principles and capacities of beings everywhere without the slightest error; he reveals the eternal, manifests the intrinsic nature, and excavates the treasury of awakening to bestow upon the assembly of his time.

If it is named according to the Buddha’s wisdom, it should be called *prajñā*; if it is named according to the established teaching, it is called the "bestowal of nirvāṇa. One should understand how the name *prajñā* serves as the realization of the bestowal of nirvāṇa.

These five practices are truly upright and straight, immovable and unshakable; furthermore, they can shatter and disperse the fetters and delusions of affliction. If viewed from the perspective of cultivation, they are called "practices"; if viewed through analogy, they are likened to a vajra. One should know that the Vajra-samādhi is the practice by which one realizes nirvāṇa.
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the reason for a name; therefore, beneath the name "Nirvana" lies the reason that it is *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature). Buddha-nature is precisely the meaning of Nirvana.

This meaning is sovereign, definitive, and fearless. Whether following the metaphor of the "lion's roar" (*siṃhanāda*) or the referent of the metaphor which is the meaning of Buddha-nature, one should know that the name "lion's roar" can be realized as the meaning of Nirvana.

Essence and function are mutually identical; within all phenomena, there is entirely the nature of peace and bliss, which is none other than Buddha-nature. By means of this essence, its function manifests as wandering and transforming within the world, gathering in the wicked and the heterodox so that they all return to the right and the good. One should know that the name "Buddha-nature" can be realized through the function of Nirvana.
Now, by dividing this according to the sūtra, the textual meaning has a basis and is not merely a product of arbitrary fabrication.
Seventh, regarding the presentation of alternative interpretations:

Emperor Wu of Liang divided the sūtra according to time into "before noon," "noon," and "after noon. While this might be acceptable for "dawn" and "after noon," upon what textual authority are "evening" and "midnight" based?
The *Upāsaka-aṣṭakavarga-sūtra* states: "This discourse was completed in one cycle. To which year—its beginning, middle, or end—does this refer?
Now, by dividing the text into chapters according to its doctrinal content, this difficulty is eliminated.
Kaishan [Huiyuan] established the *xu* (preface) and the *zheng* (main body); the *xu* consists of the invocation, while the *zheng* comprises four chapters.
Guangzhai [Jingying Huiyuan] supplemented it with the *liutong* (circulation), which merely utilizes a small portion of the chapters.
In the *Lingwei*, it is asked whether there is an origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and answered that there remains residual momentum (*śeṣa-vega*).
Since there are questions and answers throughout [the text], there should likewise be residual momentum throughout.
If, according to Hexi, the first two fascicles are taken as the "Gate of Connecting the Present and the Past through Conditions," this would mean attaining the Real while losing the Provisional.
What is now called "invocation" fully encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate.
From the third fascicle up to the "Questions of the Great Assembly," it constitutes the brief and extensive gates; this is merely based on the quantity of the text.
Now, opening this to unfold the bestowal of the *Nirvāṇa*, it includes both the extensive and the brief.
The five practices constitute the gateway to the practice of nirvāṇa, while the ten virtues constitute the gateway to the virtues of a bodhisattva.
Since both practice and virtue belong to the causal stage, combining them here into the chapter on "Practice" avoids prolixity in the text.
Taking the entire *Siṃhanāda-sūtra* as the gate of the inconceivable Middle Way Buddha-nature, its integration was difficult to comprehend;
now, by dividing its meanings and applications, the text becomes easy to understand.
The Master of the Grounds (Dishī) designates the first fascicle as the "Section on the Reversal of Supernatural Powers," which results in gaining the provisional while losing the real;
now, by speaking of invocation and invitation, there is no such partiality.

He designates the second fascicle as the "Section on Breaking Doubts and Eliminating Attachments regarding the Spiritual Lineage" (gotra), and from the third fascicle up to the "Questions of the Great Assembly" as the "Section on the True Meaning of the Correct Dharma."
Now, by bestowing a single nirvāṇa, both parts are simultaneously encompassed.

That [teaching] takes the five practices and ten virtues as the part of cultivation and accomplishment through skillful means; that [teaching] takes the lion’s roar as the part of entering realization through non-negligence. Since the preceding cultivation has already been the entry into realization, and realization itself is again the entry into realization, would this not be redundant?
Now, for the Chapter on Meaning:
Kāśyapa is taken as the section on abiding in compassion and sustaining [the Dharma], while Cundaka is taken as the section on manifesting the characteristics;
taking the evil toward the good and manifesting the deviant to return to the correct constitutes the section on function.

At the beginning of the Xinghuang period, there were six gates for receiving and guiding those with karmic connections from both past and present: first, the Gate of Receiving and Guiding Based on Past and Present Karmic Connections, which employs the intention of Master Lang;
second, the Gate of Dispelling Doubts and Eliminating Attachments, which employs the intention of Master Di;

third, the Gate of Brief and Extensive Explanations; fourth, the Gate of Practice; fifth, the Gate of the Five Stages; and sixth, the Gate of the Middle Way within Practice—all of which employ the intention of Master Lang.
The "Gate of Expedient Means" and the "Gate of the Non-duality of the Erroneous and the Correct" do not differ in their essence from the "Opening and Closing" distinction found in the Hexi tradition.

Regarding the second part, the detailed explanation: the "Chapter on Summoning and Inviting" was established by the scribe of the scripture; it was traditionally called the "General Preface" (Tongxu) and the "Specific Preface" (Bie xu). It is termed the "General Preface" because the Way is the same throughout the three periods of time, and the "Specific Preface" because the gates of teaching and the capacities of the audience are distinct.
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s single career—whether small, large, distinct, or perfect—is entirely established in this manner, it is called "common" (tong);
yet because the scriptures, their paths, and their supports all possess differences, it is called "distinct" (bie).
Furthermore, the opening of all sūtras invariably establishes the phrase "Thus [have I heard]," which serves as a common expression for encouraging faith.
Within the general introduction (sādhāraṇa-nidāna), this phrase may appear five or six times, depending on whether the primary subject and the location are treated separately or combined.
"In this manner" refers to the principle being transmitted.
"As I have heard" refers to the person capable of transmitting it.
"At one time" refers to the moment when the transmitter and the transmitted principle meet—the occasion when the opportunity and the principle coincide.
The Buddha is the master from whom one receives the transmission;
"abiding" is the place where it is heard;
and the assembly is the companions who receive it directly.
Successively verifying one another, they exhort belief that these are not false, desiring to ensure that those in the future will follow them without confusion.

Furthermore, at the beginning of all the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, there is an exhortation to believe; if one believes in the Great and believes in the Small, the Great and the Small must necessarily be distinct.
If they were not different, there would be no distinction between small and large, common and particular, or circular and unique; yet if they were different, how could one differentiate them?
Now, I shall briefly explain this.

If one says that the "transmitter" and the "transmitted" are similar to one another, this constitutes "likeness" (rú); if it is said that there is nothing that is not the transmitter or the transmitted, this is called "is-ness" (shì). This is the intended meaning of the Tripiṭaka.

If one says that the union of understanding with reality constitutes "thusness" (tathatā), and that the dissolution of the body and the stilling of wisdom constitute this [truth], this is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Sambhoga-yāna).

If one says that being in accordance with the capacities of beings constitutes "thusness," and that while phenomena may oppose it, principle accords with it, this is the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna).

If one says that the realm of Māra is identical to the realm of the Buddha as being suchness (tathatā), and that every single form and every single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way, this is the meaning of faith in the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa).
Since this is so, passages such as "Thus have I heard" and the like can be understood accordingly.
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"Those who believe say that this matter is thus; those who do not believe say that this matter is not thus.
If one believes the first three [turnings], this is the belief in the various provisional means (*upāya*) of the skillful expedients.
If one believes in the latter [of these], it is the belief that the one true reality is perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*).

This [explanation] of the general and specific introductions has been employed by all masters; it is commonly heard in the world and need not be elaborated upon further, as is fully detailed in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra).
Now, this [text] retains only the single principle of "interpreting according to the teaching" (*yōkyō*), and all other matters are to be inferred from it.
Herein we clarify the five phrases of the general introduction (*tsūjo*), which may also be correlated with the five chapters:

"Thus" (*nyorai*) introduces the request; "I have heard" (*wamon*) introduces the bestowal; "at one time" (*isshi*) introduces the practice; "dwelling at" (*jūsho*) introduces the meaning; and "together with those who heard" (*dōmon*) introduces the function.
Thus, in introducing the assembly for the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra: that which is not different is called "as it is" (*tathatā*), and that which is not otherwise is called "this.
If one does not attain suchness, then what is different is definitively different, and what is not so is definitively not so.
One who comprehends this meaning finds that what is different is not different, and what is not is not not.

Beginning from the various rows of insects and worms down to the lowest forms of life, their deceptive species and extraordinary shapes result in a chaotic mixture of karmic retributions; they range from those who reach up to the Brahma-world or cover the great trichiliocosm, to those where the large and small overwhelm one another and the refined and coarse vie for dominance.
If one views this with the eyes of ordinary cattle or sheep, then nothing would be free from contradiction; how could it be as it is?

That it can be so is because one knows that the Mahāsattvas of the Dharmakāya manifest various forms through the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, realizing both difference and non-difference; therefore, it is called "as it is" (yathābhūta).
Knowing what is not "not" and what is not "not-not," it is thus said to be "is. One should know that such an expression clearly serves as a prologue for summoning and inviting the assembly.

Regarding my hearing of the introduction to the Nirvana Sūtra and the giving of alms: that which I had not heard in the past, I now hear; I see eight *dronas* of non-glutinous rice pervading the entire assembly, and I hear that the fruits of these two kinds of giving are equal and without distinction. Having heard for the first time the various flavors of the Dharma—the four virtues of the letter "I" and the secret Buddha-nature—I know that I have heard the introduction to the Nirvana Sūtra and the giving of alms.
Regarding the practitioner of simultaneous nirvāṇa: their practice is simultaneous rather than sequential, and their realization is simultaneous rather than realized through successive stages.

As the text states: "Furthermore, there is one practice that is the practice of the Tathāgata; it is not a sequential practice, for within a single thought-moment, one is able to fully manifest bodies in the five realms of existence."
"Thus, they simultaneously realize [enlightenment]; one should know that this signifies the sequential entry into nirvana.

Regarding the meaning of 'abiding' as the sequence for entering nirvana: 'place' (sthāna) refers to the locus where the body returns to rest; it symbolizes that the Buddha-nature is the ultimate and final ground."

Driving away the heterodox and leading the malevolent toward that Kuśinagara—neither withering nor flourishing, it is the intermediate state of quiescent extinction; whether for others or for oneself, reaching the ultimate limit and coming to rest, one should know that this dwelling place illustrates the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the "Preface to the Shared Audience" (*tóngwén xù*) concerning the application of *Nirvāṇa*: the deities of mountains, forests, rivers, and seas, as well as the species of oxen, sheep, locusts, and insects, constitute the assembly of the shared audience. This indicates that the equal teaching [of the Buddha] treats the three sons together as three fields; it gathers both good and evil alike, delivering both the heterodox and the orthodox. Therefore, the assembly of the shared audience serves as the preface to the application of *Nirvāṇa*.
Having already concluded the separate assignment of the five prefaces, I shall further explain one preface for each of the five chapters.

Now, the multitude does not transcend the eight Buddhas; these eight Buddhas are no different from the manifest Buddha in their name, being "Suchness" (Tathatā). Because there is nothing that is not Buddha, they are called "This."
Because the two kinds of giving are without distinction, it is called "as" (如); because they equally enter the secret treasury, it is called "is" (是).
Because it is the practice of the Tathāgata, it is called "as"; because this single practice universally encompasses all, it is called "is."
Because the Buddha-nature is one and the same, it is called "thus" (tathā); because its essence and meaning are non-dual, it is called "this" (iti).
Because evil and the false are non-dual, it is called "thus"; because there is nothing superior to it, it is called "this."
One should know that such a general introduction consists of five chapters.
What I have heard is likewise:
formerly it was said that the fourfold assembly were not the eight Buddhas, but now it is heard that the eight Buddhas are precisely the fourfold assembly.

In the past, I heard that there are distinctions between the beginning and the end, and that the five fruits undergo transition; now I hear that the two kinds of giving are without difference, both being eternal and blissful.
In the past, I heard that rivers flow in winding curves and do not reach the ocean directly; now I hear that the continent of Aparagoyānī is like a straight line.

In the past, I heard that those with physical eyes cannot even see empty space, much less perceive the nature; yet now I hear that for one who studies the Mahāyāna, although they possess physical eyes, these are called the Buddha-eye, and with the Buddha-eye, they perceive the nature with perfect clarity.

"In the past, I heard that good and evil are as distinct as the Jing and Wei rivers, and that the heterodox and the orthodox follow different tracks; now I hear that the low-mi bird and the divine tortoise both dwell within the same waters.
This constitutes the first chapter of my 'General Preface'."

"At one time" means: at one time they were summoned by the light of the voice; at one time they assembled in the Śāla grove; at one time the Tathāgata’s secret treasury was revealed; at one time they heard the teaching on the eternal bestowal of *nirvāṇa*; at one time they heard it and received it upon their heads to practice accordingly; and at one time they were established within the secret treasury in the sense of entering *nirvāṇa*.

Having at that time heard the two characters "Eternally Abiding" (changzhu), one awakens one's parents, ancestral kin of seven generations, and all sentient beings—whether enemies or friends, good or evil; this constitutes the first chapter of the General Preface.

Regarding the "place of abiding": it means that through the invocation by sound and light, one turns together toward the Buddha’s place of abiding. When the Buddha bestows his own place of abiding upon the assembled multitude, they initiate the practice of *nirvāṇa* from the Buddha’s place of abiding; thus, to see the Buddha’s place of abiding is to see the ultimate meaning.
The first five chapters of the general introduction concerning the dwelling place consist of: the Buddha’s dwelling attracting and converting the wicked;

the fact that all alike see and hear the eternally abiding sound and light, which constitutes "Thus" (tathā), rather than hearing through other expedient means; the final question and answer regarding the constant life-force, physical vigor, peace, and unimpeded eloquence of those who hear together; the upright conduct of those who hear together, like a straight measuring line; and the meaning of the secret treasury of the Western Sea heard together. These are the five chapters of the general introduction concerning the assembly of those who hear together. The fifth set of five chapters concerning the assembly of those who hear together consists of: the fact that the wicked possess the functional application of the Buddha-nature; the fact that all alike see and hear the eternally abiding sound and light as "Thus," rather than through other expedients; the constant life-force, physical vigor, peace, and unimpeded eloquence of those who hear together as the final question and answer; the upright conduct of those who hear together, like a straight measuring line; and the meaning of the secret treasury of the Western Sea heard together. These are the five chapters of the general introduction concerning the assembly of those who hear together.

Furthermore, the five introductory sections correspond to the three points: thus, the general introduction of the three points—wherein they are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor separate—is termed "Thus" (*evam*). "I heard" introduces the *prajñā*; "at one time" introduces liberation; "dwelling place" introduces the *dharmakāya*; and "those who heard together" introduce the non-falsity of the three points.

Furthermore, regarding the five introductory sections that sequence the four virtues: this general introduction sequences the virtue of *guṇa* (merit); "I have heard" sequences the virtue of *sukha* (bliss); "at one time" sequences the virtue of *śubha* (purity); "dwelling place" sequences the virtue of *nitya* (permanence); and "those who heard together" sequences the virtue of *ātman* (self), and so forth.
For example, the essential meaning of the sūtra is arranged according to five sequences; all cases follow this principle and need not be explained further—consider other examples accordingly.
Regarding "I have heard": it refers to "I and self," "I and non-self," "non-self and I," and "neither I nor non-self."
"Hearing what is heard," "hearing what is not heard," "not hearing what is heard," and "neither hearing nor not hearing.
The first three types—my hearing this as that which was heard in the past—are the provisional meanings;
whereas "neither self nor non-self" and "neither hearing nor not hearing" regarding my hearing, as explained in the perfect discourse, constitute the true intent of the present sutra.
"An epoch" (*eka-kāla*) refers simply to the worldly meaning of "one" as a numerical category;
"emptiness as one" refers to the meaning of the Two Vehicles;
the unification of the ultimate and the conventional is the meaning of the Bodhisattva.
First, all is one; one is all; neither one nor all; yet both one and all. Of these, the latter "one" is the primary intent of this sutra.
Regarding "at one time, the Buddha," there are three bodies and four meanings.
The meaning of the latter is present here; it can be understood by analogy with what precedes it.

Regarding the "place of residence" (*vihāra*): in its full form, it should be called Kuśinagara, which has no direct equivalent in Chinese; alternatively, it may be translated as "Horn City," for it possesses three corners.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "To the south of the city of Jiao," referring to this very city.
It is also called the City of Reed Grass (*śāli-grass*) or the City of Thatch; it was so named because the city was covered with grass.
Some say it is called the City of the Rishis; in the past, because the lifespan of the rishis was long and they held those people in high esteem, the place of residence was named after them.
Furthermore, the country was also named after this [name], hence it is called the Kingdom of Kuśī.

Regarding "the birthplace of the Mallas": among humans, the strength of these Mallas equaled that of a thousand men; numbering three hundred thousand in total, they formed a confederation without any external sovereign. Governing themselves by the Dharma, they were neither violent nor chaotic; they were true gentlemen, and thus it is called their "birthplace."
The Āciravatī River—translated here as "Golden Sand"—is located south of the city; it is twenty zhang wide, though some say it is forty zhang wide.
As for the twin śāla trees, they are translated here as "Firm and Solid."
On one side were two trunks, and on four sides were eight trunks, all five *zhang* in height; four were withered and four were flourishing.

Their lower roots were interconnected and their upper branches joined together; their joining resembled "joined stems" (*lianli*), and their flourishing and withering appeared like a mutual yielding of place.
Its leaves are lush and abundant; its flowers are like chariot wheels; its fruits are as large as jars, as sweet as honey, and endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor.
Because of these eight trees, the entire grove is known by a single name, "The Firm" (Sthira).
In this single city alone there are various perspectives.
If one sees it as earth and stone, that is the perspective of human habitation, the meaning of the mundane world.
If one sees it as impermanent, suffering, empty, subject to arising and ceasing, that is the perspective of the Two Vehicles.

If one perceives this as the place for generating the bodhicitta, the place for encountering Buddhas of previous lives, the place of aspiration, or the place for practicing meditative concentration and so forth, that is the dwelling place of a bodhisattva.

If one sees these four virtues as being perfectly fulfilled and complete—compassion shown to others, the city of Kuśāgra representing permanence, the Mallas representing self, the auspicious river representing purity, and the space between the trees representing bliss.

Furthermore, regarding how each individual feature represents four virtues: the indestructibility of the city represents permanence; its abundance represents bliss; its ability to repel enemies represents selfhood; and its freedom from calamities represents purity.
The Mallas represent permanence through their lack of attachment; peace of mind represents bliss; physical strength represents selfhood;

and a pleasing complexion represents purity. As for the river: its constant flow represents permanence; its golden sand represents purity; its coolness represents bliss; and its auspicious blessings represent selfhood.

Regarding the trees, the subsequent passage states: "The pair in the east symbolizes permanence; the pair in the south symbolizes bliss; the pair in the west symbolizes selfhood; and the pair in the north symbolizes purity.
Furthermore, their lush growth symbolizes permanence; their cool shade symbolizes selfhood; their flowers symbolize purity; and their fruits symbolize bliss."
"If one can discern these four virtues both collectively and individually, that is the dwelling place of all Buddhas.

If one says it is what ordinary people who hear this together perceive as the realm of birth and death; or what the sages of the two vehicles perceive; or what the Bodhisattvas who have ascended the stages perceive; or what the eight Buddhas among the nine Buddhas perceive—these are all the perceptions of the Buddhas."
If one grasps this intent, each subsequent sentence below should be interpreted accordingly.
Regarding the assembly of those who heard the teaching together, there are two parts:
first, the gathering of the assembly; second, their deportment.

Regarding the initial passage, I [the author] privately maintain that, according to the intention of this school, the fifty-two assemblies must be taken as those who heard the teaching together; therefore, the "those who heard together" (sahāṃśravaṇa) precedes the list of the fifty-two.
Now, because the bhikṣus were at the forefront, it is said they "heard together.

There are five aspects to "hearing together," namely: the giving, the praise, the category, the assembly, and the number. In the present text, the assembly is missing, yet by implication it ought to be present.
"To share" (*sādhāraṇa*) means "together. The *Śāstra* explains this "togetherness" through seven aspects: namely, one place, one time, one precept, one mind, one view, one path, and one liberation.
Because the bhikṣus share these seven points with the Buddha, it is said that "the Buddha and [the bhikṣus].

According to the explicit meaning of the Tripiṭaka, the *śāttarī* (sixteen-foot) Buddha and the bhikṣus are identical in these seven respects: they were in the same place, Kuśinagara; they were together at the time of parinirvāṇa; they shared the same restraint of the precepts (*śīla*); they shared the same mind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); they shared the same untainted vision (*anāsrava-darśana*); they shared the same path to nirvāṇa; and they shared the same liberation with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-vimukti*). Since all seven are identical to the Buddha, it is therefore called "shared."
If one explains the meaning according to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), there are five points of agreement and two points of distinction. What are they?
The wisdom that realizes the nature of phenomena perceives emptiness within form; it is not that emptiness results from the extinction of form.
This view differs from the Mahāyāna path; it is not the same as the narrow path. Since the paths differ, one should know that there is a distinction between the two.

If one explains the meaning according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the seven aspects such as the *zhunteshen* Buddha, time, and place were not seen by the two bhikṣus previously. It is like providing a candle for a blind person; what benefit is there for one who lacks sight?
Regarding the two bhikṣus before me, my teaching on morality, mind, views, the path, and liberation is like playing music for the deaf; what benefit can it bring to those who lack ears?
This Buddha does not share [this state] with the two bhikṣus mentioned previously.
Within this context, even these bhikṣus do not share it with the Buddhas of the past, let alone ordinary bhikṣus?

If we consider the meaning of perfect illumination (yuanming), the seven aspects of a Buddha are all the realm of a Buddha; they are shared only with the perfectly enlightened Bodhisattvas and those who dwell in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi while manifesting the form of bhikṣus. Since these do not even share it with the three aforementioned Buddhas, how much less so with bhikṣus?
What is now called "shared" (sādhāraṇa) refers to the fact that all [teachings] involve great expedient means (mahopāya) and have reached the ultimate revelation of the truth.
"Great" (maha) is an exclamation of praise for its virtues.
The *Śāstra* states: "Mahā is translated as 'great,' 'much,' or 'superior.'"

He is called "Great" because he is revered by great beings such as the Heavenly Kings; he is called "Much" because he has mastered the four Vedas and the Tripitaka; and he is called "Victorious" because he excels over the ninety-five types of heterodox paths.
This is the explanation according to the Tripiṭaka.

It is called "Great" because it is revered by the noble ones (ārya); it is called "Much" because it penetrates the dharma-gate of analyzing the essence of phenomena; and it is called "Supreme" because it excels the two types of liberation—analytical and through mind-wisdom (prajñā)—this being the explanation according to the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-śāsana).

It is called "Great" because it is revered by those who are both learners and those beyond learning; it is called "Many" because it penetrates both the great and small Dharma-gates; and it is called "Superior" because it transcends the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—this is the explanation according to the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdeśanā).

It is called "Great" because it is revered by the seven kinds of skillful means; it is called "Many" because it penetrates the dharma-gates of both the provisional and the real; it is called "Supreme" because it acts as the leader among those of fixed destiny—this is the explanation according to the Perfect Teaching (Enkyō).
The manifestation of great power is as previously explained.
As for the term "bhikṣu," it refers to a class of persons.
For three reasons, one is called a bhikṣu.
Neither looking up nor looking down, neither square nor crooked, he goes on alms-round in succession to sustain his life with purity; therefore, he is called a "beggar" (bhikṣu).
By observing the seven limbs of the precepts, he chains the monkey-mind with dhyāna; fearing the wolf of impermanence and subduing the fat of the afflictions, this is called "destroying evil."

When one cultivates these three dharmas, the celestial Māras and their poisonous afflictions fear that [the practitioner] will transcend their domain and further dread that they will deliver others; for this reason, they are filled with sorrow and terror.
This is the meaning of the Tripiṭaka.

To realize the essence of all phenomena—that they are neither high nor low, neither cardinal nor intermediate directions—and thereby sustain the life of wisdom; to know that evil is not evil and that there is no knower thereof—this is called "destroying evil."
One must not experience fear or joy; one who is free from fear and joy is said to "frighten Māra.
This explanation applies generally to the meaning of a *bhikṣu*.
Seeking the Dharma-joy of the Middle Way through successive stages—from the shallow to the profound—is called "begging for food" (*piṇḍapāta*).
To successively destroy the five stages of dwelling is called "destroying evil.

Because one fears afflictions (*kleśa*), one fears karma; because one fears karma, one fears the aggregates (*skandha*); because one fears the aggregates, one fears the celestial Māra—this is what is meant by "frightening Māra."
This explains the meaning of "individual bhikṣu.

Within all dharmas, there exists the nature of peace and bliss, which is called "true milk-rice"; by using this to sustain oneself, one dwells within the nature of peace and bliss. Since this nature consists purely of the Buddha-dharma and contains no evil to be destroyed, it is termed "destroying evil."
"The Mara is like the Buddha"—this is called "Frightening the Māras.
This explains the meaning of the term *yuán* (圓) in the name of the bhikṣu.
According to various sūtras, the word "assembly" (*zhòng*) is always present; four or more persons in harmony constitute an assembly.

The *Śāstra* (Commentary) speaks of four types of Saṃgha: those who break the precepts, those like mute sheep, those with a sense of shame (*hrī*), and those who are true. Of these, the latter two Saṃghas are eligible for the one hundred and one formal acts (*karmavācanā*); the former two are incapable. Those at the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth possess a sense of shame, while those who have attained the four fruits [of the path] are the true ones; these constitute the community of the Tripiṭaka.
The stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) is characterized by shame, while from the eighth person upward is the true [stage]; these constitute the assembly of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*).
The thirty minds are characterized by shame, while the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the true [stage]; these constitute the assembly of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*).

The ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute those with a sense of shame; the forty-one stages (*ekacatvāriṃśad-bhūmi*) constitute the true assembly of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).
As for the remaining two types of bhikṣus, they exist in every teaching; since there is no distinction regarding their evil, they are not mentioned separately.
There are four meanings of "shame" (*hrī*) and "truth" (*satya*):

first, initiation; second, influence; third, responding to the capacity of the audience; and fourth, establishing karmic conditions. These are combined and elucidated, which is why the term "assembly" (*parṣad*) is used, and so forth.
"Eighty billion hundreds of thousands" refers to a number. It may refer simply to persons;
or it may refer to the emptiness of persons and phenomena; or it may refer to the enumeration of dharma-gates; or it may refer to the enumeration of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and so forth.
Next, regarding those who surround [the Buddha] from before and behind, this refers to their majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Some are moved by the application of reverence through the three karmas; some are moved by the application of entering emptiness through the four gates; some are moved by the application of entering the provisional through the four gates; and some are moved by the application of entering the Middle Way through the four gates.
From "The fifteenth day of the second month" onwards is the second, the separate introduction, which is precisely the invocation.
The text consists of three parts:
first, clarifying the invoker; second, clarifying the invoked; third, concluding the invocation.
The summoning is further divided into three types:
first, summoning by sound; second, summoning by light; and third, summoning by movement.
There are six methods of summoning by sound:

1. The single sound as the manifestation of the Dharma; 2. The double sound as responding to the occasion; 3. The origin and culmination of the sound; 4. The horizontal and vertical dimensions of the sound; 5. The resonance and response of the sound; 6. The exhortation and proclamation within the sound.
First, regarding the phrase "the second month" below, the time of the sound symbolizes the Dharma: the second month is the period of mid-spring.
"Mid" (zhòng) means middle, which signifies the Middle Way.
The fifteenth day is the time when the moon is full; "full" signifies perfect permanence.
Therefore, by using the day of the full moon during the second month, one symbolizes the dharma of the Middle Way’s perfect illumination.

Next, regarding the passage "at the time of approaching parinirvāṇa": when the time for the Dharma-mechanism approaches and the capacities of beings are ripe, there is no need to wait beyond the moment of arrival.

As the subsequent text states, "The various seers of Gandhamādana, the Mallas of Kuśinagara, Cunda, and Subhadra have their roots of goodness matured," he therefore proclaimed his nirvāṇa to enable them to enter the secret treasury.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Those who are to be saved by means of parinirvāṇa, he manifests parinirvāṇa to deliver them.
This is precisely that meaning.
3. Regarding the section beginning with "By means of the Buddha," concerning the root and the branches of sound: spiritual power is the root and the great voice is the branch.
From the root, the traces are manifested, yet all are made to realize that there is neither root nor branch.
Furthermore, it is said that "emptiness-wisdom is the foundation, the knowledge of all modes is the foundation, and the precious marks are the foundation," and so forth.

Fourth, regarding the phrase "its sound": as for the horizontal and vertical dimensions of this sound, "pervading everywhere" refers to the horizontal, while "reaching the Peak of Existence" refers to the vertical.
Another interpretation states:

"The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is merely the Brahma-world, namely the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; since it is formless and lacks a body, one should not hear sounds there, and thus it is not the Peak of Existence.
Some cite the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*), which says:

If the power of the formless meditative concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*) can transform and produce clouds of fragrant flowers and the like as offerings for the Buddha, why can it not transform and produce a body?
This too is a valid objection.
Now, three sets of horizontal and vertical dimensions are established:
first, horizontally encompassing the six realms of existence and vertically penetrating the three realms;
second, horizontally encompassing the four modes of birth and vertically penetrating the three vehicles.
The three horizontal [realms] encompass the ten realms, while vertically they penetrate as far as Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).

Thus, one should know that it is not only the *Nirmita* (Nirmita) heaven that constitutes the Summit of Existence (*bhavāgra*). If one takes the summit of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) to be the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), then the summit of the three realms of existence is the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); yet there is yet another summit, which is Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). Thus, two summits are summoned and one summit is invited.
Since this intention is so broad, how could it be compared to the Brahma-world?

Fifth, regarding the section beginning with "according to": as for the resonance of sound, the responses vary according to the different classes of beings, yet when the proclamation is universal, the response is non-dual.
To respond to manifold perceptions with a non-dual voice is indeed inconceivable.
Sixth, from "Today" onwards, the sound’s lamentation and proclamation are further divided into two parts:
first the lamentation, then the proclamation.
He praises [the Buddha] to inspire veneration and instructs [the disciples] to feel sorrowful longing.
The initial praise is twofold:
first, a double praise of the two virtues; second, a double conclusion regarding the two virtues.
First, the internal virtues are praised, followed by the external virtues.
Regarding the initial passage: although internal virtues are immeasurable, the fact that only three titles are praised is intended to clarify three specific matters.
First, by praising the Tathāgata as being truly equal to all Buddhas, one gives rise to reverence and esteem; thus he is the Father of the World.
As for the "One Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat), he is the supreme field of merit, capable of generating wholesome karma; thus he is the Lord of the World.
The One of Right and Universal Knowledge (*samyaksambuddha*) is able to shatter doubts and obstructions, giving rise to wisdom and understanding; thus, he is the Teacher of the World.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "From this day forward, we shall have no master, no kinsman, and no one to revere and look up to," and so forth.

Regarding the "external virtues" mentioned next: although external virtues are immeasurable, only the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) are cited here because it is intended to clarify that the original father, lord, and teacher possessed all four immeasurables at the time of his original vow; thus, to now benefit others, uproot their suffering, and bestow happiness is the essential purpose.
Compassion is great kindness; pity is great compassion; protection is great joy; and impartial regard is great equanimity.
Next, from "acts as" onwards, is the concluding praise.
It consists of two parts:
first, establishing the three refuges as a place of reliance; second, establishing the four immeasurables as a dwelling for the world.
Next, from the words "Greatly Awakened" (*mahābuddha*) onwards, he addresses [the assembly].
He addressed them with two responses: the first response was to cause them to sever their doubts, and the second response was to encourage them to pose further questions.
The Greatly Awakened One, possessing universal knowledge, is able to sever the former doubts; through his fourfold equanimity and compassion, he will surely listen to the subsequent questions.
When questioned later, he expounded the Way with thorough clarity, bestowing the gift of Nirvana;
when doubts were severed, the false was discarded and the true attained, so that the "New Yi" (the ultimate reality) was finally revealed.
His loud proclamation served as the introduction to the establishment of the teaching; this meaning is clear.
Previously, he fully extolled the three titles; now, he simply reports to the Great Awakened One (*Mahābuddha*).
The Great Awakened One is precisely the All-Knowing One (*Sarvajña*).
Since the Enlightened Master is both Lord and Father, there is no need for elaborate phrasing.
Furthermore, "Tathāgata" is the initial title, while "Greatly Awakened One" (Mahābuddha) is the subsequent title.
By praising the former and addressing the latter, each side is raised in turn; thus, their meaning is comprehensive.
If one follows the previous analysis, one should clarify the four meanings in each section; however, since the intended meaning is self-evident, it will not be stated again.
Next, from "At that time" onwards is the section on the summoning by light.
This text consists of four parts:
first, the timing of the light; second, the place from which it issues; third, the objects illuminated by the light; and fourth, the benefits of the light.

Regarding the first passage: At the time of dawn, when darkness and light intersect, the manifestation of the arising of wisdom and the extinction of the obscurity of delusion represent the power of *nirvāṇa*.
For this reason and for this purpose, [the Buddha] emits [light] at the break of day.
Next, regarding the "place of luminous light," this refers to the opening of the mouth.
Although the mouth itself is not of six colors, the six colors reside within it; this symbolizes that the Buddha-nature is not the six [sensory objects], yet is not separate from the six dharmas.
Furthermore, blue, yellow, red, and white are fixed colors, which signify acting according to one's own will.
Crystal and agate are indeterminate colors, which change according to the object they encounter; these signify acting according to the will of others.

Furthermore, the Great Nirvana Ocean is the dwelling place of sentient beings with vast bodies; the various tortoises and fish, as well as the various precious jewels of variegated radiance, are precisely intended to symbolize this.
Furthermore, because he saves those in the six realms of existence and purifies the six sense organs, he emits six colors.
Third, the section beginning with "The light shines everywhere here" clarifies that which is illuminated.
From the three thousandfold world system up to the ten directions constitutes horizontal illumination.
If one follows this analogy, there should be vertical illumination within the sounds; yet because it does not illuminate, the high and the broad manifest to one another.
Fourth, from "within which" onwards, is the benefit of light.
Others judge this section to belong to the new assembly.
Since these words already exist within that [text], why is it necessary to say "new"?
Furthermore, the "three karmas" and so forth can be understood from there.
The present text is divided into two parts:
First, the three obstacles are eliminated:

sentient beings in the six realms of existence constitute the obstacle of retribution; sinful defilements constitute the obstacle of karma; and the obstacle of afflictions is as explained in the text.
Next, from the passage beginning with "These various," the cultivation of wholesome states through the longing of the three types of action is easily seen in the text.

When hindrances are removed and goodness arises, one swiftly attains the vision of the Buddha; this refers to the invitation by means of light, which is the intended meaning of the sequence of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Third, from the passage "At that time, the great earth... onwards, there are movements of the land and movements of the water within the earthquake-invitation. Since water and land depend upon one another, they both move together; this symbolizes that ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving-views (*tṛṣṇā-dṛṣṭi*) mutually depend on each other. As one is about to overturn the delusion and craving that take existence as their object, the earthquake is used to represent this.

Furthermore, regarding what is called "trembling" (*zhen*): rising, surging, and shaking are its forms; trembling, roaring, and awakening are its sounds; extensively, these comprise the six movements and eighteen movements, and so forth.
However, as for sounds, lights, movements, and so forth—whether they appear before, after, or simultaneously—their perceptions vary; how can one dogmatically insist on a fixed order?
From the passage "At that time, all sentient beings... onwards, the text next clarifies those who are summoned.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, a general explanation of those summoned, referring to "all sentient beings at that time";
second, from "At that time there was... onwards, a specific explanation of those summoned, referring to their emergence according to their respective categories.
The general summary consists of four parts:
first, suppressing sorrow; second, making a request; third, explaining the request; and fourth, explaining sorrow.
Regarding the first section: having heard that the Master has passed away, how could one not be sorrowful?
To be submerged in the ocean of sorrow brings no benefit to oneself or others; therefore, it is said that one must exercise restraint.
Next, from "We should together" onwards, the request is made.
If one remains merely suppressing suffering, that too is of no benefit; thus, a request must be made, and so it is said: "One should go to the place where the Buddha is."

Regarding the kalpa of decrease (*apacaya-kalpa*): if one were to request a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), it would obstruct the appearance of future Buddhas; therefore, one requests only a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
From a human lifespan of eighty-four thousand years, gradually decreasing until it reaches ten years, constitutes one small kalpa.
Third, from "mutually grasping hands" onwards is the explanation of the request.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the initiation of the request; second, the formal explanation of the request; and third, the conclusion of the request.
As for the mention of "taking each other's hands," this is merely the beginning of their mutual expression of sorrow and lamentation.
Next, the following statement is made to correctly explain the intent of the request:
"Now, as for the Tathāgata, he comes because he rides upon the *tathatā* (suchness); thus, there is a Buddha in the world."
If the Tathāgata were to depart, the world would be without a Buddha;
therefore, saying that the world is empty is a desire to invite the Tathāgata as one's father.
The Buddha is the Worthy One (Arhat); the merit of making offerings to him is inexhaustible.
If there were no Arhat (one worthy of offerings), wholesome karma would be exhausted; thus it is said that the merit of sentient beings is spent, intending to invite the Master Worthy of Offerings.

The wisdom of universal knowledge wards off evil and reveals the good; if the One of Universal Knowledge departs, there will be no one to show the Way. Thus it is said that unwholesome states increase, intending to invite the Teacher of the Perfectly All-Knowing.
Since your intention is thus, you should go to the Buddha immediately and must not delay.
Third, the conclusion of the invitation:
"Go quickly! Go quickly!"
4. From "Furthermore, he spoke thus" onwards, suffering is explained.
Generally, when compassion covers the world, it uproots those who suffer and brings joy to those who are poor;
now, as both compassion has departed, they are simultaneously afflicted by poverty and suffering.
Chanting together that the void offers no rescue, no protection, and nothing to revere, this explains the suffering of having no master.
Being poor, destitute, and exposed, suddenly separated from the unsurpassed World-Honored One, this explains the suffering of having no kinsman.
"If there should be any doubt, whom else should one ask? [I] shall explain and dispel suffering without a teacher.
In this way, he successively explains and establishes the meaning of sorrow and suffering.
Next, from the passage "At that time, there were immeasurable... onwards, is the separate invitation.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the summoning of this land; second, the summoning of other lands.
This land is further divided into three sections:
First, the assembly of Jambudvīpa is summoned; second, the intermediate assembly is summoned; third, the assembly of the upper realms is summoned.
There are three types within the assembly of Jambudvīpa: namely, the śrāvakas, the bodhisattvas, and the mixed assembly.

The *Śāstra* clarifies that because the Bodhisattva’s practice abides in the Middle Way, he occupies the position between the eldest and the youngest sons; this should be understood in full according to the text of the *Fahua shu*, stating that there is both the literal meaning and the underlying intention, and so forth.
The preceding section is divided into two parts:
first, the ascending numerical sequence, and second, the descending numerical sequence.
Regarding the first part, which distinguishes between monastics and laypeople, the current meaning is as previously explained.
First, the śrāvakas are further divided into two:
first, monks (bhikṣu); second, nuns (bhikṣuṇī).
Monks are further divided into two:
First, the assembly surrounding the Buddha; second, the assembly of those who have come from without.
Question:
Why is it necessary to summon those surrounding the Buddha?
Answer: Although he was not summoned, he was startled into responding to the subsequent question.
Furthermore, because it occurred frequently, it may also be said that he was summoned.
The assembly surrounding the Buddha consists of three groups:
first, those who were summoned; second, those who attended the summons; and third, those who followed the summons.
Regarding the initial statement that there were "immeasurable" [beings], the number has already been established above.
Regarding the term "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*), it refers to those listed at the head above;
since this category extends to their followers as well, they are called immeasurable.
As for the "great disciples," they are like younger brothers or sons; though they occupy a position of honor between the two pillars, they are designated by a single title, and so forth.
Regarding the term "Venerable" (*āyuṣmat*): fellow practitioners of the holy life address one another with mutual respect as "Venerable.
As stated in the *Āgama*: "O Bhikṣus! From now on, those who are senior shall be addressed as 'Virtuous One' (*bhadanta*), and those who are junior shall be addressed as 'Elder' (*sthavira*)."
He was called "Elder" (*sthavira*) and so forth because his virtuous deeds were praised.
Kātyāyana is translated here as "Fan-Rope.
Bakula is translated as "Good Appearance."
Upāli (Upātta), translated here as "Great Joy" or alternatively "Repeated Joy.
He was of handsome appearance, and his parents named him Great Joy.
While at home he was a Wheel-Turning King, and having renounced the world, he became a Mara King.
The Māra King, knowing what was to come in the future, manifested eighteen transformations, saying, "If you are able to leave the household life, you shall surely attain such as this.
His parents granted him permission; he attained the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and was therefore named Joyful-Weight (Cunda).
"Next, 'encountering the Buddha’s light' refers to being summoned.
One should say that encountering sound, light, and earth tremors is a case of mentioning one while implying the other.
Third, from 'his body trembles' onwards, this refers to responding to the summons."
In the preceding passage, encountering light dispelled the three obstructions and gave rise to the three virtues;
now, as in the text, the obstructions are omitted and only the virtues are retained.
Question:
The Arhat has exhausted all sorrow and grief; why then has he suddenly reached such a state? Answer:
This is a residual habit, not an active affliction.
Furthermore, it demonstrates a model for others to emulate and aspire toward.
Moreover, these are specific delusions that have not yet been eliminated, rather than pervasive delusions.
Sorrow and grief constitute the Buddha-dharmadhātu, which encompasses all phenomena.

Regarding the subsequent passage, "Those with sorrow and those without sorrow are all within the realm of the Tathāgata," I shall not elaborate further on its analysis according to the four teachings.
Next, from the words "At that time, there were again eighty hundred thousand... onwards, the assembly from outside is summoned.
It consists of two parts:
the invocation and the response to the invocation.
The invocation has four elements: enumeration, classification, praise, and conclusion.
First, the enumeration is easy to understand.
Second, regarding "bhikṣu," it refers to a class of persons.
The explanation is as before.
All were Arhats who, upon departing, first praised the virtues of their own practice.
An Arhat is one at the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Being "mastery of mind" refers to one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), which is precisely the praise for the virtue of non-arising.
"Having done what was to be done" praises the quality of the Worthy One (*arhat*) who possesses the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

"Free from affliction and with faculties subdued"—since the faculties themselves are thieves, as the *Śāriputra-śikṣāpada-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) states, "These five faculties are thieves"—this praises the quality of being a slayer of thieves.
Next, the passage beginning with "Like a great dragon king" praises his virtue in transforming others.
Since it states that he possesses "great majestic power," it cannot refer to his own personal majesty; one knows that this refers to benefiting sentient beings and being looked up to by others.

Now, the elephant represents great strength on land, which is an analogy for wisdom (*prajñā*); the dragon represents great strength in water, which is an analogy for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Sometimes the elephant is simply called a "dragon-elephant" (*nāga-hastin*), such as the precious elephant Airāvaṇa belonging to Śakra, who walks through the void; in the blink of an eye, he traverses ten thousand *li*.

He transformed his body into thirty-two tusks; on each tusk were seven ponds, in each pond were seven lotus flowers, and upon each flower were seven jade maidens who played music that delighted the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
If one takes the dragon-elephant as a metaphor, it is even more consistent with converting others.
The sandalwood is likened to benefiting beings through precepts, while the lion is likened to benefiting beings through wisdom.
Being able to mold and perfect others through these two dharmas, one is in turn surrounded by a pure assembly.
4. From "Thus, immeasurable merit" onwards is the conclusion.
Since it speaks of "immeasurable," one knows that both self and others are being concluded.
As for "the true sons of the Buddha," their manifest traces appear as those of the Hīnayāna.
The "True Child" is fundamentally a true child of the Mahāyāna; by means of being a true child of the Mahāyāna, one binds together the clouds of merit for oneself and others, and so forth.
Next, the "Receiving the Summon.
This section has three parts:
First light, next sound, and finally movement.
First, "light-summons" (ābhāsa-āvartana).
Second, from "each at dawn" onwards, this constitutes "offering to the light-summons."
Morning is the beginning of clarity.
The use of the *yāṣṭi* (willow branch) represents practice;
its commencement signifies the movement of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) to manifest superior conduct (*viśeṣa-caryā*).
First, encountering the Buddha’s light;
next, from "they spoke to one another" onwards, responding to the light's summons.
Although there is no text regarding the removal of the three obstacles as in the preceding section, there is text concerning the virtues of the three karmas.

They said to one another: "This is goodness of verbal action (*vākkarman*); that the hairs of the entire body stand on end is goodness of bodily action (*kāyakarman*); and that great suffering and affliction arise is goodness of mental action (*manaskarman*).
*Pāṭala* is the name of a tree; its leaves are green, and its flowers have three colors: when the sun has not yet shone upon them, they are black;
when the sun shines upon them, they become red, and all the red veins become visible.
When the sun sets, it turns yellow.
This signifies that one has not yet received the summons: the three virtues do not arise, as if they were black;
having received the summons, one feels sorrow, as if they were red.
"There is no Buddha," as in "like yellow clouds," and so forth.
The phrase "desiring to benefit" excludes the intention of merely following [the teachings].

"Benefiting sentient beings" excludes that which is not for one's own practice. "Accomplishing the Great Vehicle" excludes the minor paths. "The foremost practice of emptiness" excludes that which is shallow or superficial.
This corresponds to the "True Sons of the Buddha" in the *Wen-hui* (Textual Assembly).
Next, from the passage "Manifesting the Tathāgata" onwards, is the "Receiving the Summoning by Sound.
This also has two parts:
First, he issued a great proclamation, commanding that this final question be asked.
Now, by accepting this summons, he reveals the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings of skillful means, opening up the eternal inquiry and giving rise to the ultimate final teaching.
Next, from "In order that [the Dharma] may not be interrupted" onwards, there is the invocation by means of following the Buddha's voice.
If one follows the Buddha’s vocal teachings, then the preaching of the Dharma will not be interrupted.
Third, from "For the sake of all sentient beings" onwards, there is the invocation by means of offering the earthquake.
There are also two types:
first, the "mountain-sea earthquake" which overturns the nature of false views—this is the invitation currently being offered.
Second, the "swift arrival at the Buddha's abode through the conditions of subduing"—this is the compliant invocation.
"The invoker and the invoked mutually comprehend one another; this is what is meant by 'wisdom knowing wisdom,' and so forth.
Second, the listing of the assembly of nuns is divided into two parts:
First, the assembly is enumerated; second, their origins are revealed.
The enumeration of the assembly is twofold, namely: those who pay homage and those who are summoned.
Regarding those summoned, there are four aspects: name, number, rank, and praise.
Among those listed in the equal ranks, three are preeminent:
Kuṭilā (the meaning of which has not yet been translated), Ni, and Yi-nü;
these are all general designations for women from the two regions [of India and China].
Regarding the distinctions: among laypeople, one who has received the five precepts and so forth is called an *aiyi* (aunt); among those who have left the household life, she is called a *ni* (nun).
However, within the Vinaya, they are also addressed as "A-ai" (Aunt) or "A-jie" (Sister), using these titles to express kinship based on the Dharma.
The [status of the] stages can be understood.
Within the section on praise, first, the praise of one's own practice is as described above.
Next, from the phrase "like a great dragon" onwards, the praise of the virtue of transforming others is also as described above.
Next, the phrase "also at the time of dawn" refers to complying with the three summons as explained above.
Next, the phrase "among the community of bhikṣuṇīs" marks the departure from that place.
This consists of two parts:
first, clarifying the traces of the initial bhikṣuṇīs, all of which are the fundamental basis of bodhisattvas;
first, pointing to their general stages, and second, specifically pointing to their high stages.
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s power of speech, its superior or inferior nature was not yet known; therefore, the text further explains that his original nature is lofty and his traces are vast.
When it first says "a dragon among men," if he were merely like a dragon among worldly people, this would not be particularly remarkable; rather, he is a dragon among sages and saints.
Regarding the statement that she occupies the successive stages of the ten bhūmis, this explains the loftiness of her fundamental nature.
Regarding her manifesting in a female body, this clarifies the extensiveness of her traces.
Why are her traces so extensive?
Because of the four immeasurable minds.
Why was he originally high?
Because he had attained mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"If he can still become a Buddha, why can he not manifest the forms of the nine realms?
and so forth. He divides this passage into two pairs:
first, the pair of the Original and the Traces; second, the pair of Cause and Effect.
"The cause and effect are difficult to perceive," and so forth.
Next, the assembly of Bodhisattvas is enumerated, which is also twofold, and so forth.
The six aspects of the invocation are: number, category, stage, name, praise, and conclusion.
First, "one *gaṅgānadī-vāluka*" refers to a numerical quantity.
There are four reasons why many sūtras use the Ganges as a standard of measure:
first, because most people are well-acquainted with it; [and so forth].
Second, those who enter [the water] obtain merit;
third, it is great among the eight rivers;
fourth, it is the birthplace of the Buddha, and because it is the native land of the Great Sage, it is used extensively.
This refers to the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*.
Next, regarding "bodhisattva-mahāsattva," it is a category.
This is translated as "the mind of the Way" (*daoxin*) or "the great mind of the Way" (*dàodàoxin*).

The *Śāstra* explains the ten meanings of a Bodhisattva: first, to exhaustively transform and teach all sentient beings; second, to exhaustively make offerings to all Buddhas; third, to exhaustively purify all Buddha-lands; fourth, to exhaustively uphold all Buddha-dharmas; fifth, to exhaustively ensure that the lineage of all Buddhas is never interrupted; sixth, to exhaustively discern all Buddha-lands; seventh, to exhaustively know the assemblies of all Buddha-disciples; eighth, to exhaustively discern the minds of all sentient beings; ninth, to exhaustively know how to sever the afflictions of all sentient beings; and tenth, to exhaustively know the faculties of all sentient beings.
With these ten gates as the primary ones, there are further immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* gates; for this reason, one is called a "bodhisattva.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha himself clarifies the meaning of "mahāsattva" through ten gates:
first, one should don the great armor amidst immeasurable births and deaths;...
Second, one should relinquish all that one possesses;
third, one should maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;
fourth, one should deliver all beings by means of the three vehicles.
Fifth, one should deliver all beings, and having delivered all, forget the merit of that deliverance;
sixth, one should understand that all dharmas are characterized by non-arising;
seventh, one should practice the six perfections solely with the mind of *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).
Eighth, one should study wisdom to thoroughly comprehend all phenomena;
ninth, one should thoroughly comprehend the single characteristic of all phenomena;
tenth, one should thoroughly comprehend infinite characteristics.
These ten gates are primary, and thus one is called a Mahāsattva.
Nāgārjuna explains these ten meanings as follows:

First, "Great Adornment" means that for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, measured not by days, months, or years, one benefits and delivers all sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death.
Second, relinquishing all possessions means that nothing—whether noble or base, internal or external—is spared or begrudged.

Third, having an impartial mind toward all sentient beings means treating with equal regard those one hates or loves, those for whom one feels deep affection or thinness of feeling, and those who are enemies or kin.
Fourth, regarding those delivered by the three vehicles: according to their respective capacities, they are all led to reach nirvana together.
Fifth, regarding the forgetting of merit: one does not grasp at self or other, nor does one perceive a deliverer or one who is delivered.
Sixth, regarding the knowledge of non-arising: all dharmas are non-arising.
Seventh, regarding the practice of the six perfections: with a pure and unadulterated mind, one practices the six perfections and dedicates them toward *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Eighth, "thoroughly comprehending all phenomena" means that one thoroughly comprehends all worldly activities.
Ninth, "the gate of the single characteristic" refers to ultimate emptiness; it is the characteristic of nirvāṇa, which is free from recollection, thought, and discrimination.
The ten immeasurable gates refer to the numerical progression of one, two, three, four, and so forth.
With these ten gates as the primary ones, there are further immeasurable dharma-gates; this is the meaning of "Mahāsattva."
Within this context, one should clarify the four types of bodhisattvas; as is frequently praised in the separate records, these concern the virtues of the perfected (pariniṣpanna) bodhisattva.
