Preface, Part II: "The Dragon Among Men" concludes; this clarifies the stages [of attainment].
The "dragon among men" emerges from the stage of skillful means.
Those whose rank is at the ten stages abide in the stage of reality.
To dwell peacefully and immovably is to be eternally quiescent at the primordial limit.
Regarding "manifesting through skillful means," this refers to transforming and benefiting those throughout the dharma-realm of all lower stages.
Fourth, from the phrase "Their names were" onwards, the names are listed;
although there are as many as the sands of the Ganges, only two individuals are named.

Regarding "Ocean of Wisdom" (Haide), it is as with the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, and also as with the eight inconceivables of the ocean of Great Nirvāṇa mentioned below; from this, the name "Ocean of Wisdom" is established, and so forth.

Regarding Akṣayamati, in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, this bodhisattva himself declares his own name and elucidates the meaning of "Inexhaustible Intention" through eighty kinds of dharma-gates, and so forth.
Five: From "Their minds are all... onwards is the praise of their virtues.
The text is divided into three parts:

first, a singular praise of the upward-seeking; second, an application of the Four Great Vows that encompasses the downward-transforming; third, a conclusion of both the upward-seeking and the downward-transforming.
Regarding the first passage on "reverence," this is explained from the perspective of principle; as the subsequent text states, "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he contemplated whom it was appropriate to revere."
"This is precisely the meaning of [the statement]: 'There is nothing superior to Prajñā; I shall revere it.
As for 'abiding securely,' this refers to realization; as the subsequent text states, 'All sentient beings and all Buddhas alike abide securely within the secret treasury'—this is its meaning."

"Profound understanding" refers here to the treatise on wisdom (*jñāna-śāstra*). As the subsequent text states: "It can give rise to the profound and vast wisdom of a bodhisattva; it is like a large box requiring a large lid, or a deep well requiring a long rope. This is precisely its meaning.

Regarding "delighting in [practice]," this refers to the actual conduct of practice; as the subsequent text states: "The eight characters of the Snowy Mountains were not considered difficult, and though he cut himself three *liang* daily, he never complained of suffering"—this is precisely its meaning.

Regarding "guardian" (*rakṣa*), this is discussed according to the teachings; it refers, for instance, to the meaning found in the passages below concerning Xianyu’s execution of punishment and Juede’s destruction of the enemy ranks.
When the great aspiration of the bodhisattvas to seek the supreme [enlightenment] reaches such magnitude as the ocean, five meanings are briefly cited to demonstrate its characteristics.
Next, from the phrase "skillfully conforming" onwards, the virtues of downward transformation are praised.
First, there is a general praise of the Four Great Vows; next, they are praised individually.

The Bodhisattva has already ascended the Ten Stages and dwells therein immovably; rather than realizing nirvana, he enters into birth-and-death. Recalling his original vows, he conforms to the world, giving rise to two of the Great Vows through conformity with great compassion, and giving rise to two of the Great Vows through conformity with great kindness—this is the meaning of the general praise.
Next, from the passage "making this vow" onwards, there is a separate eulogy.
The phrase "to deliver those not yet delivered" is a separate eulogy of the initial vow.
Because he maintained the precepts in the past, and because the precepts are the antidote to the defilement of transgression—by means of this antidote, one is liberated from the bonds of defilement.
Regarding the phrase "explaining the unexplained," this is a specific praise of the second vow.
Regarding "continuing the lineage of the Three Jewels," this is a specific praise of the third vow, as the dharma-gate is immeasurable.

If one says that carving sandalwood, casting precious metal, copying the *sūtras*, shaving the head, and dyeing the robes merely constitutes the non-interruption of the Three Jewels through their outward manifestations in ritual matters;

If one gives rise to the bodhicitta, it is called the Buddha Jewel; if one realizes the Great Way through its essence, it is called the Dharma Jewel; if phenomena and principle are harmoniously integrated, it is called the Sangha Jewel. This is precisely the uninterrupted continuity of the Three Jewels of Principle-Nature.
The *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā* states: "Wherever this scripture is located, there is the Buddha and his honored disciples.
The subsequent passage says: "If one knows it to be eternally abiding, one should know that this household is as if it possessed the Buddha."
Inferring from this, the non-interruption of the Three Jewels is itself an immeasurable dharma-gate.
The phrase "in future ages" refers to the vow to achieve the unsurpassed path of the Buddha; this separately extols the fourth vow.

Third, the phrase "by means of great adornment" serves as a summary of the Four Great Vows; it also simultaneously summarizes both the upward seeking [of enlightenment] and the downward transformation [of sentient beings], which is why it is called "great adornment."

If one makes the fourth vow separately, it means that in the future, when becoming a Buddha, one will have a body adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, and a mind adorned with the ten powers and fearlessnesses; this is called "Great Adornment."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Large Version) frequently employs the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) as adornments; the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Small Version) takes non-adornment as its adornment; and the subsequent text identifies the merit of the six perfections and the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as the two types of adornment.
Below "The Six Accomplishments," there is the conclusion.
This further consists of two parts:
first, the general; second, the specific.
The first part summarizes the seeking of enlightenment above and the transforming of sentient beings below through merit and wisdom.
Next, from the passage "viewing all sentient beings as equal to an only son" onwards, is the specific summary of the four great vows for the transformation of sentient beings below.
Next, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, at dawn" refers to being summoned by the light of offering (*pūjā-prabhā*).
Next, the passage beginning with "The hair on his entire body stood on end" refers to being summoned by the light of compliance (*anuloma-prabhā*).

Maintaining the body and mind, one briefly [mentions] the excellence of speech, the three obstacles, and so forth; this reveals the invocation through the sound of "departing" and "reverently following.
The section beginning with "for the sake of all sentient beings" indicates the invocation through the movement of the earth in reverent accordance; the explanation is as stated above, and so on.
III. From "Two Ganges-sands" onwards, the miscellaneous assemblies are enumerated. This is divided into three parts:
first, twenty-one assemblies with increasing numbers; second, eight assemblies with identical numbers; third, one assembly with no fixed number.
The first two [sections] concern the Ganges; the text states "threefold," and so forth.
Within the initial "summoning" (of the assembly), there are likewise enumeration, categories, names, praises, and conclusions.
The first two are constant enumerations; because they are not known by the world, they are measured by means of the "Ganges."
"Upāsaka" (lay follower) is the next category below [the monastics].

The *Śāriputrābhidharma* calls them "men and women free from desire"; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* calls them "pure-faith men and women"; the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* calls them "meritorious men and women," or alternatively, "virtuous men and women."
Although there are many types, they are collectively termed the two groups of householders.
To speak of them specifically: though their outward form remains that of laypeople, they have never married and constantly follow the Tathāgata.
Regarding "for the two assemblies," these are the two assemblies that have departed from desire.
If one has previously married but now observes the five precepts and permanently severs worldly ways, they are of service to the Buddha-dharma and are called an *upāsaka* (lay practitioner).
If one does not violate worldly laws while observing the five precepts and further the eightfold fast, they are called a "virtuous male or female lay follower" (śrāddha upāsaka/upāsikā).
Furthermore, those who merely take the three refuges are called "unclassified lay followers" (anupāsaka).
If one or two [precepts] are observed, it is called "partial"; if three or four, it is called "majority"; if all five are fully maintained, it is called "complete.
The Sūtra states that "endowment" (samanvāgata) refers precisely to the "complete" category.
Furthermore, if one fully upholds the five precepts yet seeks only the realms of humans and devas, one has no share [in the higher path];
if, in addition, one fears birth and death and aspires to seek nirvana, this is a small share;
if one does so for the sake of sentient beings, it is a great share.
If one knows that the precepts are the Dharma-realm, encompassing all phenomena solely for the sake of the Buddha-way, this is the fulfillment.

One who is "fully endowed with dignified deportment" possesses such deportment as to be constantly accompanied by ritual propriety, constantly accompanied by the precepts, constantly accompanied by impermanence, constantly accompanied by compassion, and constantly accompanied by the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Constantly abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they are able to manifest various forms throughout the ten realms; whether lifting or lowering their feet, they are always endowed with the Buddha-dharma. Even in brothels or taverns, there is nothing that is not the Right Path. Abiding in the Buddha’s deportment is what is called being "fully endowed."

One should know that the five precepts and the codes of dignified conduct have both a fundamental basis and manifest traces; to remain unmoved within the fundamental basis while universally manifesting all traces is called being fully endowed with the precepts and dignified conduct.
Question:
If the meaning of an upāsaka is as such, what then are the meanings of śrāvaka, bodhisattva, and buddha? Answer:
The principle is necessarily so, yet it has not been seen in the formal teachings; thus, those who are deluded do not believe it. Let me now attempt to explain:

the four roots of goodness constitute the "undivided" stage; the first fruit of the śrāvaka constitutes the "small portion"; the second and third fruits constitute the "large portion"; and the stage of no-more-learning constitutes the "complete portion."

Furthermore, regarding these four parts: if, within the Mahāyāna, both are without parts, it is the "small part"; if one has severed the dust-like afflictions (*rajas*), it is the "partial part"; if one has severed one or two grades of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is the "majority part"; and if one has exhausted all ignorance, it is the "complete part."
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "We of today are truly śrāvakas. Because they cause all to hear the sound of the Buddha-way, they are for the most part śrāvakas.

If the stage of dry wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*) constitutes the "undivided" bodhisattva, then from the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*) up to the sixth stage, where the severance of afflictions is equal to that of an arhat, it is "partially divided"; on the seventh stage, the cultivation of the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*) is "mostly divided"; and on the eighth stage, where the path and contemplation flow together, it is "fully divided."
Furthermore, the thirty minds are without portion; the first and second stages are of small portion; from the third to the ninth stages are of great portion; and the tenth stage is of full portion.

Furthermore, the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) are the stage of no-part; the ten abidings (*vihāra*) are the stage of a small part; the ten practices (*caryā*) and ten directions (*abhimukha*) are the stage of a large part; and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*) are the stage of fullness.

Moreover, according to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), the ten grounds and the distinct thirty minds are the stage of no-part; the distinct ten grounds and the Perfect ten abidings are the stage of a small part; the Perfect ten practices and ten directions are the stage of a large part; and the Perfect ten grounds are the stage of fullness.

All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; yet, when this nature lacks manifest function, they are Buddhas without partiality. At the first dwelling and the first stage, one can act as a Buddha within a hundred realms, and is thus a Buddha with limited partiality. From the second dwelling and the second stage upward, one is a Buddha with greater partiality. Perfect Enlightenment is the Buddha of full partiality.
For this reason, every single dharma-gate possesses both the provisional and the real, as well as the original and the manifested; this is precisely that meaning.
Question:
As for the terms "earthworm" (*kēyí*) and "viper" (*fùchài*), what is their significance?

Answer: Generally, a single wholesome dharma consists of four degrees; by analogy, a single unwholesome dharma should likewise be so. I have not yet seen any scriptural teaching that omits this and fails to discuss it.

To speak in terms of provisional designations: the deeds performed by a small bodhisattva constitute the "no-part" (amśa); those performed by one at the initial stage and initial dwelling of the *vṛścika* (venomous serpent) stage constitute the "small-part" (*alpa-aṃśa*); those performed up to the tenth stage and tenth dwelling constitute the "great-part" (*bahu-aṃśa*); and the deeds performed by a Tathāgata constitute the "fulfilled-part" (*paripūrṇa-aṃśa*).
Therefore, there are assemblies of both provisional and ultimate [beings]; because the ultimate summons the provisional, it is called "summoning and inviting" (*zhàoqǐng*).
Regarding the section beginning with "Their names were," thirdly, as for the listing of names, only two individuals are listed.
The King Vimalakīrti was likely the very person who, as the Vimalakīrti of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, rebuked eight thousand bodhisattvas and censured five hundred bhikṣus;
and the one named Śubhavyūha was likely the very person who provided the facilities for the assembly at his father’s house.
These are the foremost leaders among the two Ganges [of bodhisattvas].
From "Deeply delighting in contemplation" onwards is the fourth section, praising their virtues;
it first praises them and subsequently provides a summary.
This praises both the superior seeking above and the transformation of those below; from the "thirteen antidotes" onwards, it is the praise of the superior seeking.
The old commentary states:
taking suffering as medicine to treat the disease of pleasure, the same applies to [the contemplations on] permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Now it is clarified that this is merely the initial teaching and does not represent the intended meaning of the present sutra.
Furthermore, the ancients have said:

"These various counteractive measures constitute the contemplation of the six aspects. They cite the following passage: "That which is impermanent is birth-and-death; that which is permanent is Great Nirvana."
"Non-self" refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; "self" refers to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
"Suffering" refers to all non-Buddhists; "bliss" refers to Great Nirvāṇa.
"Impurity" refers to all conditioned phenomena; "purity" refers to the true Dharma possessed by Buddhas and bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, these six modes of contemplation were not previously explained; they are only discussed in the second fascicle, where, within the parable of the birds, the simultaneous flight is first clarified. One should not use this to praise the virtues of the upāsaka; rather, this is the compiler of the sutra taking the general meaning from later in the text and applying it here as a praise.
Xinghuang said:

"When the bhikṣus first arrived, none of them were yet arhats; the author of the sūtra took their later realization of the stage of no-more-learning and projected it back to praise them at the outset."
The bhikṣus are not so; how could the lay assembly be like that?
You should know that the Buddha’s fellow practitioners have long mastered this contemplation, which is why he praised it.
Furthermore, [the text] discriminates:
First, the mutual correspondence between medicine and illness constitutes a remedy; however, how could the simultaneous movement of the six practices constitute a remedy?
The explanation says:
when medicine and illness correspond, the illness departs while the medicine remains; this is a partial remedy.

When the six practices are cultivated as pairs, moving back and forth, each serving alternately as medicine and as disease, so that when the disease is gone the medicine perishes—this is perfect counteraction (*paripūrṇa-pratipakṣa*).

If this is so, then for those who have long practiced alongside the Buddha and are thoroughly proficient in the six contemplations, their praise would not be subject to doubt; but what then of other practitioners of reality?

The provisional may also lead to the ultimate, as the following passage states: "Those who receive the preceding teaching use the medicine of impermanence to counteract the disease of permanence; yet, although the disease of permanence has been removed, they again cling to impermanence."

"Hearing that the medicine of permanence cures the disease of impermanence is precisely what is employed in the present teaching; the subsequent passage on the three cultivations using the superior to overcome the inferior is of this very same meaning."

Second, those who from the outset do not receive the prior teaching but practice the Great Nirvana through its successive stages—first practicing impermanence to remedy permanence, then practicing permanence to remedy impermanence, thereby destroying the twenty-five states of existence and attaining the twenty-five samādhis, abiding in Great Nirvana—this is called the ocean of Great Nirvana gradually deepening.
This already fully possesses two kinds of antidotes; why then do you infer that one is taught by the former teaching and the other by the latter teaching?

Thirdly, there is furthermore a single practice which is the practice of the Tathāgata, fully endowed with permanence, impermanence, both permanence and impermanence, and neither permanence nor impermanence.

By practicing the six contemplations in a circular manner, one simultaneously remedies both permanence and impermanence; as these alternate as medicine and disease until the disease is eliminated and the medicine perishes, both the remedy and the affliction are abandoned. This is why it is called the "Gate of Counteractive Treatment" (*pratipakṣa-mukha*).
If one discusses practicing all modes of conduct through a single mode, it is as explained in the "Noble Conduct" (Ārya-caryā);
if one discusses practicing both simultaneously, it is as described in the "Bird Simile.

The lay followers (upāsakas) are endowed with these virtues; while the former two are still shallow, the latter one is profound. As the text states, "They deeply delight in contemplating the various gates of counteractive measures," this praises the meaning of the third [mode].
The fifty-two classes of beings differ in their faculties and natures, yet they do not exceed three types; those who employ skillful means lead them toward Nirvana through the same reality.
When even a single type cannot be found upon entering Nirvana, how much less could there be three?
This is the meaning of the gate of true antidotes, and it also reveals the intent of the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings on skillful means.
Within this text, there is a formal praise of how the provisional leads toward the ultimate; for if there were no practice of the ultimate, what would the provisional lead toward?
If there were no provisional [teachings], there would truly be nothing to rely upon.
Since you praise the provisional, you must also praise the ultimate; how then can you judge them as belonging to earlier and later teachings?

If one were to analyze this phrase by phrase, one should say that adhering to the conventional is suffering while sinking into the ultimate is bliss; sinking into the ultimate is suffering while making distinctions is bliss. The same applies to permanence, self, purity, and so forth.

Furthermore, to sink into emptiness is suffering while Great Nirvana is bliss; to sink into emptiness is bliss while Great Nirvana is suffering; and even so it is for the superior and the non-superior.
Question:

That which does not arise from causes and conditions is eternal; that which remains unchanged from beginning to end is constant.

3. Below "Virtue of Longevity" (*āyus-guṇa*), the names of three persons are listed.

First, the superior seeking.
The text consists of two parts:

The contemplation of phenomena is divided into two sections:
First, the objective realm is indicated; next, the five gates are set forth.
Regarding the first, the reproach of the "household dharma" (kula-dharma), this refers to the object of contemplation.

If one takes merely the ritual of the mat and broom—that is, the duties of a wife—as the household dharma, it is too narrow; if one takes the cycle of rebirth within the three realms as the household dharma, it is too expansive.
Now, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are taken as the household dharma.

Their retribution is constricted and confined within a cage and a pen; they are what the ignorant and foolish cherish and nurture, but what the sages and worthies despise and reject. Therefore, they are termed "reproach."

Next, following the section "Observing One's Own Body," the first part concerns the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkha-vipaśyanā*): the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) harm one another, various parasites further gnaw at them, and as the elements mutually devour each other, the body becomes a thicket of suffering.
"This body is foul and filthy" refers to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), which consists of the five kinds of impurity.
"Bound by craving" means that it is covered by a thin skin and thus called "pure"; because one is entangled in attachment without end, it is called the "bond of desire."
That which dies and perishes is ultimately impure.
That from which the nine orifices flow is impure by its own nature.
"Departing like a city" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

This body is a provisional construction based on conditions such as tiles, wood, earth, and stone; within it dwell the evil spirits of the three poisons. Because it deceives others externally and is full of guile internally, it is called "empty.
To realize that this body is not solid is the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).
"This body is impermanent" refers to the contemplation of impermanence.
The two contemplations, coarse and subtle, are as explained in the text.
Next, from the passage beginning "Would one rather [use] a cow's footprint," the text concludes by summarizing its merits.
Combining these matters with their respective contemplations results in seven points:
first, citing an analogy to conclude the contemplation on these matters, observing that the faults and afflictions of this body are exceedingly vast;
second, citing the three samādhis to conclude the contemplation on the profound and subtle nature of this principle.

Regarding causes and conditions, they are observed as phenomena; that is to say, because one seeks and examines them internally and externally and finds them unobtainable, they are empty. Being empty, they lack the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) and likewise lack the characteristic of emptiness itself. Because they are without characteristics (*animitta*), they are therefore without volitional action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

The *Śāstra* states: "The two vehicles contemplate the three samādhis by taking the Truth (tattva) as their object; the bodhisattvas contemplate the three samādhis by taking the true mark (lakṣaṇa) as their object," and so forth.
Third, this citation from the Mahāyāna concludes the discussion on the objects and contemplations, bringing it into accord with the *Sūtras*.

4. Fourth, by citing the "ability to preach," he concludes the contemplation on the superior seeking [of enlightenment] without losing the task of transforming those below; this is the method for instructing others. 5.

Sixth, "Censuring" and below raise the specific instances of such reproach and disparagement; these are the fundamental matters of the Bodhisattva, which, when examined, are seen to be the result of his vow-power.
Seventh, the conclusion: this contemplation of the matter itself is right contemplation, capable of destroying birth and death.

This can be seen in the text, as stated at length. This meaning constitutes entirely the gates of remediation within the Chapter on Upāsakas: because the male nature is upright and firm, it discusses only remediation; because the female nature is characterized by attachment, all five gates are provided. These five gates equally take the object-condition as their focus upon the true reality (*dharmatā*); thus, principle is present within the phenomenon, which is the sublime remediation.
In the chapter on Bodhisattvas, this refers to one who deeply delights in the Mahāyāna and protects the Mahāyāna, which is the same as the aforementioned [category].
Although manifesting in a female body, she is in reality a Bodhisattva; this corresponds to the aforementioned "abiding securely in the Mahāyāna."
Next, from "skillfully conforming" onwards, he praises his virtue in transforming those below, as explained above, and so forth.

The explanation is as stated above, etc.

*Vaiśālī* is translated as "Good Road"; Master Zao translated it as "Extensive and Majestic" (*Guǎngyán*); Master Shi translated it as "Extensive and Broad" (*Guǎngbó*). All of these names derive from the fact that the streets and lanes of the country were magnificent and orderly.
Licchavi is also rendered as Li-chang (黎昌) or Mi-li (彌離); these are different dialects of the Chu and Xia regions.

Regarding "the former ones," this refers to the thirty-four assemblies previously mentioned.
As for the two assemblies singled out, there are both circumstantial and explicit reasons.
The circumstantial reason is that when Kāśyapa entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), he did not come because he was sustained by that absorption.
Ānanda did not come because he was ensnared by Māra.
As for that which was revealed: it was revealed so that Kāśyapa would not abandon the minor precepts.
Since Kāśyapa is the eldest son and is currently upholding the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha, as he approached his parinirvāṇa, should have pardoned the minor precepts; thus he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"After my parinirvāṇa, it is well for those who can uphold the subtle precepts; those who cannot may let them go.
Later, Kāśyapa asked:
"What are these subtle precepts?"
Ānanda replied, “I do not know.
He then rebuked Ānanda, saying:
"You have personally received the Buddha's instructions; now that you say you do not know whether they may be abandoned or not, you are further being ridiculed by the non-Buddhists:
'The precepts established by his teacher were all abandoned after his passing.'"
Furthermore, it could not be abandoned.
If Kāśyapa were to come, how could he possibly uphold this matter correctly?
Ānanda acted thus to manifest the final Buddha’s praise and entrustment, as well as the power of the divine mantra.
If Ānanda were to come, he would neither inquire after him nor offer praise, nor would he have Mañjuśrī hold the mantra to untie the snare.
That the two assemblies did not come was intended to manifest this meaning.
Question:

What was the reason for this opposition between teacher and disciple?
Answer: Not so.

thus, there was no act of defiance or rejection.

Although the text does not explicitly mention the three continents or the ten billion sets of four continents, by logical inference they must exist.

If beings from the ten directions still come, for what reason do those from the ten billion sets of four heavens not come?
If one infers from the intermediate statement, they should be the most numerous; this can only be known through the mind and cannot be recorded in writing, and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "and the various mountain deities," others claim that the mountain deities take the form of mountains; however, this is not necessarily so.

Just as tree deities manifest half their bodies without taking the form of trees, mountain deities do not necessarily take the form of mountains; they simply have their divine way associated with the mountains.

These trees, once flourishing and lush, suddenly turned white, resembling white cranes.
In the grove there is a crane; when the grove undergoes transformation, it is no different from the crane.
This has a symbolic significance: if its flourishing were fixed as flourishing, it should not suddenly change; if its withering were fixed as withering, it should not be like the crane.
Since withering is like that of a crane, withering is not truly withering; since flourishing suddenly changes, flourishing is not truly flourishing.
That which is neither flourishing nor withering—the nirvana between them—manifests arising and ceasing while signifying neither arising nor ceasing.

At the twin śāla trees, a single transformation was understood differently by each according to their capacity: those of superior faculties reached its fundamental essence, while those of inferior faculties grieved over its traces;

those of middling faculties dwelled between grief and realization. As the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness" states: "Those of the lowest ignorance and commoners see it as necessarily entering nirvana; only the bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī can know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and immutable."
This is precisely that meaning.

Next, the fact that the pavilions and halls in the void are exquisitely adorned and clearly defined represents the physical marks of the Buddha’s body, which are the most supreme in all the heavens above and the heavens below.
Now that the conditions for this present body have ceased, the unsurpassed wisdom no longer dwells within it to govern; this is what those of inferior capacity lament.

Furthermore, the hall’s foundation and framework remain while its current occupant is absent; thus, there is a hall within the void, where the carvings, engravings, and exquisite decorations are clearly manifest.
Immovable and unfalling, it is wondrously adorned and magnificent; it manifests as the treasury within space, complete and without deficiency—this is what the person of middling capacity prizes.
Furthermore, that there is this flowered hall, solemn and orderly, radiant, pleasing, and beneficial, is its very existence.
That which is high up in the void and not utilized by anyone is its "non-existence.
If there is existence, once the task is finished, one should withdraw this empty existence back into that which is neither empty nor existent; this is what the superior person (upāsaka) realizes.
The lower class possesses compassion but lacks penetration; the middle class possesses both compassion and penetration—this lies between the "junior" and "senior" ranks.

Third, the presence of many flowing springs and bathing pools beneath the hall symbolizes that the Buddha’s body and speech descend to reach those below, flowing forth immeasurable teachings just like a bathing pool.
The bathing pool has two functions:
first, it can wash away defilements; second, it removes feverish distress.
This symbolizes how the Buddha's teaching can cause adventitious dust to be exhausted externally and ignorance to be eliminated internally.
The presence of exquisite lotus flowers symbolizes adherence to the Buddha’s teachings, which constitutes the cultivation of causes.
Since the fruit transcends the world of causes, both locations are cited as metaphors.
As the conditions for transformation are nearing their end, it is like a hall rising high into the air.
The flow of the verbal teachings moistens all like a clear spring in a pond.
Regarding its fundamental essence, it neither departs nor remains; yet, speaking in terms of its benefits, one speaks of departure and remaining.
As the text says, "All behold the marks of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa," this is, for the time being, what those of inferior capacity perceive.
If one were to provide a complete exposition, there should be superior [compassion] directed toward those below, as fully explained previously.
Although these three characteristics differ in their sequence, their meaning remains the same as before.
Previously, by exhorting you with a great voice to inquire, the secret teachings were revealed;

now, like clear springs flowing from beneath this hall to benefit many, the gate before you emits five-colored light that shines everywhere, removing the three obstructions, giving rise to the three virtues, and causing your practice to advance.

Within the first pair, the first section—where that Buddha speaks of this Buddha—is divided into four parts:

first, terror; second, consolation; third, seeing that assembly; and fourth, crying out "Alas, suffering!

Hearing that Buddha say this Buddha should enter parinirvāṇa was the omen of the preceding voice;
feeling the earth tremble and quiver was the omen of the preceding earthquake.
Seeing it as the radiance of a mirror, it was still the auspicious omen of the previous light.

Question:

Now, regarding the discussion of reality, the intent does not lie in expedient means.
Furthermore, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are superior and inferior grades; that which is performed by a superior grade is not known by an inferior grade.

As for what is accomplished through the power of a Buddha, if the Buddha lends his supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*), even insects can know it; if he does not lend his supernatural power, they cannot know it.
This Anantagātra, having received the Buddha’s spiritual power, manifested this auspicious sign; why then should Śūra be terrified or harbor further doubts?
This is the second pair.
First, from the great assembly, they saw each and every pore of Anantagātra, illustrating that this bodhisattva manifests the inconceivable—seeing by not seeing.
To perceive a single hair-path is to see the small; to perceive the magnificent splendor of seventy-eight thousand cities contained therein is to see the large.
Yet the dimensions of that body are equal to space; since space itself is neither large nor small, how can it be fully described?
Furthermore, it did not prevent them from coming from there.
The large and the small were mutually contained; the pores were not widened, nor was the city diminished.

Again, one heard the sounds of joy and the enjoyment of pleasure; again, one heard the cries of "Alas, what suffering! and again, one heard voices exclusively preaching the Mahāyāna. Thus, neither suffering nor pleasure existed, and they did not obstruct one another.
The reason the Bodhisattva manifests this matter is to signify that the present Buddha’s entry into parinirvāṇa is likewise inconceivable.
Next, from that time, the Bodhisattva Boundless Body (*Anantagātra*) and immeasurable Bodhisattvas appeared; those Bodhisattvas came by means of an inconceivable non-coming.
Next, regarding the third pair: first, making offerings to the Buddha; second, not receiving [offerings], as stated in the text.

Question:
Since the body is already boundless, both this land and other lands are contained within a single hair-tip; why then would it suddenly come here from there?
This would mean coming from that side to this side. While the great assembly here sees it coming from that [other] side, it is precisely from this side that they see that [other] side.
The old [commentary] states:
"Because it is partially infinite, there is coming and going. This should not be so.
Since it is said that its measure is equal to empty space, how could empty space have either a small portion or a large portion?
If one speaks of a "small portion," then it would not be the same as space.
Now, we clarify that the inconceivable form of the Bodhisattva is such that the finite is the infinite, the infinite is the finite, and it is neither finite nor infinite.
The limit is itself the limitless; their measure is equal to empty space.
The limitless is itself the limit: from that "other" comes this "self," and by seeing this, one perceives that which comes from there.
Although it is both the limit and the limitless, neither the limit nor the limitless, yet it can manifest as both the limit and the limitless; therefore, it is called inconceivable.
If there were fixedness, it would not be inconceivable.
For example, in the case of the sixteen-foot [Buddha], Brahmā could not see the crown of his head; it is neither seen nor unseen, yet capable of being both seen and unseen.
It is like when one carries a mirror with them: the body is within the mirror; it is not "within" yet is "within," and though not "within," it is "within.
It is also like the sun that does not descend into the pond, nor does the water rise up, yet its reflection appears in the water.
Since even the stubborn and obstructed aspects of form are still difficult to conceive, how much more so the inconceivable—how could it ever be grasped through ordinary sentiment?
From "The Pair of Śāla Trees" onwards begins the third major section: the conclusion and invocation.
The middle section has two parts:
first, the conclusion of the assembly’s gathering; second, the conclusion of the auspicious signs.
Since the auspicious signs originally served to gather the assembly, once the assembly has gathered, the signs also reach their conclusion; therefore, both must be concluded.
The initial gathering of the assembly is further divided into two parts:
first, clarifying that the location is inconceivable; second, clarifying that the persons are inconceivable. Regarding the first section:

within an area of thirty-two *yojanas*, it can accommodate a multitude of fifty-two thousand people; long banners and great parasols do not obstruct one another, and the ritual implements suffer no damage.

Furthermore, it is already inconceivable that the tip of a needle or a single mote of dust can contain boundless bodies; how much more so when they receive bodhisattvas with boundless bodies from the four directions and the ten directions?
Moreover, how many retinues and offerings there are, such that no one encounters obstruction and none suffer injury!
This is the inconceivable locus.
Next, the people are divided into four groups;
first, from "the ten directions" onwards, the assembly from other quarters is concluded.
Those gathered on the tip of a needle and those from Jambudvīpa— this assembly of beings in this land gathered beneath the twin trees—
is inconceivable for humans. Second,
there is the distinction between those who should have gathered but did not, and those who should not have gathered but did.

Those who should be assembled are the three assemblies of Kāśyapa and his followers; those who should not be assembled are the three assemblies of venomous insects, wicked people, and malevolent spirits.
This clarifies that both assembling and not assembling are inconceivable.
Third, the elucidation of the benefits of the assembly’s gathering.
This refers to generating a mind of compassion toward both those who have gathered and those who have not, and purifying both the places where they have gathered and those where they have not.
The Rāṇava deity represents those who have gathered; the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm represent those who have not gathered.
Furthermore, one must distinguish and exclude both the compassionate and the non-compassionate.
The "non-compassionate" refers to the icchantikas, who do not give rise to a mind of compassion.
Both the compassionate and the non-compassionate are inconceivable.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, by the power of the Buddha, the three-thousandfold world system... onwards, the location is further elucidated.

The three-thousandfold world system is the place where the assembly gathers; the worlds of the ten directions are places where they do not gather. Since all are equally adorned and purified like the Land of Ultimate Bliss, it is said that "the ten directions are likewise so."
Because the assembly has gathered, this benefit has been brought about.

Even the state of not gathering in a place, the non-assembly of a multitude, and the non-arising of the resolve for enlightenment are already inconceivable; how much more so, then, can the Tathāgata’s manifestation of birth and manifestation of extinction be conceived?
This concludes the assembly of the congregation.

From the preceding section up to this point, there are nine auspicious signs in total, which together form three thematic meanings; however, they are all subsumed under a single summary.
The reason for this is that sound, light, and wind all issue from the mouth.
If one draws the light back into the mouth, the same applies to wind and sound; by withdrawing the sound, the teaching of cessation is realized.

When the wind-energy was withdrawn, his spiritual transformations ceased, and there was no way for his inverted states to be overturned; this signified that he had truly departed.

The great assembly saw him resolve one thing and understand three others, and seeing the sound of his withdrawal enter his mouth, they knew he would surely lose his teacher; therefore, they wailed and wept.
He cried out, "I shall no longer receive the offerings of devas and humans; this weeping is for the loss of my refuge, lamenting that there will be no food of the Dharma.

Seeing the collected light enter his mouth, he knew the Master would surely pass away; therefore, he wailed, "The sun of noble wisdom has now forever set; who will remove the three obstructions, and who will give rise to the three virtues?"

Seeing that the wind of death had entered his mouth and knowing he would surely lose his kinsman, he wept and said: "The Dharma-ship has sunk; who will now shatter ignorance to ferry us from this shore to the other shore of Nirvana?"
There are three kinds of weeping: weeping for one's lord, for one's kin, and for one's teacher.

"Alas! is the anguish of the mind; wailing and crying out is the sorrow of the mouth; trembling and convulsing is the suffering of the body. Thus, the compassionate attachment of the three karmas reaches this state.

Chapter on Cunda (3–5). Part One: Chapter on Cunda (Upper). The commentary on this chapter is divided into three sections:
first, distinguishing between the exoteric and esoteric; second, distinguishing between conduct and virtue; third, explaining the title.

The initial interpretation relies on the Indian text, which still belongs to the "Chapter on Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) as it opens up and refutes the meanings of the eternal and the non-eternal regarding the present and the past; thus, it is dense in meaning but loose in its textual arrangement.
Xie’s version follows the person and the event, titling it the "Pureḍa Chapter" (*Cūḍā-paṭala*); thus, it is dense in its textual arrangement but loose in meaning.

Now, regarding the chapter on the gift of *nirvāṇa*, it is clear that there is no loss of meaning in either the Sanskrit or Chinese texts; according to the former [Sanskrit] version, it is "the gift of constant life," while according to the subsequent [Chinese] version, it is "the gift of constant cultivation," and so forth.
Regarding the next point on virtuous conduct: Cunda is included among the two groups of *asaṃkhyeya* beings; for what reason is he established as a separate chapter?
Briefly, ten differences are clarified:
first, while the assembly first made offerings and subsequently requested [the teaching], Cunda first requested and subsequently made offerings.
1) On two occasions the assembly requested the Buddha three times, yet he remained silent; on the single request of Cunda, the Tathāgata immediately accepted.
2) Because of the third [request], he accepted the great assembly.
3) Because of the food, he revealed the eternal.
Fifth, he requested to remain of his own accord;
sixth, he conveyed the request of the assembly;
seventh, he praised him with his golden mouth.
1. The eight great assemblies offer praise;
2. The ninefold questioning and answering by the disciples;
3. The vows made in the past.
