Regarding dregs: the clarity of wine is likened to the concentration of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-samādhi*), while its turbidity is likened to the concentration of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-samādhi*).
The Buddha does not indulge in or become defiled by the samādhi of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), just as one does not consume wine.
"Not savoring" means that the samādhi of conventional truth is like not eating dregs.
"Slippery grass and wheat bran": the wisdom of nirvāṇa is easy to attain, like slippery [grass]; the wisdom of discernment is difficult to produce, like bran.
The Buddha’s wisdom is neither the knowledge of all things (sarvajñatā) nor the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā).
This well-trained calf attains the Middle Way, being gentle, virtuous, and compliant.
Not dwelling in high plateaus or low marshes, it does not take nirvana as a final realization, nor does it abide within saṃsāra.

To drink from the clear water means it is neither the mud of the five desires nor the turbidity of the darkness of ignorance; being free from these two extremes, it is the clear water of Buddha-nature, which does not gallop toward the emptiness of the ultimate nor rush toward the conventionality of the mundane.
"Not herding with the bull" means that the bull has no milk; this is a metaphor for the absence of compassion, clarifying that the Buddha possesses unique (asādhāraṇa) compassion.

"The food and drink are well-adjusted" means that entering emptiness is hunger and emerging into the conventional is satiety; in the Middle Way, there is neither entry nor emergence, which is thus neither hunger nor satiety.

Regarding "conduct and abiding reaching their proper place": abiding in the Secret Treasury is "abiding reaching its proper place," while the two birds flying together is "conduct reaching its proper place.

Interpreting it in this way accords with the scripture and harmonizes with the meaning; it constantly subverts the impermanent so that both principle and expression coincide—how could this be the same as others?
From "At that time, the Great King" onwards, sentient beings receive transformation. This further divides into four parts:
first, receiving the teaching and transmitting it to others; second, other people not receiving it; third, explaining it repeatedly for them; and fourth, their believing and accepting it.
Regarding the preceding text: first, one attains self-confidence and realization; subsequently, one further transmits and transforms others.

That is to say, once those of superior capacity have attained understanding for themselves, they transmit and transform those of middling and inferior capacities, causing them all to attain awakening.
First, from "The people of the country heard this" onwards, those of middle and lower capacities do not receive it.
Second, from "The king said" onwards, the transformation is transmitted and propagated again.
Third, from "At that time, the great king" onwards, those of superior, middle, and lower faculties all attain realization simultaneously.
Next, from "You, monks... onwards, the analogies are unified.
In the preceding text there were two medicines and two diseases; here, in this unification, only the two medicines are unified, while the two diseases are not.

The reason for this is that I originally doubted whether the scriptural teachings contained such an exposition or not; if it had not existed in the past, there would have been no need to speak of it now, but if it did exist then, why was it not spoken earlier?

Now, employing this intention to remove doubts, [I previously] did not speak of emptiness early on because it would have been mistaken for eternalism; now, having further refuted the disease of false eternalism, I can only speak of the past emptiness and impermanence.
Now, to simply synthesize these two medicines so that they may be understood within the gateway of the teaching, I shall not speak further.
In the text concerning illness, the medicine of impermanence is synthesized first, and subsequently the medicine of true permanence is synthesized.
In the preceding analogy, it was first clarified that they were the same at the beginning, and later clarified that they differed at the end.
Now, I shall likewise combine these points; here, I first combine the similarity at the beginning.

The present statement that the Tathāgata is the Great King of Physicians precisely corresponds to the previous description of the time when there was a skilled physician who understood the eight branches of medical art.
Regarding those who appear in the world, they should now be understood as having come from afar.
Following the section "Subduing All," the end should differ from the beginning.

Initially, they should be combined as gradually differing; that is, they should be combined as entering together to see the king and speak of various medical prescriptions, as well as other arts such as governing the state and treating illnesses.
Next, from "desiring to subdue the non-Buddhists" onwards, it corresponds to the sudden teaching and differs [from the gradual].
This very meaning of the teaching—selflessness and impermanence—corresponds to the aforementioned compounding of various medicines, namely the five flavors: bitter, acrid, salty, sour, and sweet.
Next, from "Bhikṣus, you should know" onwards, the intent of this teaching is summarized.

Having previously concluded that the non-Buddhist paths are erroneous and subsequently concluding that the present teaching is correct, [the Buddha] must speak of this "non-existence" in order to harmonize sentient beings and because he knows the proper time.
Regarding the single phrase "Thus there is no self," there are two interpretations:
first, that this statement points toward what follows;
second, that it still belongs to the preceding section, and because there are specific causes and conditions, it is joined with the prior teaching on the true and eternal.
The subsequent section consists of three parts:
first, the formal exposition; second, the refutation of the errors of non-Buddhists; and third, the elucidation of the correctness of the Tathāgata.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle Six.
Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Compiled by Dharma Master Zhǎng'ān Zhǐng of the Sui Dynasty;
revised by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Zhànrán of the Tang Dynasty.

4. Chapter on Longevity (7–8). Regarding the first three chapters, they were arranged according to the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*. This present chapter follows the original text, with the sole modification that "life" (*ming*) has been changed to "long" (*chang*), and "vitality" (*shou*) has been moved to a subsequent position. It would have been equally appropriate not to move it, as the word order in the Western language (Sanskrit) is inverted; there was likely no intentional difference in the translator’s handling of these terms.
Based on the preceding text, one should understand that the Tathāgata is indeed long-lived.
Alternatively, based on the opening of the verse, "How does one attain long life?"—since "long" (長) simply means "constant" (常), why not use "constant" as the name?
The correct explanation is that because one attains this long life through the qualities of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, the name is established based on what has been attained.
Now, the long life is explained in four ways:
first, it is called "long life" because the Dharma-body, wisdom, and lifespan of all Buddhas are entirely equal.
Second, because beings delight in the long and loathe the short, it draws them toward the cultivation of virtue.
Third, it counters the ineptitude of one-sided cultivation of impermanence by clarifying the excellence of the constant, perfect cultivation.
The fourth [aspect], the mutual relation of long and short, is the gate of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*).
Because it realizes the "long" that is neither long nor short, it is called "long life.
This is the third application within the gift of *nirvāṇa*, wherein the Bodhisattva assembly grants according to the questions asked.

There are fourteen chapters in total; among the various questions and answers, the Chapter on Longevity (*Āyuṣmat*) is the first, followed by the Chapter on Life (*Jīvita*), with the others arranged according to their respective topics.
The text contains both exhortatory inquiries and formal inquiries: first, an exhortation to the bhikṣus, and subsequently, an exhortation to the great assembly.
The initial exhortations are threefold because the Buddha-dharma culminates in three stages;
furthermore, they manifest the Buddha’s earnestness;
and moreover, the first exhortation removes doubt, the second exhortation concerns receiving the entrustment, and the third exhortation concerns benefiting sentient beings.
When his doubts were completely resolved, he remained silent at the first exhortation;
when he realized he could not bear the responsibility of entrustment, he declined at the second exhortation;
and when he lacked the power to transform others, he deferred at the final exhortation.
Regarding the opening passage: why is he specifically encouraged to inquire about the Vinaya?
Hexi said: "The Buddha-dharma consists of two parts: first, the Sūtras; second, the Vinaya. Previously, he has already inquired about the Sūtras; now, he is encouraged to inquire about the Vinaya."
This interpretation is not correct.
Since the Sūtras are profound and the Vinaya is shallow, if one is capable of inquiring about the Sūtras, how could one be unable to inquire about the Vinaya and thus require encouragement?
Master Guan said:
The Vinaya is the foundation of the Śrāvakas and is also the primary tenet of this present sutra.
Because non-killing serves as the cause for attaining the fruit of longevity, [the Buddha] specifically exhorted [Śāriputra] to inquire about it.
This, however, is not the case.

Now, examining the sutra which states, "Regarding all precepts and regulations," it follows that the restraint of the Pratimokṣa (śīla-vinaya), the meditative discipline (dhyāna-saṃvara), and the discipline of the Path (mārga-saṃvara) are all termed "precepts" (śīla).
Since these various expressions are not uniform, how could it refer to the Pratimokṣa alone?
Furthermore, using what follows to verify what precedes it, this is not merely an exhortation to inquire about the Vinaya.

"Emptiness" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), and "quiescence" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); one should understand that this is an exhortation for the bhikṣus to inquire about morality (*śīla*), concentration, and wisdom.
Some interpret this through the lens of the two truths,
but this is also incorrect;
the text concerning the two truths is obscure, whereas the text concerning the three truths is clear.

What are these? The three—precept, concentration, and wisdom—are the rungs of the ladder for entering the truth; thus, they exhort one to inquire about the truth. That the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent is the inquiry itself. That there is clear understanding and thorough penetration is the simultaneous illumination of the two truths; thus, it exhorts one to inquire about the conventional.

Furthermore, when it is said that one should not claim that the Tathāgata cultivates only emptiness and quiescence, this implies that since the Tathāgata does not exclusively cultivate either the ultimate or the conventional, he is instead exhorting one to inquire into the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) which is neither ultimate nor conventional.
The second part, the repeated exhortation, consists of two sections:
first, the exhortation; second, the refusal.
Regarding the exhortation to inquire about the beginning of the precepts (*śīla*), one version says it is merely brief, while the full explanation is as given above.
Furthermore, taking the meaning of the subsequent passage, because the Buddha intended to entrust [the teachings], he used the precepts and discipline as the basis for his exhortation.
As for the following expression, since one is unable to inquire regarding the precepts and discipline, one then declines on the grounds of being incapable.
There are the thesis, the example, and the application.
Furthermore, the statement of the thesis consists of three parts:
the formal proposition, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Regarding "Correct Words" (*zhèngcí*): if words lack wisdom, one cannot inquire into the three titles, as stated in the text.

Next is the explanation of the words: the explanation of the three titles is that they are all inconceivable; because the profound and subtle Dharma of the Tathāgata’s realm accords perfectly with that of all Buddhas, he is titled "Tathāgata."
That I cannot inquire further means that his original nature is empty and quiescent.

All his meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) are inconceivable; having reached the ultimate depths of profound and subtle dhyāna, he is able to serve as a field of merit for all beings, and is therefore called "Worthy of Offerings" (*Arhat*).
When I cannot ask, my words are clear, lucid, and penetrating.

The teachings and instructions he expounds are inconceivable; they exhaust the very limits of all speech and discourse, guiding sentient beings as to what is the path and what is not the path, and are thus called "Right Universal Knowledge" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
If I am unable to ask, I shall decline the higher precepts.
Furthermore, I shall decline to ask about the Three Truths,
for the realm of the Buddhas lies within that which cannot be asked.
All meditative concentrations are unable to inquire into the ultimate truth;
all the teachings and instructions that are expounded are unable to inquire into the conventional.
Regarding the statement in the "Threefold Refutation" that there is "no wisdom," it means there is no possession of the three types of knowledge (*trividya*).
Next, the analogies are fourfold:

first, that the śrāvakas are incapable of being entrusted; second, that the Tathāgata should not entrust [it]; third, that the śrāvakas forcibly accept the entrustment; and fourth, that the Tathāgata loses what was entrusted.

First, it clarifies his incapacity. Regarding the term "old man," this refers to the years when the karmic retribution of Jambudvīpa is nearing its end; it is likened to the śrāvakas' contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination, where each of the twelve branches spans from the past to the present, thus totaling one hundred and twenty.
Because the past and present have ceased, old age and death cease; because ignorance ceases, up to and including old age and death, one enters parinirvāṇa.
As for one whose body is afflicted by a chronic illness, even though the [active] disease may be exhausted, the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) still remain.
Furthermore, because the specific delusions of ignorance have not yet encroached even by a hair's breadth, it is called a "chronic illness.
As for "lying prostrate upon a bed," this refers to sinking into emptiness and stagnating in stillness, thereby losing the playful mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
"Unable to rise or sit" means being unable to enter [the Dharma] as if unable to rise, and being unable to sustain the Three Jewels as if unable to dwell.

"With feeble and inferior strength" means having no permanent life-force as if lacking breath, and lacking the heroic power of the Ten Strengths as if lacking physical strength; it is called "feeble" because of the paucity of reality, and "inferior" because it is not a superior cultivation; with little life remaining, one is about to enter the cessation of ashes.
Next, regarding the passage beginning with "There was a wealthy man," it is as follows: he should not be entrusted [with the task], just as the Tathāgata should not be so entrusted.
He is called a "wealthy man" because his wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) are perfected.

Regarding the phrase "desiring to act on account of business": he is said to have "business" because he is appropriately engaged in manifold transformative activities; he is said to "desire to act" because he gives rise to responsive manifestations based upon suchness (*tathatā*).
"By means of a hundred *jin*," refers to the liberation of a hundred phrases.
The *Book of Han* (*Hanshu*) states that ten thousand [cash] constitute one *jin*; thus, having "a hundred *jin*" amounts to one million.
Since one phrase of liberation has ten thousand liberations as its retinue, one hundred phrases of liberation have one million liberations as their retinue.
Regarding the phrase "perhaps ten or twenty years," there are three interpretations:
first, that it refers to ten *kalpas* or twenty *kalpas*;
second, that it refers to ten human years or twenty celestial years.
Third, [some] say that the True Dharma lasts for ten years and the Semblance Dharma for twenty.
This interpretation is incorrect.
If that were so, how could there be a subsequent period for returning to and assembling [the teachings]?
Now, it is explained that the pervasive afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) constitute ten, while the specific afflictions (*kleśa*) constitute twenty.
To eliminate both the pervasive and specific afflictions by responding to conditions and benefiting sentient beings is called "entrusting the household affairs.
When the one who receives the entrustment eliminates these pervasive and specific afflictions, they immediately cause me to return.
Regarding the phrase "returning to give it back to me," there are two traditional interpretations.
The first states that this refers specifically to Śākyamuni;
once all other regions have been reached, when he returns to this land, he will still see my former Dharma-treasures as they were inspired and manifested here.

The second [interpretation] says: "Even when Maitreya descends to be born, one still perceives the true Dharma of Śākyamuni; because the Dharma-body is not different, it is said that 'one returns to me.
Now, the explanation is as follows:
the exhaustion of both general and specific delusions is itself the time of returning, which is itself 'returning to me'; this meaning is somewhat more convenient."
3. Regarding the passage beginning with "This old sick man," it refers to the false acceptance [of offerings] by Śrāvakas.
As for the phrase "having no heir," there are two traditional interpretations:
first, that it means there is no son of virtuous mind or daughter of compassionate mind.
Second, it is said that there are no disciples to receive his transformation and succeed him.
Now, regarding those who lack children with steadfast faith and whose illnesses are terminal and life has ended, their bodies are reduced to ashes as they enter extinction.
4. From "The Wealthy Master Returns" onwards, the Tathāgata has lost what was entrusted to him, and the Dharma-treasure is forfeited.
Regarding the "deluded person," there are two interpretations:
first, it refers to the one who received the entrustment; being a deluded person, they were unable to exercise due deliberation and thus unworthily accepted the entrustment.

The second [position] says: "One who can entrust [the teaching] is called a foolish person. This is a hypothetical statement; if one were to actually entrust it to a śrāvaka, then one would be a foolish person, but if one does not entrust it to them, then one is not a foolish person.
Next, from "World-Honored One" onwards, the analogies are applied.
Only the loss resulting from false reception is applied; the preceding two are not.
Within the latter two [analogies], the third is applied first; next, from "I now" onwards, the fourth is applied.
From "The Buddha said" onwards is the third section, the exhortation to benefit sentient beings.
It is divided into three parts:
first, the exhortation; second, the inference; and third, the praise.
The first part is as stated in the text.
The second part, which deduces the merit, is divided into two sections:
first, the analogy; second, the application.
There are another four parables:
the first praises the Bodhisattva.
The "twenty-five" refers to the twenty-five samādhis.
Those who are vigorous and handsome are the kings of all samādhis.
Those who possess abundant wealth and treasures are those into whom all samādhis enter.

As for parents: the three truths and one truth constitute the mother, while the one truth and three truths constitute the father; the joy of the Dharma is the wife, the virtuous mind is the son, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas) are the kinsmen, and the Buddhas of the ten directions are the paternal relatives.
Next, from "At that time there was a person" onwards, it is an analogy for the formal entrustment, explained by way of comparison with the preceding section.
Third, from "At that time the strong man" onwards, it is an analogy for upholding what has been entrusted.
Fourth, that a person encounters illness is analogous to not losing the True Dharma.
From "World-Honored One" onwards is the application of the analogy: first the non-appropriate is raised, followed by the application of the appropriate through entrustment.
3. From "At that time, the Buddha praised... onwards, this is the section on praise.
Regarding the "outflow-free mind" (anāsrava-citta), which refers to the mind of an Arhat: it is characterized by forgetting the self and attributing merit [to others].
As for the "two conditions," those pertaining to Śrāvakas are incapable [of fulfilling them], whereas Bodhisattvas are capable.
Whether it be excelling at question and answer or the long endurance of the Dharma-treasure for the benefit of sentient beings, all these have been set forth in the preceding text.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the Buddha addressed the entire great assembly" onwards, the second general exhortation for the great assembly to inquire is presented.
Since the Buddha is universally equal, if he encounters those who seek instruction, he benefits them all.
Furthermore, whereas there may be partial exhortation in certain instances, here there is universal exhortation.
By first presenting the partial and subsequently the universal, it is shown that the partial and the universal are not fixed, thereby revealing that which is neither partial nor universal.
Question:
A bhikṣu of meager virtue may be earnestly exhorted three times.
Why is it that a bodhisattva does not do so, yet requires two or three exhortations?
Answer:

The Buddha is like a lion; whether killing an elephant or a rabbit, he exerts his full strength in both cases and never shows partiality, which is why he offers the threefold exhortation in all instances.
If this is so, then a Bodhisattva should likewise act without hesitation, yet still practice yielding and deference.
Answer: Bhikṣus have none at all, whereas Bodhisattvas possess them all.
Because there is a question, we know that there is doubt.
Therefore, a bodhisattva may be entrusted with this task; because of their compassionate heart, they are able to benefit others.
Furthermore, although the examples are constructed as if non-existent, the underlying intent differs: the bodhisattva has long understood this, and thus remains free from doubt.
To speak of oneself with humility carries the sense of retreat, whereas to praise the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is to attribute merit to them.
Question:
Why is it that regarding "life" one says it is immeasurable, regarding "eloquence" one says it is inexhaustible, yet regarding "precepts" and "refuge," one offers exhortations and inquiries?
Answer: There are many points involved; briefly stated, there are four meanings.
First, the Tathāgata is a great and wealthy donor who bestows gifts according to whatever is requested.
If one asks about life, he then elucidates the meanings of longevity, the adamantine body, and the secret of the body.
If one asks about eloquence, he then elucidates the meanings of the four aspects of *prajñā* and the secret of speech.
If one asks about returning to the precepts, it immediately opens up the meaning of wholesome karma.

The Śūraṅgama Samādhi is able to establish great principles, including the meanings of the hundred phrases of liberation, the secret intention, and so forth, even extending to the opening of the four inversions of the heterodox and orthodox, the Four Noble Truths, the Tathāgata-nature, and the meanings of the moon, the bird, and letters; thus, the Nirvāṇa-sūtra attains its full manifestation.

Second, the Tathāgata’s skillful means as a donor are immeasurable: if one asks about life, he reveals the practice of the heavens; if one asks about eloquence, he reveals the Brahma-practice; if one asks about taking refuge and precepts, he reveals the noble practice and the infant-like practice; and regarding what is guarded by taking refuge and precepts, he reveals the practice of illness.
If the five elements are established, the ten virtues manifest of themselves, and the practice of nirvana becomes clear.

Third, the Tathāgata, the Master of Giving, adorns the precious city of the True Dharma with the immeasurable; the Tathāgata can pose questions where there is nothing to be questioned, and the Tathāgata can provide answers where no one is able to question.

When seeking to entrust the hundred pieces of exquisite treasure, one first finds a person capable of inquiry: inquiry into life is the adornment of constancy; inquiry into eloquence is the adornment of joy; inquiry into precepts is the adornment of purity; and inquiry into refuge is the adornment of the self.

Being able to both question and answer, one possesses the two adornments; thus, the meaning of the *nirvāṇa* beneath the twin trees is made manifest. Fourth, the Tathāgata is a donor whose compassion is immeasurable;

he takes pity on the heterodox and feels deep sympathy for those who are unwholesome. If one asks about taking refuge, he employs the power of constant eloquence to gather them in; if one asks about the precepts, he employs the power of constant exhortation to restrain evil. Thus, the function of *nirvāṇa* is made manifest.
For this reason, these three types are raised as the opening of the inquiry.
Question: Does this opening of the inquiry apply only to what follows, or does it also apply to what precedes?

Answer: To inquire about life is to cultivate the virtue of permanence; to inquire about eloquence is to cultivate the virtue of bliss; to inquire about taking refuge in the precepts is to cultivate the virtue of self.

Furthermore, to inquire about life is to inquire about the virtue of the permanent Dharma-body; to inquire about eloquence is to inquire about the virtue of the blissful Prajñā; to inquire about taking refuge in the precepts is to inquire about the pure virtue of my liberation.

Furthermore, it asks whether life is eternal, and whether life, form, and strength are eternal; it asks whether eloquence is eternal speech, and whether taking refuge in the precepts is eternal peace.
Moreover, the text states: "To be able to inquire in this manner brings great benefit to all sentient beings."
Thus, encompassing both what precedes and what follows,
the scope of the inquiry is as extensive as this.
Second, the formal question is divided into four parts:
First, the desire to inquire; second, the granting of permission to inquire; third, the humble inquiry; fourth, the formal inquiry.
Regarding the desire to inquire, there are two parts:
first, the introduction by the narrator of the sutra; second, the personal initiation of the question.

The introduction consists of four parts: first, the description of the fundamental status; second, the description of the manifested doctrine; third, the description of responsive manifestations; and fourth, the description of majestic deportment.
Regarding the first, the fundamental status, there is both a general and a specific aspect: the general status of a bodhisattva and the specific status of a youth.
The treatise states: "That he was able to inquire despite being twelve years old involves four intentions:
first, the True Dharma is not material form; one cannot discard the Dharma because a person is young, for it is both the Dharma and the person that are revered;
second, his birth as a bhikṣu was virtuous, and his faith and resolve regarding the bodhisattva path were firm."
"Third, it subdues haughty pride;
fourth, it clarifies the greatness of the Buddha's power.
If categorized according to the *Daśabhūmika*, this corresponds to the ninth stage (*bhūmi*).
If one were to categorize Mañjuśrī Kumāra according to his textual descriptions, he would belong to the summit of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Since the status of a sage is difficult to discern, I shall provisionally explain the term "Kumāra" by means of the ten stages.
Next, regarding the term "Brahmin" mentioned in the context of the *jieti* (trace) school, it refers to a lineage that relies upon a noble ancestral tradition.
Mahākāśyapa was born into a noble family, like the prominent clans of this world.
Regarding the "three times by the Buddha's spiritual power," this refers to the correspondence of karmic response.

Acting as the leader for the assembly of those seeking certainty, he was moved by the Buddha’s majestic empowerment to serve as the master of the proclamation, enabling the fifty-two assemblies to together drink the nectar of immortality.
Were it not for one of such great capacity, who could have accomplished this?
Fourth, [Subhūti] rises from his seat and describes his majestic demeanor.

Next, from the passage "He addressed the Buddha," onwards, he inquires on his own behalf: although the Buddha has offered general encouragement, would he perhaps grant permission for him to ask questions?
Therefore, there is an inquiry.
Next, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the Buddha grants permission as the text describes.
Third, from "At that time, Kāśyapa" onwards, this is a humble inquiry.
The text consists of three parts:
first, "great" and "small" form one pair; second, "high" and "broad" form one pair; third, "aiding" and "relying" form one pair.
Regarding the first part: the Tathāgata’s compassionate pity is precisely great compassion, the greatest among the great.
With the meager wisdom of a mosquito or gnat—the smallest among the small—I ask a great being about great matters;
how could this possibly be commensurate? As for the subsequent pairs:

"The Buddha’s virtue is towering" clarifies the loftiness of the Buddha’s majesty; "the lion is difficult to subdue" clarifies the vastness of his assembly. The Tathāgata’s body is like true adamant; because the Buddha’s physical form is great, his wisdom is likewise great. That the ocean of wisdom surrounds him indicates that the wisdom of the great assembly is also great.
The Buddha and the great assembly are as lofty and vast as this; how could I, who am like a mosquito or a gnat, be able to withstand them?

As for this third pair, if one were to discuss their magnitude and minuteness, it would be impossible to speak of them at all. Now, by borrowing the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, assisting with the strength of wisdom, and relying on the roots of goodness of the great assembly, my eloquence has been augmented, and thus I am able to pose these questions.
The fourth section, from "Right before the Buddha," constitutes the formal inquiry.
Regarding this, there are three traditional explanations for its distinct components:
first, the division of verses; second, the number of questions; and third, the causal origin.
Regarding the differences in the initial verses, Hexi says:
"The first nineteen verses constitute the questions, and the final four verses constitute the request for an answer.
Another master says:
The first twenty-one lines constitute the questions, while the final two lines express self-deprecation.
Furthermore, another master says:
from beginning to end, there is nothing that is not a question.
Furthermore, another master says:

To maintain both views with composure, it is not that the subsequent [passage] is not a question; rather, it is the lingering momentum of Kāśyapa’s skillful posing of the question, serving as the introduction to the various chapters.

Furthermore, "inquiring about profound practice and so forth" refers to inquiring about the five practices and ten virtues; "inquiring about the nature of peace and bliss" refers to the inquiry concerning the lion’s roar of Kāśyapa and others, and so forth.
Regarding the second point, the difference in the number of questions: Emperor Wu of Liang had thirty-two questions;
the thirty-four questions from Hexi were used by Lingwei Liang, Yecheng Su, and Zhuangyan Min;
and Zhongsi An had thirty-five questions.
The thirty-six questions of Kaishan;
the thirty-seven questions of Guangzhai.
Regarding the difference in how the three causes arise, Kaishan says:
Each question arises from Cunda’s expressions of sorrowful lamentation.
Taichang Zong says:
"All are questions posed according to the immediate circumstances; none arise from the preceding text."
Linggenlingzheng said:
"Some [attainments] arise from previous lives, while others do not; how can they be treated as one and the same?
As for those that arise from previous lives, how can one ask how they attain long life? This arises from the 'Cundadatta' chapter."
One should know that the Tathāgata is long-lived; he has generated a vajra-body through inquiry, born from the Dharma-body, the eternal body, and the vajra-body.
We pray that the Buddha will reveal the subtle mystery, which is born from the secret treasury of the "Chapter on Lamentation."
How does one attain vastness? It arises from taking Kāśyapa as one’s refuge for the sake of the assembly.
Those who possess the appropriate connection may arise from above;
those who lack the appropriate connection do not arise from above.
Xinghuang said:

"This question should not be restricted solely to Cunda; rather, it concerns the teaching gate of Śākyamuni’s single transformation as a whole, beginning from his birth in the royal palace and ending at the twin śāla trees."
Why is this? The text says: "In the great ocean of birth and death, how does one become a captain?
This is the question regarding the beginning, referring to the time when he first attained enlightenment.
Later, he asked: "How does one abandon birth and death, as a snake sheds its old skin?
This question marks the end; it concerns the time of his final nirvana.

During the intervening period of his transformative teachings, the Dharma gates were manifold; [the Buddha] wished to reveal the Tathāgata’s skillful means and secret teachings, manifesting various appearances of coming and going.
This intention is vast and magnificent, encompassing the great; it clearly illuminates the path of awakening, spanning from antiquity to the present.
Now, observing these twenty-three verses: although the first nineteen are questions, within those questions there is a request, namely, "I only pray that the Great Sage will speak of this."
Although the final four verses constitute a request, they contain questions within that request; these include such topics as the nature of peace and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, there are differences in how they are condensed or expanded: for instance, the first verse is condensed into two questions but expanded into four.
How is it that the single verse of the celestial Māra, when combined, forms one question, yet when expanded, forms two questions?

If one simply counts the "how many" (kathaṃ), there are thirty-two questions; if one counts by combining the verses, there are likewise only thirty-two questions. If one counts by expanding the verses, there are thirty-four questions.

If one counts the three questions within the request and adds them to the combined verses, there are thirty-five questions. If one counts the three verses within the request and adds them to all the "how many," there are also thirty-five questions. If one counts the three verses within the request and adds them to the expanded verses, there are thirty-seven questions.
Each has its own criteria for inclusion or exclusion, resulting in different expansions and contractions; this is the point.
These are merely variations in the enumeration of phenomena; it is up to the person not to labor over them by giving rise to contention.

Now, following the numerical arrangement of the verses from Hexi, rather than counting the individual requests for verses, we shall provide thirty-four question-and-answer pairs that exhaust the entirety of the "Mahāparṣat-paripṛcchā-parivarta.

Regarding the distance of the causal origins: if one were to claim that these questions arise because they follow from the preceding text—arguing that the Śrāvakas have never heard of the eternal [nature] and thus may give rise to doubt, whereas the Bodhisattvas have heard it for a long time, so why would they harbor doubt?—[the response follows].
Furthermore, if the Śrāvakas have already broken through their doubts and attachments upon hearing the teaching,
why has the Bodhisattva, possessing such sharp faculties, not yet attained understanding?
To this, the defense is offered:
Doubt arises because of conditions.
If that is so, then the question does not depend on what precedes it.
Furthermore, it says:

If the Bodhisattva, knowing that the Buddha should preach this Dharma, inquires about it in advance by virtue of the Buddha’s spiritual power—since the Buddha’s power reaches everywhere—why is it limited here to these two chapters?
Furthermore, it is said:
To ask about the beginning and end of a single transformation is entirely inconsistent with the practice of the Sūtra.
The Sūtra asks about the cause of longevity, and the Buddha answers that listening to the Dharma with a sincere mind and observing the precept against killing in the past are the causes of longevity.
Now, you have taken one transformation that came from the royal palace; where did the Buddha stay to hear the Dharma?
From whom did he receive the precepts?
And at the end by the twin trees, from whom did he again hear the sutras?
By receiving what precepts?
If this were not the case, a single transformation would not be accomplished.
That is the ultimate discourse.
Now, it is said that this does not accord with the text, and therefore it is not the ultimate teaching.
Let us now attempt to set forth its intended meaning.
How is long life attained?
This question concerns the causal basis for the eternal fruit.
The Buddha replied:

"If karma can serve as the cause for Bodhi, then having heard it with a sincere mind and received it, one explains it further; 'I have cultivated this karma and attained supreme enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi),' and now I again expound this meaning extensively for others."
Such causes as these are by no means of recent origin; even as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, kalpas as numerous as motes of dust cannot be fully known.
Now, we specifically inquire into this cause from such a remote past: if the original [cause] were impermanent, the fruit could not be permanent;
if the original [cause] were permanent, it could not be cultivated.
Yet, one has not yet understood what the cause of the eternal fruit of long life is.

If this meaning is questioned, it will spontaneously reveal itself: that by means of a cause that is neither eternal nor non-eternal, one obtains an eternal fruit that is neither eternal nor non-eternal.

The meaning of the permanence of cause and effect having been thus revealed, it follows that all the myriad virtues within the fruit are the result of causes that transcend both [existence and non-existence], thereby attaining a fruit that transcends both.

Although these meanings are boundless, to summarize them briefly: this concerns the inquiry into the original causes and effects of the past, the stages of practice and vows, merit and wisdom, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and other such Dharma-gates.
If one asks how to reach the ultimate further shore through this sutra,
it is to ask about the beginning and end of a single cycle of transformation— the various teachings bestowed according to conditions in the present.
Why is this? If there were no beginning, there would be no end.
Since you have now asked about the end, the beginning is naturally entailed by that question.
Since the beginning and the end have been discussed, the middle may be understood by implication.

One should know that throughout the beginning and end of a single cycle of transformation, the verbal teachings bestowed upon immeasurable sentient beings according to their various capacities are inexhaustible.

Although this cannot be fully exhausted, to summarize it briefly: this question concerns the immeasurable dharma-gates of following others, following oneself, and following both oneself and others in the present life.
If one asks how one may attain vastness and become a refuge for the multitude?
He then inquired about the skillful means to be employed in future ages for guiding sentient beings—those who serve as national preceptors, Daoist masters, and patriarchs of the Confucian academies.

Abiding in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he manifests in various ways in measureless and boundless ways that are inexhaustible; yet, to summarize briefly, this refers to the question of the provisional and the real, the subtle and the ingenious skillful means used to attract, guide, support, and deliver sentient beings through these and other Dharma gates.

To briefly cite three phrases to demonstrate that the intent of this question does not transcend the three periods of time, the text states: "Such profound realms of the Buddhas, and the immeasurable Dharma-gates for self-benefit and benefiting others—how could these transcend the three periods of time?"
If one seeks its ancient beginning, it is primordial and inexhaustible;
if one seeks its present state, it is vast and boundless;
if one seeks its future limit, it is eternal and endless.

Thus, this indeed encompasses the great illumination of the Path of Awakening throughout antiquity and the present; it may be called the realm of all Buddhas, for how could it arise merely from two proximate causes, nor solely from a single distant transformation?

Now, the intent of these inquiries is as vast and profound as this; yet I still fear that the clear explanations of the Buddhas' realm have not been fully grasped—how much less could what the various masters say possibly accord with the Buddha’s intention?
Xinghuang mocked people, saying:

"To not know whether a rabbit's horns exist or not, yet to vainly dispute their length; to not know whether various questions are advanced or not, yet to dispute the number of questions—what benefit is there in this?"
Now, regarding the questions from Hexi, I have divided the twenty-three verses into two parts:
the first nineteen verses constitute thirty-four actual questions, while the final four verses are a request for answers.
The first line asks about the Buddha’s cause and fruit.
Since the Buddha cultivated the cause to attain the fruit, it cannot be said to belong to the present or the future; it can only be pointed to as belonging to the past.
The subsequent line asks how one should approach this sutra; this refers to the teaching of the present.
The present teaching is spoken according to the specific capacity of the audience; it cannot be said to belong to the past or future, though one might insist on calling it the present.

As for the seventeen lines beginning with "How can it be vast and great," although their meaning applies to all three periods of time, since the preceding section has already concluded with two periods, one might insist on naming this the future.
Why is it said that [this] is "forced"?
Great Parinirvāṇa is not subsumed within the three periods of time; it is not that bodhi has past, future, or present—it is merely described by means of worldly words as if it were so.
The final four verses request answers to the three preceding points.

The first verse among them expresses the wish for the Buddha to explain the subtle practices and so forth for the sake of all bodhisattvas. Since the previous question concerned the fruit of long life, and a fruit must necessarily have a cause—wherein the cause being these very practices—it is understood that this verse requests an answer concerning the dharma-gate of past causes.
The next line requests an answer concerning the present. While the previous question asked how the secret is revealed, this one requests an answer regarding the nature of bliss (*sukhatā*).
Since the nature of bliss has not yet been revealed, it is known that this is a request for an answer concerning the present.

The final two verses request an answer concerning the future; whereas the preceding inquiry concerned the vast basis (*āśraya*), this request seeks an answer regarding the future dharma-gates, which is exceedingly clear.
Having finished listing the number of questions and concluding the text of the request, the next section indicates the location of the response.
"How does one attain long life?"—these four questions are answered in the subsequent sections of this chapter and in the "Chapter on the Vajra Body.
"How does one reach the ultimate perfection in this sutra?"—this is answered in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Name."
"May the Buddha reveal the subtle and secret [teachings]" is answered in the "Chapter on the Four Marks.
"How can one attain vastness to serve as a refuge for the masses, while in reality not being an Arhat or the like? is answered in the "Chapter on the Four Reliances."
How does one know? Regarding the two questions posed by the celestial Māra, the "Chapter on Perversity" (*Sai-zheng-pin*) provides the answer.
How do all the Tamer-Teachers joyfully proclaim the True Truths? The "Chapter on the Four Truths" (*Si-di-pin*) provides the answer.
The exposition of the four inversions is answered in the "Chapter on the Four Inversions.
As for how one performs wholesome karma and is able to perceive the nature that is difficult to see, this is answered in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature."

"How does one understand the full syllables? is answered in the "Chapter on Syllables" (*Akṣara-parivarta*). "What is the shared noble practice? is answered in the "Parable of the Birds" (*Śakuntaka-parivarta*).
"How are they like the sun, the moon, Venus, and Jupiter? is answered in the "Parable of the Moon" (*Candraprabha-parivarta*). Thus end the fifteen questions.
Regarding the twelve questions following "How is it that one who has not yet resolved [to attain enlightenment]?"—all of which are answered in the "Bodhisattva" chapter:
the answer to "How is it that one who has not yet resolved sees a rākṣasa in a dream and is compelled to resolve? is as follows.
How does one attain fearlessness in the great assembly? This is answered by three verses.
How does one abide in a defiled world? This is answered by the metaphor of four flowers.
How does one abide amidst afflictions? This is answered by fourteen similes, beginning with the physician.
"How does one become a helmsman within the great ocean of birth and death?"—this is answered by the four analogies of the Wind King.
"How does one abandon birth and death as a snake sheds its old skin?"—this is answered by two analogies of the goldsmith. That a dragon can shed its bones may be used as an analogy for *nirvāṇa*.
How does one contemplate the Three Jewels? This is answered by the *Amra* and *Jambu* trees.
If the three vehicles lacked intrinsic nature, Mañjuśrī raised his doubts, which were answered with verses on primordial non-existence (*mūlābhāva*).
How do all bodhisattvas attain an indestructible assembly? This is answered by citing the causes and conditions for protecting the Dharma.
How does one act as eyes and a guide for those born blind? It is answered: it is like a person whose sense of taste is impaired who cannot distinguish the six flavors.
How does one manifest many heads? It is answered: it is by constantly acting as parents to sentient beings.

"How does the Dharma-preacher increase like the waxing moon? and "How is it that a person has a son who is six months old?"—these and others constitute seven questions concerning the manifestation of ultimate nirvana; all are answered in the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly."
"How does he further manifest the ultimate attainment of nirvana? "By emitting light and receiving offerings," he replied.

"How does the courageous one know the paths of humans, devas, and maras? "If there is a bhikṣu who can make vows through the vows of the Tathāgata, he is the most supreme in the world; one who cannot perceive the eternal is a caṇḍāla," he replied.
"How does one know the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and experience the joy of the Dharma? To this, twenty-one verses are spoken in response.
"How do all bodhisattvas remain free from all illness? To this, the three sick people respond.

How does one expound the secrets for the sake of sentient beings? How does one extensively explain those verses that have a remainder (*śeṣa-gāthā*) by answering with verses that have no remainder (*niḥśeṣa-gāthā*)?
How does one speak of the ultimate (*atyanta*) and the non-ultimate? By what means is the meaning of "without remainder" defined?
Furthermore, what is meant by "all meanings"?
With the sole exception of the wholesome dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity that assist the path, all others are termed "answers with remainder."
How does one attain proximity to the most supreme and unsurpassed path? This is answered by the previous response concerning how the aforementioned bodhisattvas remain free from all illnesses.

Furthermore, the answer to this question is provided concurrently with the account of how the three types of sick persons, after attaining the extinction of their offenses, draw near to the unsurpassed path.
If there are sick people who recover whether they encounter [a physician] or not, they are closest to the Buddha;
if they recover only when they encounter one and do not recover when they do not, they are next closest;
if they do not recover whether they encounter one or not, they are far from the Buddha.
Furthermore, it is said that the answer to this question consists of the assembly’s arousal of the bodhicitta and the Tathāgata’s bestowal of the prediction of enlightenment.
Now, ten proofs are cited to demonstrate that the answering of the question is complete.

First, the sequence of questions was raised within the verses, and the prose section provides answers corresponding to that sequence; therefore, we know that the answering of the questions is exhaustive.
Second, having finished posing the questions within the verse, he immediately expresses self-effacement, saying:
"The profound, subtle, and wondrous nature of peace and bliss, and so forth, are not within my knowledge; I pray that the Tathāgata will expound them himself for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
If one follows this intention, it is known that the answering of questions has been completed.
Thirdly, if the answering were not yet finished, one should not express gratitude.

Since the answering of questions has concluded, the assembly has gained benefit; they rise to prostrate, burn incense, and scatter flowers as offerings. Thus, it is known that the answering of questions is complete.
Fourth, since the previous convocation of the assembly and the earnest exchange of questions and answers were not yet concluded, how could he have leaned on his side to enter nirvana?
Once he lay on his right side and ceased speaking, it was known that the answering of questions had come to an end.
Fifth, he entrusted [the teaching] to Mañjuśrī; [Bodhidharma] then lay down and remained silent, refusing to speak.

When the great assembly requested him once more, and he had accepted their request, he sat cross-legged with a serene and joyful countenance before discussing the Five Elements (*pañca-dhātu*). Thus, we know that his answers to questions were exhaustive.
Sixth, when addressing King Guṇarāja, there is a distinction between guest and host; one knows the response and the question are exhausted.
Seventh, when the Lion asks further questions, since the questioner is distinct [from the previous one], one knows the response and the question are exhausted.

Eighth, the text states that when the Tathāgata first expounded the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he spoke of three types of persons; however, these three types of persons appear at the conclusion of his response to a question and were not actually taught at the very beginning.
Now, it is said that "the initial opening" refers to the beginning of the subsequent teaching, not the beginning of the primary teaching;
since there is thus a distinction between the initial and subsequent teachings, we know that the answers to the questions are exhaustive.

Ninth, the questions at the beginning were numerous while the answers were few, whereas the questions at the end were few yet the answers were many; thus one knows that the answering of the questions was complete.

Tenth, at Hexi, Kumārajīva personally received the oral instructions on the Sanskrit text face-to-face, and Dharmakṣema guided him in its teaching; Kumārajīva earnestly and personally stated that nineteen verses constitute the *praśna* (questions) and the four subsequent verses do not. If this man did not believe it, who could be trusted?
From "At that time, the Buddha praised him" onwards is the third section, the Buddha’s response.
This is further divided into two parts:
first, the praise for the question; second, the answer to the question.
The praise and inquiry consist of two parts:
first, the praise; second, the humility. The praise, in turn, consists of two parts:
First is the general praise, followed by the specific praise, in response to the two requests—specific and general—made above.
If the thirty-four questions constitute the specific request concerning each phenomenon (*dharma*) individually, then the subsequent part constitutes the general request.
First, he responds to the general invitation; therefore, at the outset, he says, "Excellent, excellent.

The reason this praise is necessary is that in the world, when answering questions or responding to others, one employs words of commendation. The Buddha does not contravene worldly conventions; thus, he first praises the person.
Seeing only that he was young, one would not expect his wisdom to be profound; yet when one encounters his inquiries into the deep and mysterious, one then realizes he is no shallow person.
Furthermore, seeing him praise the Buddha causes all to give rise to a sense of the extraordinary; for this reason, it is necessary to offer praise.
When the assembly from other regions saw that this minor bodhisattva was able to inquire about such momentous matters, they all felt reverence and submission; therefore, he must be praised.
Furthermore, each of these questions accords with principle; for this reason, he must be praised.
All [the preceding] has been presented as a general comparison, and so forth.
Next is the specific praise, which refers to the specific praise of the inquiry concerning the three periods of time.
First is the praise for the inquiry regarding the dharma-gate of the past, which contains three meanings:
First, praising the cause by means of its fruit:

when it says "you have not yet attained," this does not mean you have not attained anything at all; rather, it refers to a partial realization within the causal stage, as opposed to the ultimate state of the fruition stage, and is thus said to be "not yet attained."
Second, he praises the question by citing the profound and secret treasury:

"You ask about longevity; the Buddha takes omniscience (*sarvajñā*) as his life-force. This wisdom-life is realized at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*); therefore, I say that I have attained it."

That which has already been attained is not newly acquired; once attained, it is perfected. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom it; therefore, it is called the profound and secret treasury. Since you are able to inquire about this, I praise the Dharma you have asked.
Third, he praises that which has been empowered.
Regarding the request above, it says: "Relying on the Buddha's spiritual power, I now empower and praise it," and thus it is said to be "equal and without difference.
As for "one who sits at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this praises the manifestation of his inquiry.
He then asked: "How does one reach the ultimate further shore regarding this sutra?
The Buddha immediately praised him by citing three meanings:

First, by citing the beginning to establish the subsequent, he praises his skillful questioning as encompassing the entirety of the manifestation from beginning to end; thus, he says, "I sat at the site of enlightenment when I first attained perfect awakening."
2. To praise one individual so as to bring harmony to the entire assembly, it is said: "There have been many bodhisattvas who have also asked me about this profound meaning.
3. To praise his present attainment of the assistance and support of the great assembly.

The request made therein states: "Furthermore, by the power of the roots of goodness of the great assembly, the phrases and meanings of merit are now clarified as being without difference. This constitutes the praise and inquiry concerning the Dharma-gate of the present.
One who asks such questions is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings; this praises the inquiry regarding the future.
The preceding question asked:
"How does one attain vastness to serve as a refuge for the masses?"
The statement that "this benefit can be understood" and so forth is explained by the old commentators as follows:
regarding the phrase "one who also once questioned [the Buddha] while sitting at the site of enlightenment," some say:
In this *Avataṃsaka*, the questions regarding the incomplete translation remain unanswered, as their texts have not yet arrived. Some say:
"This is a partial and non-definitive teaching, and its texts likewise have not arrived."
Some may say:
"This is a secret teaching and is not included among the revealed teachings.
This interpretation is in every respect incorrect.

It is now clarified that this site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) is the original, primordial, and perfect place where he first sat; it is not a site of enlightenment belonging to the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*).
The second fascicle states: "I have long since attained Buddhahood throughout immeasurable kalpas."
This is also like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which states: "Since attaining Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed.

Formerly, various bodhisattvas asked about this meaning; it is no different from the present inquiry. This directly addresses past questions and does not pertain to the beginning of a single cycle of transformation (*ekavyūha*). One should not rely on the site of the terrace of tranquility (*śāntimārgamaṇḍala*) or on partial, esoteric teachings.
"From 'At that time, Kāśyapa' onwards is the second section, his self-deprecation.
The Buddha had just praised him as being equal to the Tathāgatas above and on par with the Bodhisattvas below.
This self-deprecation is also twofold:"
First, that which was asked by One-Humble-Who-Asks could not reach [the goal] either horizontally or vertically; second, his vow to hear the Dharma and carry it upon his crown increased.
Regarding the first passage: being unable to fly across the great ocean means he could not reach it horizontally.
It cannot pervade the entirety of space; it does not reach its vertical limit.
The subsequent text states that "wearing on the crown" signifies protecting what is lofty and profound, while "increasing" signifies protecting what is vast and expansive.
How is this known? The text subsequently explains: "May I attain profound and vast wisdom.
From the passage beginning "The Buddha said to Kāśyapa" onwards is the second part, the formal answer to the question.
The main section is divided into two parts:
first, the sequential answers to the thirty-four questions; second, the offerings of the great assembly.
Regarding the first part, the answers: from the beginning up to the end of this chapter constitutes the answer to the question concerning longevity. This, in turn, is divided into two sections:
The first part answers the cause of long life, and the latter part answers the fruit of long life; it further explains the terminology of "cause" and "fruit.
One interpretation states:
if cause and fruit exist, one falls into the view of eternalism (śāśvata); if cause and fruit do not exist, one falls into the view of nihilism (uccheda).
If one says that the causes and effects are taught because the secret of causes and effects is revealed, this statement is somewhat superior;
if it is said that causes and effects are mentioned incidentally in order to manifest nirvana, this statement is most excellent.

Nirvana is without cause or effect; it is through skillful means that cause and effect are spoken of. By calmly suppressing [conceptual proliferation] to reveal the True Dharma, one speaks of cause and effect.
Now it is clarified that if the cause were inherently a cause and the effect were inherently an effect, one would fall into the view of self-nature (*svabhāva*).
If the effect exists because of the cause and the cause exists because of the effect, one falls into the error of other-nature (*parabhāva*).
If the cause exists because of the causal conditions of the effect and the effect exists because of the causal conditions of the cause, one falls into the error of common-nature (*sabhāva*).
Because it is neither cause nor effect, yet is called "cause and effect," it falls into the nature of causelessness.
It thus falls into both the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.
It is only by means of the four *siddhāntas* that one designates "cause and effect" to reveal that which is neither cause nor effect; therefore, it is called "cause and effect."

The preceding text is not unclear regarding the fruit, nor is the subsequent text unclear regarding the cause; these two sections are distinguished according to what is predominant and what is primary.
The initial response concerning the cause is divided into three parts:
first, the exhortation to listen; second, the formal response; and third, the discussion of the meaning.

First, the instruction to listen is given because one is about to be taught the wondrous medicine of the nectar of long life; if one covers their vessel, they will not hear it, and thus both reflection and cultivation will be lost—therefore, the assembly must be cautioned.
The *Śāstra* states: "Focus your gaze and listen to the Dharma as one who drinks when thirsty; with a single mind, enter into the words and their meaning," and so forth.
From the passage beginning with "the karma for long life attained by the Tathāgata" onwards constitutes the direct answer.

The text consists of five pairs: first, pointing to the person who has realized the fruit and the person who follows the cause to define their karma; second, pointing to the dharma that is the fruit and the dharma that is the cause to exhort them toward their karma; third, clarifying one's own practice and the transformation of others to verify their karma; fourth, employing metaphors and their applications to illustrate their karma; and fifth, showing the retribution of the fruit and the provisional rewards to conclude their karma.
The person of the first fruit is the Tathāgata;
the person who relies on causes is the Bodhisattva.
If one lacks this karma, one is not called a Bodhisattva; if the Buddha lacked this karma, he would not be called a Tathāgata.
When this karma acts as a cause, it is called a bodhisattva;
when this karma acts as a fruit, it is called a Tathāgata.

If karma were fixed as a cause, it could not become a fruit; if karma were fixed as a fruit, it could not become a cause. One should know that this karma is neither cause nor fruit, yet it is capable of being both cause and fruit.

Although there are causes and effects, causes and effects are ungraspable; the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; even bodhisattvas of diligent application cannot know it, so how could it be fathomed by the darkened minds of ordinary people?
Unable to restrain myself, I shall now set forth what I have heard.
Regarding the dharmas of the fruit, these are bodhi.
Regarding the dharmas of the cause, these are the three types of wisdom.

Listening to this is the wisdom of hearing; receiving it is the wisdom of reflection; and explaining it to others is the wisdom of cultivation. If bodhi lacks these activities, its fruit cannot be attained; if the three wisdoms lack these activities, their causes cannot be established.
Supreme and without peak, vast and without limit, it accomplishes much; what are its characteristics?
If karma can destroy karma, this is called the destruction of karma.
From non-abiding action, all actions are established; this is the establishment of action.
To neither destroy nor establish, yet to destroy while establishing, is correct action.

Such correct action cannot be said to be three, nor can it be said to be one. To speak of it as one is to lose its function; to speak of it as three is to harm its essence. It is the function within the essence, and the essence within the function.
Functioning as the very essence itself, it is said that this karma can serve as the cause for Bodhi and attain the fruit of Bodhi.

Before the Path, the essence and function are extensively explained to people; after the Path, the essence and function are such that function is itself the essence—neither cause nor fruit, neither self nor other.
Therefore, the preceding passage states, "By the power of the jewel, the water immediately becomes clear"; is this not the function [arising] from the very essence?
The subsequent passage states, "Great kindness and great compassion are called Buddha-nature"; is this not the essence [manifesting] through the function?
The third section, from "Good son, by my cultivation... onwards, cites one's own practice and the transformation of others to establish the accomplishment of the activity.
Because I cultivated it, I attained Bodhi; this is the realization of the essence and function prior to the Path.
Now, I further expound this Dharma extensively for the sake of others; this refers to the essence and function [attained] after the realization of the Way.

However, since my fruition was accomplished long ago, the karma prior to that realization no longer pertains to the present time. Therefore, it should be known that this clarifies the past Dharma-gate in order to answer the initial question.
Within the four similes, there is first the illustration and then the application of the illustration.
"Like a prince" is a partial simile for the stage prior to the Path.
The king represents the Bodhisattva; the son represents sentient beings; committing a crime represents the arising of evil causes; and being imprisoned represents the undergoing of evil effects.
Compassion is like a natural bond of kinship; loving concern is like uprooting the causes of evil; and personally visiting the place of confinement is like uprooting the effects of evil.
Now, as for a prince, though he is of the Kṣatriya caste, he may become a prisoner for his crimes; sentient beings are likewise:

though they share the same Buddha-nature as the Buddha, they are constrained by their sinful karma and wander through birth and death. Thus, they both possess Buddha-nature and yet seem to lack it—just as a prince may be a prisoner, and a prisoner may be a prince. For this reason, compassion provides rescue and deliverance.
The passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva is also like this" applies the analogy.
Generally, three dharmas are cited to apply the analogy:
first, the stage of the only child (ekaputraka-bhūmi) applies the great compassion of identical essence (*tatsvabhāva-mahākaruṇā*), illustrating how function is inherent in that very essence.

Next, the four immeasurable minds uproot the causes of suffering and provide the causes of goodness; they uproot the fruits of suffering and provide the fruits of happiness. With great joy and sublime equanimity, how much more so when their application is inseparable from their essence—such that they are the essence through their very application.
Third, the Four Great Vows apply universally to the Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the Truth of Suffering, it extends beyond the four realms of existence; regarding the Truth of Accumulation, it extends beyond the ten unwholesome actions; regarding the Truth of the Path, it extends beyond mere preceptual virtue; and regarding the Truth of Cessation, it extends beyond the extinction of ashes.
The scope of the great vows encompasses all things; therefore, three dharmas are employed to provide analogies for karmic action.

Regarding the fifth point, which concludes with the two types of retribution: the Sage takes wisdom as his life-force, and because his wisdom is sovereign, his lifespan is long; this is an analogy for the fruit of retribution.
"Receiving pleasure in the heavens is like the provisional fruit," and so forth.
From the passage "At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha" onwards is the formal discussion, consisting of four rounds of question and answer.
In the first section, there is first the question and then the answer.
The question contains three intentions:
first, stating a lack of understanding; second, asserting that [the position] is untenable; and third, formally raising an objection.
Regarding "not understanding": since the karma of longevity is neither cause nor effect, and neither self nor other, it is said to be profound and hidden.

Next, regarding "inappropriate": on the ground of the "only son," there is great compassion of identical essence (*samatā-karuṇā*) which is devoid of both attachment and aversion; how, then, could there be the notion of "son"?
If one conceives of [the mother] as being the same as one's child, this is the arising of attachment. How can there be attachment toward that which is of the same substance?
How can there be attachment toward that which is of the same substance? Therefore, it is said that this is not appropriate.
Regarding the third difficulty: those who break the precepts or commit acts of rebellion ought to be punished; yet if punishment contradicts compassion, how can one speak of "regarding all equally"?
If there is equality, there would be no punishment; so how can one speak of "governing"?

To govern while being partial violates compassion; thus, governance and compassion both deviate from their essential nature, mutually obstructing one another, making it difficult for [the state] to arise therefrom, and so forth.
Next, the Buddha answered these three points with a single statement, saying:
"I regard all sentient beings as my only child."
As in the case of Rāhula, this is the compassion of the same essence.
This compassion is pure, subtle, and supreme; it is not the compassion of defiled attachment.
This compassion is profound and hidden; it is not only difficult to understand, but also difficult to explain.
Function is identical to essence; thus, one may regard others with impartiality, just as one regards Rāhula.
Since function is identical to essence, compassion is likewise so.
The single phrase that answers three questions has its meaning in this.

However, while Kāśyapa asked about the bodhisattva’s cultivation of loving-kindness—which pertains to the stage prior to the Path—the Buddha answered with the fruit of loving-kindness realized after the Path, saying: "I regard all sentient beings as my only child."
Citing the latter response to the former, the preceding and succeeding parts do not differ.
Next, from the point where "Kāśyapa spoke again" onward, this constitutes the second question and answer; first the question is posed, followed by the answer.
In the initial question, an ancient event is cited to challenge the present meaning.
The story of the wrestler who, lacking compassion, crushed the earthen toy of a novice monk until the boy’s life was cut short—this is the ancient event.

If one relies on the Buddha’s power, it is as if the Tathāgata were to dispatch harm or injury, or release poison against his compassion, suddenly violating the [feeling for] his only son; this would contradict the present meaning.
Next, within the Buddha’s response, he clarifies the compassion of the three periods of time as threefold:
first, he clarifies that the "child" refers to a past event, and answering regarding this matter corresponds to the compassion of the past.
The youth and Vajrapāṇi are both illusory beings created by transformation; using an illusory vajra to destroy an illusory life—how could there be anything real in this?
To employ expedient means to punish evil is precisely the Great Compassion that uproots the causes of suffering;
to provisionally assume a form to rescue those in peril is precisely the Great Benevolence that bestows the fruits of happiness.
Supreme compassion and supreme skillfulness do not pertain solely to the meaning of having only one son; what, then, are they?
Another interpretation states:
even when observing the capacities of others, he caused harm to five hundred practitioners of pure conduct; thus, there were indeed instances where he performed harmful deeds.
If one applies this interpretation, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Next, from the section beginning with "Kāśyapa," the compassion of the present life is elucidated;
the "Original Ground" (Mūlabhūmi) refers to the practice of compassion through the three types of action.
Furthermore, there are three [points]:

first, the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings with the thought of them as his only son; even those who slander the Dharma, icchantikas, those with false views, or those who violate the precepts are all regarded as his only son, let alone others.
The mind being constantly impartial is what constitutes mental loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Following this, from the passage beginning "For example, like a king," the practice of verbal loving-kindness is clarified; this is further divided into two parts:
first, citing the laws of the state; second, clarifying the Buddha-dharma; and finally, concluding with the administration of punishment.
First, the severe punishments of the state take cruelty as their foundation;
second, the Dharma-net of the Buddha takes compassion as its principle.
This contrasts the improper to manifest the correct.
The Buddha-dharma has three [stages]:
if one is expelled (*pārivāsika*), they are permanently excluded from the assembly.
If one undergoes the four *karmavācanā* procedures but is not excluded from the assembly, they simply may not serve as the presiding officer of a *karman*.
Regarding the fourteen types of administrative officials, they are now collectively termed *karmavācanā*, yet in reality there are degrees of gravity among them.
The first mentioned, the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), is precisely what is referred to in the Vinaya as the *niḥsaraṇa-karman* (act of expulsion).

The two bhikṣus, Aśvakapada and Pūrṇaśaya, had defiled families and committed evil deeds within a village; the Buddha therefore ordered that they be subjected to the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) and expelled from this village.
"Rebuke" refers to the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) found in the Vinaya.

The bhikṣu Paṇḍuluka delighted in quarreling, inciting strife, and instigating disputes between two parties; he would go to the city to lodge complaints, repeatedly doing so by fastening legal petitions to his waistband.
The Buddha ordered that the *kukṛtya-karman* (act of censure) be performed against him—a rite of painful and urgent admonition.
"To set aside" refers specifically to the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence).
The bhikṣu Śreyaka was frivolous by nature; he repeatedly committed offenses requiring confession and frequently troubled the Saṃgha.

The Buddha ordered that the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) be performed for him, requiring him to rely upon a person of firm integrity and virtue to provide guidance and instruction, so as not to commit offenses repeatedly.
"Bringing forth the charge" refers to the *avakāśana-karman* (act of subduing the mind) found in the Vinaya.
The bhikṣu Uttara was the master of the Āmra Monastery for the householder Citta, and he constantly received excellent food.
Later, when the householder encountered Upasena, he made offerings to him at his own home, without informing the monastery’s master.
Uttara became angry and said to the householder, "Although the food and drink are delicious, they lack the sesame *modaka*.
This was because, when the householder was young and poor, he had once engaged in this very trade; thus, Uttara stung him with these words.

The householder then spoke a parable: "It is like a chicken and a crow that have together produced a single chick; it may utter the cry of a chicken or the sound of a crow. So too, you may speak words that are good or words that are evil."
Because this bhikṣu’s parents lived in another country, he was thus ridiculed.

The Buddha, knowing this, ordered that the *adhyāśaya-karman* (ceremony of humble submission) be performed for him; one person from the Saṃgha was sent to lead this bhikṣu to the layperson’s residence to perform an act of humble repentance.
"Unwillingness to see [one's fault]" constitutes the three types of *pravāsanīya* (expulsion).
Among the eight categories of disciplinary measures (*aṣṭadharmāḥ*), these three expulsions are clarified:

first, expulsion for not seeing [the fault]; second, expulsion for not confessing; and third, expulsion for not abandoning evil and heterodox views. Within this context, there is no mention of the term "not confessing."
Regarding this single matter of *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), the instructional methods differ.
One must not assume that "not seeing" is identical to the *adarśanīya-karman* (act of suspension for refusal to see an offense).
The bhikṣu Chandaka repeatedly committed offenses, and the other bhikṣus exhorted him to repent.
He replied,
"I do not see my offense. The Buddha ordered that he be subjected to the formal act of *apraticchanna-ukkhepanīya-kamma* (suspension for not acknowledging an offense).
Those who did not repent returned.
Chanda had repeatedly committed offenses; when others exhorted him, he replied, "Although I see my transgressions, I am unable to repent."
The Buddha ordered that he be subjected to the *apraticchanna-āpatti-pārivāsa* (exclusion for not confessing an offense). He was then subjected to the *nihsargika-pārivāsa* (expulsion).
Since he had not abandoned his evil views, he was subjected to the *drṣṭy-asthita-pārivāsa* (exclusion for not removing wrong views).

When the incident arose, Līlā said that desire does not obstruct the Path; though he was admonished three times, he did not comply, and thus he was subjected to the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment) for his unremovable evil and heterodox views.
From the passage beginning "Good son, for what reason the Tathāgata... onwards, this summarizes the meaning of the offense of having no remedy (*apratikarmaka*).
