Since "measurable" and "immeasurable" refer merely to the two conditions of small and large, why should they be grounds for rejoicing?
Furthermore, since that which is measurable is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how can you say that three are conditioned and one is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
If that were so, the meaning of "conditioned" would not be established.
If the immeasurable were unconditioned, how could there still be the death and rebirth of transformation?
The explanation says:

Because it is not produced by means of a fragmented body or life-force, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*); yet, it is not devoid of the three characteristics [of arising, abiding, and ceasing].
If that were so, it would truly not be unconditioned.
If the unconditioned is not established, then the uncreated (*akṛta*) is also undermined.

Although the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* contains this name and teaching, it was intended for a specific occasion; one cannot employ the doctrine of the four truths of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) to explain the text of this sūtra, as their meanings do not coincide.

Furthermore, the five periods and four truths are clarified: in the first period, they are treated in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), such as the definition of suffering as the characteristic of oppression, and so forth;

from the second through the fourth periods, they are treated in terms of principle (*li*), such as the meaning of suffering being the thorough penetration of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as empty and non-existent—here, "meaning" (*yi*) is equivalent to "principle."
The explanation states:

At the time of entering contemplation, names are extinguished and marks are severed; these four matters do not exist. It is only by relying on the four skillful means that one speaks of the Four Truths.
Just as one enters the truth upon seeing it, there are no eight patiences or eight knowledges, but rather one contemplates solely cessation.
Regarding the term "patience-wisdom" (*kṣānti-jñāna*), it is designated by way of its skillful means (*upāya*).

For this reason, during the first four periods, the Buddha-nature was not clearly revealed, and the Buddha’s mind was not yet satisfied; it was in the fifth period that wisdom was established as the truth.
The text states: "Because there is no suffering yet there is reality, it is called Buddha-nature; thus, the Buddha-mind rejoices.
Now I ask: if this is still the same as the previous [discussion on] the finite and the infinite, it has already been refuted as before.
If it is neither finite nor infinite, what other truth could it be such that it has no distinct name?
Since there is no distinct name, there is no distinct principle; furthermore, why employ this to explain the present sutra?
Now it is clarified that this chapter shares both similarities and differences with the "Chapter on Noble Practices" (Śrīkṣānti-parivarta).
While the "Noble Practices" fully elucidates four sets of the Four Truths, the present text elucidates only the single reality of the Four Truths.
What are its characteristics?

The true mark of Buddha-nature pervades all places; only when one clearly realizes the true mark regarding these four matters can it be called "Truth. If one does not realize it, it is inverted and not Truth.
The sutras contain explicit teachings; why then should you fall into confusion?
It is said that knowing the Tathāgata’s profound realm—the eternally abiding and unchanging, subtle, and secret *dharmakāya*—is what is called the Truth (*satya*).

This is merely taking the fruit of Buddhahood as the primary illustration; in reality, it extends to all realms of existence, including the animal and hellish states, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*). To fully realize that the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* is unchanging is called the Noble Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-āryasatya*). To give rise to true wisdom within impurity and not destroy the True Dharma is called the Noble Truth of Origination (*samudaya-āryasatya*). To recognize the *tathāgatagarbha* amidst cessation and annihilation is called the Noble Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-āryasatya*). To clearly recognize the Triple Gem and right liberation is called the Noble Truth of the Path (*mārga-āryasatya*).
The Truths (satya) are not four in number; rather, they are called the Four Truths because they are understood by way of four aspects.

The Tathāgata appeared in the world primarily to expound these. Having previously concealed their characteristics, they are now revealed; like applying ointment to a wound or washing away filth, one’s mind is filled with joy as the True Truths are proclaimed.
The title is established based on this; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Four Truths.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the elucidation of the Four Truths; second, the acknowledgment and understanding [of that teaching].
The four truths constitute the first four chapters, each chapter containing six sections; they differ only in that some follow a sequential order while others do not.

Regarding the six sections of the Truth of Suffering: first, clarifying delusion; second, clarifying the fruit of delusion; third, clarifying understanding; fourth, clarifying the fruit of understanding; fifth, concluding with understanding; and sixth, concluding with delusion.
"One is four and four is one" is called the inconceivable; this text clarifies it.
The initial clarification of delusion is twofold:
first, directly clarifying suffering; second, explaining that because [beings] do not understand, there is suffering.
The following clarifies that suffering is of three kinds:

first, that which is suffering but neither a truth nor real; second, that which is suffering and a truth but not real; and third, that which is neither suffering nor a truth but is real, and so forth.
"Know that such a person will certainly fall" below explains the fruit of delusion.
"If there is one who is able to know" below explains understanding.
"If it passes through the ear even once" below explains the fruit of understanding.
"‘If one knows thus’ and below concludes the resolution;
‘If one does not know’ and below concludes the delusion.
Next, the chapters on collection also consist of six [sections], their sequence being as before."
This first section clarifies delusion.
The passage beginning with "Because of this ignorance" clarifies the fruit of delusion.
The passage beginning with "If there is profound wisdom" clarifies understanding.
The section beginning with "By these causes and conditions" clarifies the fruit of understanding.
Furthermore, it reiterates the former state of delusion to negate it and thereby reveal what is correct.
The section beginning with "If one can know" concludes the explanation of understanding.
"Regarding the passage 'If a person cannot' and below, the delusions are summarized.
Next, the Chapter on the Truth of Cessation also consists of six sections, with the sequence slightly different.
The first clarifies the delusions."

Regarding the statement "those who cultivate emptiness excessively," there are two types: first, those of the Two Vehicles who sink into emptiness; second, non-Buddhists who negate existence. These are those who cultivate emptiness excessively.

Next, regarding "cultivating the cessation of suffering," this refers to clear understanding; one should also say that this is directed against the Śrāvakas, while specifically addressing non-Buddhists.
There are two meanings:
first, the preceding section censured the śrāvakas; second, it shows that those śrāvakas who deviate from the principle are themselves outsiders (*bāhya*).
From the words "If there is cultivation" onwards, the text clarifies the fruit of delusion.
The section beginning with "If there is that which is not done" clarifies the understanding of the fruit.
The section beginning with "If one can thus" concludes the explanation.
The section beginning with "If there is that which cannot" concludes the discussion on delusion.
The Chapter on the Truth of the Path also consists of six sections, following the same sequence as before, with only a slight difference in the final conclusion.
First, it clarifies delusion by first presenting that which is deluded;
next, it correctly elucidates delusion itself.
The section beginning with "By these causes and conditions" clarifies the fruit of delusion.
The section beginning with "If one can resolve the mind" clarifies understanding.
The section beginning with "Riding upon this single thought-moment" clarifies the fruit of understanding.
The passage beginning with "If anyone says that the Three Jewels are impermanent" concludes the section on delusion.
The passage beginning with "If one cultivates this Dharma" concludes the section on liberation.
In reality, these conclude the Path and Cessation.
Regarding the Four Truths: since the Path and Cessation follow the [other] two truths, they should be placed fourth.
From the passage "Kāśyapa said to the Buddha" onwards, the second part concerns the comprehension and realization [of the meaning].
11. Chapter on the Four Perversions (11). Regarding the four perversions, "perversion" refers to delusion (*moha*).
The previous passage, which speaks of a drunken person’s dizziness causing the sun and moon to appear to revolve, serves to clarify the meaning of delusion.
However, the number of inversions is not fixed; they may be one, two, three, four, eight, or even many.
The first is merely ignorance, which is a false snare that entangles oneself.
The second is the attachment of views and perceptions, which leads to injury and ruin.
Third, the deluded mind is an inversion of mind, the deranged and narrow-mindedness is an inversion of perception, and the discriminative views are inversions of view;
fourth, the counterfeit arts of permanence, bliss, self, and purity are devoid of reality;
eighth, impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity are like tiles and pebbles, not the truth.
O multitude, it is only that the *nirvāṇa* and the Buddha-nature are ultimately pure, being neither inversion nor truth.
It is from the causes and conditions of delusion and awakening that one speaks of inversion and truth.

Although the teachings of former Buddhas who appeared in the world to destroy inversions remain as the Dharma in this world, as time passes and the distance from the Sage grows, people cling to the literal words and lose the intended meaning. Not knowing that the medicinal expedients have turned into poison, they give rise to the four inversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

When the Buddha first appeared in the world, he administered the medicine of impermanence and poured it out; yet when the illness was cured but the medicine remained, they clung to it as being the truth. Thus, deluded regarding the Buddha’s skillful means, they gave rise to views such as impermanence. The Buddha observed this illness and realized that he should instead apply the medicine of permanence and other such qualities to treat their disease.
If, in the future final age, views such as permanence become a sickness, only by entrusting [the teaching] to a subsequent Buddha can it be cured.
Throughout both the past and the future, these are all termed the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*).

If one treats the sickness of permanence and so forth, it is according to the ancient teachings; if one treats the sickness of impermanence and so forth, it is as in the "Chapter on Lamentation" (*Śokavarga*).
This chapter clarifies only the disease of delusion; if one understands the disease, one can then understand the medicine.
Since there is no truth apart from the overturning of perversions, and because the conditions for their cessation require separate explanation, the four perversions are elucidated here.
The eight inversions of civilization are categorized under four headings; the compilers of the sutra have abbreviated them by combining them into four.
I now follow this combined classification because it is intended to correspond with the Four Noble Truths so that they may mutually support one another.

The preceding treatise established the three aspects in their entirety, discussing in general terms the false and the correct regarding what is spoken by Māra and what is spoken by the Buddha; it specifically clarified the correct understanding through the Four Noble Truths and specifically clarified the delusions of error through the four inversions.

If one merely understands the truths and their inversions, it is like a person who enters a place while identifying it only partially; knowing it merely as a tree stump rather than as a person is not complete knowledge. Such a person is not said to be correctly and fully accomplished, and thus cannot perform wholesome deeds.

The simultaneous resolution of the false and the correct, as well as the inverted and the true, constitutes the complete accomplishment of what is right and wholesome. That which is capable of performing wholesome karma is precisely the *tathāgatagarbha*.
These factors arise in succession and combine to form the four inversions; since this meaning is thus established, it is called the "Chapter on the Four Inversions."
The text consists of two parts:
first, the clarification of the four inversions; second, the summary and understanding.
Regarding the initial section on the four inversions, it is further divided into four chapters.
The first chapter is divided into three parts:
first, identifying the state of suffering; second, identifying the essence of suffering; and third, the conclusion.
To regard that which is not suffering within the fruit of Buddhahood as suffering is itself a delusion, which ought to invite the retribution of suffering.
Thus, to say this is liberation is to give rise to the perception of pleasure within suffering.
That which is impermanent and subject to change refers to the Buddha’s *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of conditioned formations).
His relinquishing the body and entering parinirvāṇa refers to the Buddha’s *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of transformation).
He says that to regard the Tathāgata as permanent is an inversion, while to regard him as impermanent is the truth.
The passage beginning with "If I were to say... refers precisely to this inverted mind, such as conceiving the idea of suffering regarding what is pleasant, and so forth.
The perception of permanence in what is impermanent is the second inversion.
Within the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), both perceptions are presented together; within the essence (*svabhāva*), only one perception is specifically explained.

Since both were already presented above, there is no desire to further burden the text by restating the objective sphere of the inversion; later, when the essence of the inversion is clarified, it may be seen that the conclusion is likewise established.
What is called "non-cultivation" refers precisely to the non-cultivation of the wisdom of *prajñā-śūnyatā*.
The latter two inversions may be sought [in the commentary].
The second section, the comprehension and understanding, also has two parts:
First, I shall provide an understanding of the meaning, and subsequently describe the delusions.
Specifically, to deny cause and effect is termed wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); Kāśyapa has long been free from this.
Generally, however, all inverted states of mind are taken as "wrong"; in this sense, Kāśyapa still possesses such [inversions], and so forth.

12. Chapter on the Tathāgata-nature (11). Regarding this title, the term "Tathāgata" is used instead of "Buddha" to accord with the three periods of time; for all Buddhas of the three periods of time were initially designated as Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, by citing the beginning, one indicates what follows.
Also, as with the name being non-different, this refutes all theories of difference.
Since the Tathāgata is the Buddha and the Buddha is the Tathāgata, it is called the "Tathāgatagarbha Chapter"; thus it is said, "according to the four *siddhāntas*," and so forth.
Furthermore, "Tathāgata" is the supreme designation for the ultimate fruit, and its nature is the fundamental name of the ultimate principle.
Not only is the ultimate fruit called Tathāgata, but the original nature of sentient beings is also called Tathāgata.

Furthermore, "Tathāgata" refers to the fruit and "nature" (prakṛti) refers to the cause; although both cause and fruit are listed, the intent lies in the cause, and thus it is called the "Chapter on the Nature of the Tathāgata.

Moreover, because the fundamental nature of the fruit is hidden and difficult to discern, the manifest is used to designate the hidden, and thus it is called the "Chapter on the Nature of the Tathāgata."

Furthermore, the nature-principle contains and preserves all varieties of natures—good, evil, and the three vehicles; by highlighting the superior and setting aside the inferior, it is called the "Tathāgata-nature Chapter.

Moreover, the name "Tathāgata" is universal: indeed, all who possess a mind will become future Tathāgatas, the four reliances (catur-yoni) bodhisattvas are like Tathāgatas, and the Buddhas of the ten directions are all equally designated as Tathāgatas.
Regarding a single Buddha, there are the transformation, response, and recompense bodies, all of which are designated as Tathāgata.
In the present text, we specifically distinguish the Tathāgata within the *tathāgatagarbha*.

All beings within the twenty-five realms of existence possess a self; because this self is identical [to the nature of reality], it is called "Tathā" (Thus); because it reveals this "Thusness" to people, it is called "Lai" (Come). This permanence that cannot be destroyed is termed its "nature" (*dhātu*); based on this, the title is established as the "Chapter on the Nature of the Tathāgata."
One should know that this Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu).
Various masters offer different interpretations of the meaning of "garbha" (matrix/storehouse). The Śāstrins say:
The fruit of Buddhahood exists in the future and does not yet exist at the present moment; therefore, it is called a "store" (*garbha*).

Furthermore, it is said that Buddha-nature is the sentient being's mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*); this mind-consciousness is naturally capable of avoiding suffering and seeking happiness, and it is precisely this mind-consciousness [that constitutes Buddha-nature].
Kaishan said: "The claim that the six dharmas constitute Buddha-nature is entirely incorrect.
This chapter [treats] the self-nature of the Tathāgata, not the mind or spirit, nor the six dharmas."
Furthermore, while the Tathāgatagarbha is hidden, the six dharmas of the mind and spirit are all manifest;

moreover, while the Tathāgatagarbha is eternal, the six dharmas of the mind and spirit are subject to change and impermanence, having no connection whatsoever with the nature of the Tathāgata, and thus they are now all discarded.
The followers of the *Yogācārabhūmi* say:
"That which obscures the principle is called 'store' (*ālaya*).
This interpretation is not correct; my own view is as follows:
It is not that one side is non-existent; rather, it simply does not accord with the title of this chapter.
That [system] holds that afflictions and principle are distinct, and thus afflictions can obscure principle;
however, according to the sūtra, the nature of peace and bliss exists within all phenomena. How could an affliction that lacks this nature obscure a nature that is itself free from affliction?
Because they do not understand the purport of the sutras, they do not employ it.
I privately maintain that this is not merely a matter of delusion regarding the identity of nature and characteristics; what, then, would there be that is not subsumed?
"In what dharma is nirvāṇa not present?
All sentient beings are the very mark of nirvāṇa; all lands are the very mark of nirvāṇa," and so forth.
Furthermore, a commentator says:
That which has the nature of being a present fruit is external;
that which has the nature of the six dharmas is internal.
The *Dìrén* (Earth-People) say:
Delusion obscures the ālayavijñāna; this, too, is internal.
Xinghuang says:
"Neither internal nor external," as it refers exclusively to the fundamental nature (dharmatā).

The followers of the *Dharmatrāta* school (the "Earth-people") rely exclusively on what is inherently existent, while the followers of the *Vasumitra* school (the "Treatise-people") rely exclusively on conditions and causes, further relying on future fruits; yet the nature of the fruit and the nature of the fruit-of-fruits are both condemned by the Sūtra, for they are like blind men touching an elephant, failing to grasp its profound essence.

Now, it is called "Tathā" (Thusness) because the four propositions are equal, pure, and without contention; it is called "Lai" (Coming) because it skillfully manifests to sentient beings through the four *siddhāntas*; and it is called "Nature" (*prakṛti*) because it is eternal and unchanging. How could the *dharmakāya* (the Dharma-store) be the nature of only a single dharma?
Furthermore, some people maintain that the Tathāgatagarbha must necessarily exist.
This interpretation is incorrect.
The Buddha-nature is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent; how then can it be said exclusively that it exists?

Although it is not any of these four [positions], when there are causes and conditions, one may speak of it through a single gate by means of the four *siddhāntas*; therefore, it must be said that the *tathāgatagarbha* exists. It is by means of "existence" that one receives those who are nihilistic, by means of "existence" that one refutes eternalism, and by means of "existence" that one brings about awakening.
When awakening to Buddha-nature, Buddha-nature is not something that exists; the three gates are likewise so. Why then do you cling to existence and thereby harm the three gates?
It is like a person asking about a bridge—what is the use of much contention?
Now, the meaning of clarifying the Buddha-nature is as follows:
if one grasps this meaning, it exists in the original nature, in the intermediate stage, and in the ultimate fruit; it is both hidden and manifest, and both external and internal.
This is precisely the meaning of the sutra passage: "In the house there is a treasure of gold, whose size is unknown;
one who is skillfully able to excavate it and bring it forth is to be revered."
Question:
Regarding the three principles of the nature of the storehouse (ālaya), what are their similarities and differences? Answer:
It is simply a single principle.

If one wishes to differentiate it: when discussing both principle and delusion together, it is called a "storehouse" (pitaka); when not discussing delusion at all, it is called "principle"; and when it cannot be altered, it is called "nature," and so forth.
A disciple gave rise to five analogies, first asking whether there is a self within the twenty-five states of existence.
The Buddha answered by citing the example of the poor woman’s hidden treasure, clarifying that while a self exists, it is merely concealed and not manifest.
If that is so, why was this not stated earlier?
The Buddha raised the analogy of poison being applied because the chronic illness had not yet subsided, and thus the breasts could not be washed.

The two illnesses—the former and the latter—are discussed in terms of sentient beings, while the concealment and manifestation, as well as the application of poison and the washing, are discussed in terms of the Buddha’s teaching.
If that is so, for what reason are sentient beings divided into the six realms with such vast differences in their ascent and descent?
The Buddha cited the cause of losing a pearl during a fight, which led to unequal feelings of sorrow and joy.
If that is so, why do they fight?

The Buddha raised the example of sweet medicine remaining truly pure while on the mountain; it is only when brought into contact with those of meager virtue that it turns into something salty or sour.
If that is so, since the true flavor does not change, who could possibly harm it?
If it were impossible to injure or wound, there would be no offense of killing.

The Buddha cited the example of a sharp pickaxe that can pierce stone and sand but cannot damage a diamond; just as the Buddha cannot be harmed, yet one incurs the sin of rebellion by giving rise to a hostile mind toward him;
so too, while his nature cannot be destroyed, one incurs the offense of violating the aggregates (skandhas) by destroying them.
However, a single answer would suffice for understanding; why then are they presented in such rapid succession?
It is solely because the Buddha-nature is difficult to clarify, requiring ten thousand axes to split a tree.
The arising of these five analogies is the result of his ingenious thought, and for this reason they are preserved here, and so forth.
However, this single chapter answers the two preceding questions:
first, it answers how one performs wholesome karma; second, it answers how one is able to see the nature that is difficult to see.
These two aspects complement one another, for it is precisely through wholesome karma that one is able to see the nature.
Nature arises from wholesome karma; karma begins and nature ends, so this chapter is titled according to its conclusion.

Regarding those who explain the meaning of wholesome karma: it is provisionally named that the practitioner is able to govern both good and evil. By governing what is good, one refines the mind and spirit and attains perfect enlightenment.
A proponent of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* asks:
"Is the provisional person who exists within birth and death the Buddha-nature? He answers:
If one cannot obtain this Buddha-nature, then one likewise cannot obtain a self.
Since there is no self, who would govern wholesome karma?
Furthermore, you clarify that the "provisional person" (prajñapti-pudgala) is not autonomous, whereas the "self" (ātman) is autonomous; these two matters are mutually contradictory.
The *Diren ming* states:

"The essence of the dharma-realm possesses both good and evil functions; this essence and its functions are fully present even within delusive afflictions, just as gold covered by earth cannot be destroyed."
If delusive confusion were thus, this activity would be useless; how could it perform karma?

To clarify this point, as the sutra says that a treasury of gold cannot be seen, at such a time one cannot perform wholesome karma. Once the treasury has been excavated, what further need is there for wholesome karma to weed out the weeds and filth?

The functioning of the Hīnayāna is not a wholesome karma; rather, it is like a stranger using skillful means to show one's son that there is a treasure of gold buried in the house and instructing him to dig it up—this is precisely the meaning of being able to perform wholesome karma.
If categorized according to the six stages, the first stage is incapable and the final stage is unnecessary; the four intermediate stages constitute the stage of performing action.

If categorized according to the four propositions, the first [stage] conceals incapacity, the second manifests necessity, and the third—where both are concealed and manifested—is precisely the stage of performing action.
The response regarding wholesome karma is further divided into two parts:
first, clarifying that Buddha-nature acts as the condition for wholesome karma; second, clarifying that Buddha-nature directly gives rise to wholesome karma.
Regarding the first point—that it acts as the condition for wholesome karma—there are again two sub-sections:
First, the clarification of karmic conditions; second, the discussion of doctrine.
Within the first section on karmic conditions, there is further question and answer.

The question arises from the preceding "Chapter on the Four Perversions": although all worldly beings speak of a self, it is not called Buddha-nature; the supramundane true self is what is called Buddha-nature.
For this reason, he raises the question:
"If there were a fixed self within the twenty-five realms of existence, then 'existence' would not be existence;
if there were no fixed self, who would perform wholesome karma?"
Therefore, when it was asked whether there is a self within the twenty-five states of existence, the Buddha answered with two parables.
The first parable clarifies that what is originally present cannot be seen; the second parable explains that [the self] cannot be immediately described, thereby resolving the doubt.
The initial analogy consists of the subject (*dharma*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*).
The exposition of the subject is twofold:
first, that which exists inherently; second, that which is invisible.
However, the Buddha-nature is neither original nor future; it is spoken of for the sake of conditions.
The subsequent analogy consists of four parts:
first, an analogy for its inherent existence; second, an analogy for its being invisible; third, an analogy for its being evoked by conditions; and fourth, an analogy for its manifest exposition.

The meaning of the initial passage is as follows: it is called "poverty" because the conditions and causes are deficient; it is called a "woman" because she possesses the power of procreation; it is called a "house" because she dwells within and relies upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); it is called "gold" because she possesses the true Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*); it is called a "treasury" because this nature is all-encompassing; and it is called "abundant" because this nature is vast and extensive.

Next, regarding "the family members, both great and small, who do not know": the traditional interpretation holds that the noble ones of the four fruits are the "great" and the ordinary beings of the three realms are the "small"; all of these do not know.
The proponents of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* say: "To claim that only Bodhisattvas are great and only Śrāvakas are small is likewise ignorance.

Now, it is clarified that humans and devas are small while the two vehicles of analytical emptiness (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*) are great; the two vehicles of analytical emptiness are small while the two vehicles of essential emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) are great; the Śrāvaka of mere emptiness is small while the Bodhisattva of mere emptiness is great; the Bodhisattva of mere emptiness is small while the Bodhisattva who has emerged into the provisional (*niryāta-prajñapti*) is great—all of these [positions] remain unknown to them.
3. "At that time, there was another person" who departed; this illustrates the conditions that provoke [the teaching].
Within this, the dialogue first employs the Lesser Vehicle to accommodate him, which is why it says, "weeding out the weeds and filth."
Because he was unwilling to accept it, he said he could not.
If one were to show gold to his son, that would be due to the power of transformation.
To desire to precede others is itself to put oneself last.
4. "This person" then departs and explains it clearly.
The third section, the application of the analogy (*upanaya*), has two parts:
first the application, followed by the correspondence (*yoga*).
The application [to the teaching] is as follows.
The second analogy consists of two parts:
first, the illustration; second, the application.
The initial analogy consists of four parts:

first, clarifying the arising of the disease of the self; second, expounding the medicine of non-self; third, the cessation of the disease of the false self; and fourth, the emergence of the teaching of the true self.
The meaning is the same as in the *Śokānuśaya-sūtra*; however, that parable is explicit while this one is implicit.
Regarding the "woman" and the "skilled physician," there are four masters who offer explanations.
The first says:
The woman is a metaphor for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and the physician is a metaphor for the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Another interpretation states:
the woman is a metaphor for ultimate wisdom (jñāna), and the physician is a metaphor for expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna).
The third says:
"The woman represents the former Buddha, and the physician represents the latter Buddha.
The fourth says:
The woman is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom, and the physician is a metaphor for the opportune conditions.

In the preceding passage, the poor woman was used as a metaphor for the bodies of sentient beings; since this woman is not described as poor, she is employed here as a metaphor for the superior response of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The procreation of a single son is likened to sentient beings receiving the teaching and giving rise to understanding; because this understanding is slight, they are called infants.
Because they cling to false permanence, they are said to have fallen ill.
Next, from "This woman was distressed" onwards, there is an allegorical exposition on the medicine of non-self, which is further divided into three parts:
first, the Buddha’s wisdom observing the capacities of beings; second, providing transformation according to those capacities; and third, severing false notions of self.
Regarding the first passage: because expedient wisdom gives rise to compassion, it is said that there is "grief and affliction.
Because one seeks those with the capacity for non-self (*anātman*), it is said that one "seeks a physician.
Next, once the skilled physician has arrived, the capacity [of the patient] is immediately reached and transformation is applied.
The provision of three kinds of medicine is an analogy for the threefold cultivation of impermanence.
From the passage "Then he addressed the woman" onwards, there is the teaching to sever the false notion of self.
Within this context, milk serves as an analogy for the true self.
Because the true self is not subject to time, it is said that one should not give rise [to conceptualization].

Regarding the analogy of bitter-tasting milk: this illustrates how the absence of self (anātman) covers over the true self, just as bitterness and sweetness are diametrically opposed in their natures.
In the previous combination of the three medicines, why is there also milk?
This too is the bitter taste of non-self (*anātman*), which is contrary to the notion of permanence.
Third, from the passage "the child was thirsty and exhausted" onwards, it is a metaphor for the cessation of the illness of false selfhood.
First, the sickness and the breath are clarified; next, the medicine and its elimination are clarified.
Because the true self arises through conditions, it is called "thirst and exhaustion"; because the self and non-self are mutually contradictory, it is called "poisonous vapors.
Non-self serves as the remedy for the false; when the false is eliminated, the medicine subsides, and thus it is called "the elimination of the medicine."
The four mothers then washed their breasts, which is analogous to the arising of the teaching of the True Self.

Furthermore, there are four aspects: first, the explanation; second, the contradiction with worldly sentiments; third, the repeated explanation; and fourth, the reception and practice, as can be seen.
"Next, 'the Tathāgata is likewise' is the application of the analogy.
However, it applies only to the two medicines and not to the two illnesses.
The original intent was to resolve the doubt regarding the difference between self and non-self; therefore, the medicines are applied."
Treating illness is peripheral; therefore, it is not appropriate.
The same applies to the "Lamentation" (Śoka).
Question:
Regarding the statement, "The hidden name is the Tathāgatagarbha; I am the Buddha-nature," does this mean that all sentient beings possess my nature? Answer:
All sentient beings indeed possess this nature, yet they are not yet Buddhas; therefore, while there is "I," it is not yet the virtue of "I."
Why is this? Because persons are distinct while dharmas are universal.
Because dharmas are universal, there is self-nature and there is a self.
Because individuals are distinct, [the Buddha] is neither a person nor a virtue.
Question:
Since the Dharma is the Dharma of a person, and there was previously no distinct person, whose Dharma is it?
The commentary states:
"The dharmas belong to the dharma-nature," and so forth.
From the passage "Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha" onwards is the second section: the discussion of principles through questions and answers.
Regarding the initial inquiry: previously, it was explained that within the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) there is a self; now, this doctrine is challenged.
First, there is a general proclamation of non-existence.
Following the phrase "For what reason," there are twelve specific challenges, which together constitute four points of argumentation.
The first four objections concern the fruit; the next two concern the cause; the third and fourth objections again concern the fruit; and the final two objections concern the locus.
The first consists of two pairs: namely, birth and death, and distinction and superiority-inferiority, which are evident.
Next, there are two further difficulties:
the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) and so forth pertain to unwholesome causes, while being under the influence of alcohol pertains to unwholesome conditions;

this is evident. Regarding the fourfold difficulty concerning the threefold fruit: first, it refers to the fruit of suffering; second, it refers to the conditions for suffering; third, it refers to forgetfulness; and fourth, it refers to recollection.
Regarding the four points of censure and the two difficulties: where does the first difficulty specifically lie?
Does the second difficulty pervade the entire body?

Alternatively, one might formulate six pairs to constitute twelve difficulties; or one might apply ten difficulties to challenge the present function [of the breath] and two difficulties to challenge its location, and so forth.
The section beginning with "The Buddha said" is the response;
it answers the twelve difficulties.
First, two analogies are presented to answer the inquiry regarding its present function; second, the analogy of the sharp hoe answers the inquiry regarding its location.
Regarding what is called the "objection based on manifest function": if the true self were permanent, it should be without arising or ceasing.

Next is the objection concerning distinctions of superiority and inferiority. The Buddha’s intended response was that the true self indeed exists, but because it is shrouded by hatred and delusion, one is unable to perceive it; therefore, there is death, rebirth, ascent, and descent.
The former analogy refers to gaining and then losing; the latter analogy refers to losing and then gaining.
Yet, regarding this wondrous understanding, how can one suddenly speak of "losing" it when ordinary beings have not yet attained it?

This is a statement concerning the nature of reality (*dharmatā*): because one ought to attain but does not, one speaks of "gaining and then losing. There is no separate gain that exists apart from regaining what was lost; there is no separate loss that exists apart from losing what was gained. Thus, in gaining there is nothing gained, and in losing there is likewise nothing lost, and so forth.
Within the first two similes, the first simile consists of three sections: the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).

The analogy has four parts: first, the principle of the originally existing nature; second, the arising of delusion upon encountering conditions; third, the mutual invocation of the faculties and the conditions; and fourth, the Sage’s response to destroy the delusions.
Regarding the phrase "royal household" in the initial passage, it refers to the domain governed by the Buddha.
As for the "wrestlers," they are a metaphor for sentient beings who possess the capacity to subdue Māra and restrain external adversaries; hence, they are called wrestlers.
The space between the eyebrows is the Middle Way.

As for the "Vajra-jewel," some say it refers to principle (*li*), some say it refers to understanding (*jie*), and others say it refers to the perfect purity of both principle and understanding, which cannot be destroyed, just like a Vajra-jewel.
Regarding "next, with other strongmen": this refers to encountering conditions that give rise to delusion, thereby losing the fundamental principle.
This further has two parts:
first, the arising of delusion; second, the loss of the principle.
Regarding the phrase "the other wrestlers" at the beginning of the text: this refers to the celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, and various evil associates, and so forth.

Regarding "wrestling and grappling": the views of annihilationism and eternalism deviate from correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), whereas correct contemplation destroys annihilationism and eternalism; therefore, it is called "grappling."
"Touching it with the head" means that by touching it with the body-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one attains liberation through the Middle Way.

The subsequent section, "The pearl upon his forehead," clarifies that he has lost the correct principle and is submerged within a body of false views characterized by the extremes of nihilism and eternalism.
Third, having a wound at that location refers to the experience of suffering through karmic conditions.
Second, seeing injury to one's correct understanding as a wound—formerly it was said that experiencing the fruit of the suffering of birth and death constitutes the wound.
He immediately summoned a skilled physician to invoke the Buddha.
At that time, there was a wise physician who, through his holy wisdom and penetration, understood that the loss of principle had invited suffering.
He then remained still, clearly discerning what was a loss and what was not.
4. From "At that time, the skilled physician" onwards, the teaching is presented to shatter delusions, which is further divided into two parts:
first, an analogy for partial teaching; second, an analogy for complete teaching.
Regarding the initial partial teaching: the doctrine of non-self is used to examine and rectify errors, just as one searches for a pearl.
The strongman answered in astonishment; this is likened to receiving the teaching and practicing the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).
Because he attained liberation from delusion, it is said that he "answered in astonishment.
That which is not a magical illusion is precisely the contemplation of non-self.
To regard whatever exists as impermanent is the contemplation of impermanence (*anicca*).
To regard sorrow and weeping as suffering is the contemplation of suffering (*dukkha*).
This is explained as a partial teaching (*pāṭiyekka-dhamma*).
Next, from "At that time, the skilled physician" onwards, there is an allegorical exposition of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), which is further divided into four parts:
first, the teaching; second, non-acceptance; third, repeated teaching; and fourth, immediate acceptance. This allegorically illustrates how the Buddha-nature is not accepted at the outset.
Regarding the phrase "within the skin" in the initial text, it means hidden within the [extremes of] annihilationism and eternalism.
Regarding "manifesting externally," the traditional explanation states:
"the future fruit exists in the present."
Xinghuang said: "The Buddha’s wisdom is silent illumination.
Now, it is clear that the nature and principle are empty and pervasive throughout all places; this is what manifests externally as reflections."
Next, from "At that time, the strongman" onwards, it describes sentient beings who do not accept [the teaching].
The older commentary states:
"The interior of the skin is a metaphor for the present; the interior of the sinews is a metaphor for the future."
If it were in the present, why would one not break through delusion and emerge?
If it were in the future, it should not be visible.
Xinghuang said:
When delusion is slight, it is called "skin"; when delusion is heavy, it is called "sinew.
Third, the physician's departure with the mirror represents the Tathāgata’s repeated instruction.

The mirror is a metaphor for the circular scripture; it reflects the face of the faithful mind, where the patterns are clear and the principles manifest, such that faith and the truths are clearly understood.
Upon seeing this, the four strongmen immediately believed and accepted it.
Following the section beginning with "Good sons," the parables are correlated;
however, only three are correlated, while the first is not.
The first section corresponds to the second [point], where encountering conditions gives rise to delusion;
this is analogous to having two [beings] in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), whereas now there is only one, who gives rise to delusion and engages in a physical struggle.
Next, from "Therefore he falls into hell" onwards, it corresponds to the third [point], which involves the loss resulting from the induction of suffering.
Within this, the preceding ten objections are answered collectively.
Regarding the third point, just as that wrestler [was struck], the fourth noble one (*ārya*) should have been told to preach the Dharma;
however, in the first instance, he was told to preach specifically.
Previously, the Buddha spoke of sentient beings practicing the contemplation of non-self; now, this merely combines with what follows.
Furthermore, there are two points to the intent:
first, the practice of the combined contemplation; second, the clarification of ignorance.
The section beginning with "Among these, the citation of the analogy" constitutes the formal correspondence.
The passage starting from "For example, those who are not noble ones" below shows that although they contemplate selflessness, they are still unable to understand it. Why is this?
If one understands the true self, then one recognizes non-self; since one does not understand the reason for the self, non-self cannot be established.
First, the analogy is restated, and subsequently it is applied.
Next, from "The Tathāgata is thus" onwards, the application is made to explain the perfection.
The preceding parables consist of four parts, yet only the latter two are combined here.
This first section combines the third part, the Tathāgata’s repeated teaching.
The passage beginning with "These sentient beings" combines the fourth part, their faith and acceptance; first the text provides the combination, and then it cites the parable as a corroboration.
In the section on "Correctly Entering," first it clarifies the lack of faith when delusions are present, and subsequently it clarifies the faithful acceptance when delusions are eliminated.
Third, it concludes with a praise of its inconceivability.
Next, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, good son," follows the analogy of the sweet medicinal herbs of the Snowy Mountains.
The old commentary says:
This assists in answering the preceding question.
Master Guan says:
It is like losing something and then finding it again.
This consists of the opening analogy and the concluding analogy. The opening analogy is divided into four parts:
First, loss; second, gain; third, repeated loss; fourth, repeated gain.
Within the initial clarification of loss, there are two parts:
first, the principle of nature (*li-xing*); second, the analysis of loss.

Regarding the initial passage: the Snowy Mountains are a metaphor for the bodies of sentient beings; the single-flavored medicine is a metaphor for the Middle Way of non-duality, hence it is called "single-flavored.
Because this principle can eliminate inverted delusions, it is called "medicine" and is termed the "flavor of bliss."
That its flavor is extremely sweet means that the teaching and the principle correspond to one another; this is the sweetness of the principle within the joy of the teaching.
Next, the phrase "beneath the dense thicket" clarifies that it is obscured by afflictions (kleśa), which is why the principle is lost.
The afflictions are profound and inverted delusions are intermingled, causing one not to see.
Following the section "Someone hears the fragrance," this is the second part, which clarifies the attainment of light; it further has two sections:
first, partial attainment, and second, complete attainment.
Regarding the statement in the *Chufen* (Initial Section) that "one who smells the fragrance" is mentioned, one interpretation says:
it is called "smelling the fragrance" because one relies on the sutras to know [the truth] with faith.
A second interpretation says:
Because the vision of Bodhisattvas in the Ten Abodes is not yet clear, it is said that they "smell the fragrance.
The section beginning with "In past lives" clarifies the second point: the full attainment;
that is to say, the former Buddhas have already realized this principle.
The construction of wooden tubes refers to the teaching itself.
It is likened to the "revealing cause" (liao-yin) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); because the cause receives the fruit, it is called "connecting the medicine.
"In every place" means cultivating the causes of the ten stages throughout successive lifetimes in the past.

Regarding "flowing from the ground and collecting in wooden tubes": because cause and effect correspond and the clarifying cause (*vyañjana-hetu*) is correctly applied, it is said that they "flow out.
Third, from "Once the king has passed away" onwards, the loss is further elucidated.
This means that when the previous Buddha passed into extinction, sentient beings became heedless and gave rise to various afflictions, thereby causing them to lose it.
The six flavors are a metaphor for the six realms of existence.
The original flavor was true and correct, but after the arising of delusions, they flowed into the six realms, becoming either sour or salty.

The true flavor of this medicine remains within the mountain; this is analogous to the fact that the fundamental nature of sentient beings' bodies does not differ [from that of the Buddha], yet they appear different because they follow the currents of the six realms.

That ordinary people of meager merit fail to obtain it despite their efforts is analogous to those with attached minds who, through asceticism, meditation, and wisdom, seek the ultimate truth but are unable to find it.
This is also like various kinds of digging and excavating; one wishes to seek the fundamental nature and principle, yet finds them entirely unrelated.
Fourth, from "Furthermore, there was a holy king" onwards, it is a re-acquisition;
that is to say, the present Buddha again realizes this principle.
From "Good son" (*kulaputra*) onwards is the second section, the synthesis of the parables; however, it only synthesizes the two faults and does not synthesize the two gains.
This initial part synthesizes the fault regarding that which possesses principle.
The previous statement regarding being "beneath deep thickets" is now correlated with being "covered by the thicket of afflictions.
The previous sequential analogy regarding "no one seeing [it]" is now correlated with "sentient beings of ignorance not seeing [it]."
The section beginning with "by means of afflictions" below consolidates the third level of clarification regarding the faults.
That is to say, it addresses either acidity or salinity, directly responding to the prior question concerning the distinctions between victory and defeat.
From "The Buddha-nature is heroic and fierce" onwards is the second [section], which answers the latter two of the twelve preceding challenges regarding the question of seeking its location.
While previously there were both specific and general challenges, here the general question is directly answered.
Although this nature is discussed in terms of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the body may be destroyed while the nature cannot be destroyed.

The body is the dwelling place of the nature; the nature belonging to the body is precisely the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and the body belonging to the nature is nothing other than the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the formal exposition; second, the discussion of the meaning.
Regarding the initial formal exposition, it is divided into three sections:
first, restating that which is indestructible; second, an extensive analysis; third, a concluding summary.
From "Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha" onwards, there are two sections of doctrinal discussion consisting of questions and answers.
Regarding the question: as previously stated, since the Buddha-nature is valiant, fierce, and indestructible, there should be no sin of killing.
Next, the Buddha’s response is twofold:
first, the teaching by way of principle (*dharma*), and second, an analogy. The initial teaching by way of principle consists of four parts:
One interpretation holds that because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) can be killed, one incurs evil karma.
As for the statement "dwelling within the five aggregates," others take six dharmas to be the Buddha-nature; this is not a correct understanding of this text.
The six dharmas are nothing other than the five aggregates; how could it be possible for the five aggregates to abide within the five aggregates?
Or for sentient beings to abide within sentient beings?
If you take the mental consciousness as the Buddha-nature, then since the mind consists of four aggregates, the mental consciousness would simply be abiding within the mental consciousness itself.

Regarding his interpretation that the future fruition (*bhāvin*) constitutes the Buddha-nature: since the future fruition is contingent upon sentient beings, it is said to "abide within the five aggregates.
If this future fruition exists, it is no longer a "future fruition";
if this future fruition does not exist, to what could it be contingent?
The people of the land take the *ālaya* to be the Buddha-nature, which is shrouded by delusions.
To explain this is convenient; yet it must still face the aforementioned objection:
if there were a Buddha-nature, one should possess knowledge from the very day of birth.
I shall now explain this by means of the following passage:

Buddha-nature is neither identical to the six dharmas nor separate from the six dharmas. Because it is not identical, it is not as the various masters have interpreted; because it is not separate, it is said to abide within the five aggregates.
Speaking in terms of ultimate reality, how could Buddha-nature have either abiding or non-abiding?
These differing explanations are merely made for the sake of specific conditions; if one were to cling rigidly to them, it would obstruct the preceding and following passages of the text.
Since it is ultimately pure, how could there be internal or external, the past and the present, or abiding and non-abiding?
I submit that this teaching reaches the ultimate limit.
Furthermore, regarding "within the five aggregates," this nature exists as discussed in relation to the five aggregates, not in relation to grasses and trees.
[My] private opinion is that one who makes such a statement still relies upon expedient means (*upāya*).
Next, from "by the causal conditions of karma" onwards, the doubts are resolved.
The doubt is as follows:
some may claim that one should fall into hell solely for the act of killing; why, then, can there be twenty-five realms of existence?
Therefore, the present commentary explains:
because karmic conditions differ, the various realms of existence (gati) become distinct.

The section beginning with "those who are not noble ones" serves to distinguish them from various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) who falsely claim to have attained sainthood and hold differing conceptions of a self (ātman).
4. From "The World-transcending Mark of Self" below, the true mark of self is clarified.
Second, from "Furthermore, good son" below, there is the analogy.
This also has two parts:
First the analogy, then the application.
The initial analogy is divided into two parts:
first, an analogy for the five aggregates (*skandhas*) as being subject to destruction; second, an analogy for the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) as being indestructible.
In the first analogy, it is said that "one who well knows the hidden treasure" is like the person capable of killing;
the sharp pickaxe is like the instrument of killing, and the frequent digging into bedrock, sand, and saline soil represents the process of slaughter.
The subsequent section, beginning with "Only reaching the diamond [level]," serves as an analogy for the indestructibility of the Buddha-nature, which is evident.
In the subsequent section on "Combining," only the non-destruction is combined.
From the passage beginning with "Good son, as for the Vaipulya sutras" onwards, this is the second chapter, which correctly elucidates how the Buddha-nature can give rise to wholesome karma.
The text consists of two parts:
first, an explanation of performing wholesome karma; second, a discussion of the meaning.
Regarding the first part, some say:
The Buddha-nature is capable of giving rise [to activity]; it gives rise to the wholesome karma performed on the Right Path.
Now, observing the previous analogy, the Buddha-nature serves merely as the condition for wholesome karma;
however, the present text clarifies that one is taught to perform both wholesome and unwholesome karma by means of the Buddha-nature, and thus it is illustrated through these metaphors.
From the passage "Kāśyapa again addressed the Buddha" onwards, there are two sections of doctrinal discussion.
First, the dual inquiry regarding the sweet and the poisonous, as in the text.
Second, the Buddha’s response, which is threefold:
First, the two types of persons—the wise and the ignorant—are clarified; next, the single essence of the Triple Gem is clarified; third, the perfect contemplation of the Middle Way is clarified.

Wondrous understanding arises through this successive progression: because the wise are not deluded, they recognize the single essence of the Triple Gem through the teachings, whereby wondrous contemplation is perfected and they are able to perform wholesome karma;
the ignorant act in the opposite manner, and thus wholesome karma is not accomplished.
The first section, concerning the ignorant and the wise, consists of three parts:
first, the Buddha further questions; second, Kāśyapa answers; third, the Buddha provides an explanation.
Within the explanation, there are seven and a half verses, which are further divided into two parts:
The first four and a half lines distinguish the ignorant and the wise in pairs; the subsequent three lines exclusively clarify the wise.

In the initial passage, there are two analogies and two applications: the first line shows that those who consume the same ambrosia may have either a premature death or a long life, while the following half-verse shows that those who consume the same poison may have either death or birth.
There have been three traditional interpretations since antiquity.
The first states:
the first part equally addresses those who receive the Mahāyāna and both gain and lose from it; the latter part serves as an analogy for those who receive the Hīnayāna and both gain and lose from it.
The second says:

In terms of teacher and disciple, when the teacher expounds the Mahāyāna teaching of non-attainment, the disciple who understands it is "long-lived," while the one who is deluded is "prematurely deceased.
When a Hīnayāna teacher expounds the teaching of attainment, the disciple who forms a great understanding is "born," while the one who clings to the small teaching is "dead."
Third, this is simply a single Mahāyāna sūtra; for those who attain it, it is given the name "Amṛta" (Nectar), while for those who lose it, it is given the name "Poison.
Furthermore, it is given the single name "Amṛta" to explain that those who receive and practice it have both attainment and loss;
it is given the single name "Poison" to explain that all who receive it have both birth and death—these aspects mutually complete one another in turn.
Now, to clarify what constitutes these faults: both are designated as ambrosia and poison.
That which is cherished, attached to, and clung to is called ambrosia; that which causes injury, destruction, and ruin is called poison.

For those who have attained it, it is called both nectar and poison: it is called nectar because entering into principle gives rise to goodness; it is called poison because revealing the essence destroys evil.
Possessing these two meanings, it is called the "Teaching of Wholesome Karma.
Each section of the text contains its own corresponding analogy, which can be seen by consulting them.
It is like a leper who takes aconite and recovers from his illness, or one who, having taken poison, regains consciousness through an antidote.
For example, one who studies impermanence, suffering, and emptiness to sever delusions knows this to be a great skillful means and thereby enters the Mahāyāna.
From the passage "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" downward, the text specifically elucidates the wise.
All of these are distinguished in terms of persons: first in terms of the two vehicles, next in terms of bodhisattvas, and finally in terms of ordinary beings.

It appears that they perform wholesome karma by means of the three truths: the bodhisattva advances in wholesome karma through the Middle; the follower of the two vehicles performs wholesome karma through the Middle by means of emptiness; and ordinary beings perform wholesome karma through the Middle by means of the conventional. Thus, the intent behind citing these three types of persons may lie herein.
From the passage beginning "Kāśyapa, you should now," the second section distinguishes the Three Jewels as being of one essence (*eka-rasa*).

However, in the initial teachings of the past, the non-existent was raised to manifest the existent, and the heterodox was refuted to lead back to the orthodox; therein, the Three Jewels were clarified as having distinct essences (*pṛthag-rasa*), a meaning that is easy to understand.

In the previous section on "Longevity," the protection of the Dharma was clarified; by taking refuge in the Dharma, one recognizes that all Buddhas have already become a single embodiment of the Triple Gem, and thus taking refuge in anything else is not permitted. To take refuge in a separate entity is to take refuge in something where the precepts are incomplete.

The current text encourages one to take refuge in one's own body as the Three Jewels in a single essence, because it reveals that by perfecting wholesome karma within one’s own nature, one is also freed from the bonds of Māra;
each [text] has its own basis.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the exhortation; second, the discussion of the doctrine; and third, the acknowledgment of understanding.
Regarding the initial section, the phrase "skillfully discerning" exhorts one to discern the single essence of the Triple Gem within one's own person.
First the exhortation, then the explanation.
The first is as the text states.
As for the second, "if one can contemplate with truth," this explains the exhortation.
To attain entry into the secret treasury is the meaning of the nectar of the principle of goodness;
that such a person has already transcended the world is the meaning of destroying the poisonous medicine of evil.
Both possess attainment; this is precisely what the explicit text clarifies.

Furthermore, that which knows "I" is the Buddha Jewel, and that which belongs to "mine" is the Dharma and Sangha Jewels; although these two jewels do not differ in essence, they are explained as three from a conventional perspective.
Furthermore, the Buddha is awakening, the Dharma is non-awakening, and the Sangha is harmony; these three meanings are explained within the single Buddha-nature.
Second, from "At that time, Kāśyapa" onwards, the meaning is discussed.
There are two rounds of question and answer.
In the first, he refuses both [the precepts and refuge]; in the latter, he seeks refuge for both; the Buddha does not permit either.
The first inquiry consists of ten verses, divided into four parts:

The first one and a half lines express ignorance; the next two lines inquire about the distinct entities of the past; the third and fourth lines and a half inquire about the single entity of the present; and the final two lines conclude the inquiry by requesting an answer.
Regarding the first point, it is stated generally that [they] do not know.
Next, regarding "unsurpassed," it is specified that they do not know how to take refuge in the Buddha.
Regarding "fearlessness," it is specified that they do not know how to take refuge in the Sangha.
Regarding "How is it that those who practice non-self do not know where to take refuge in the Dharma?
Next, regarding "How is it that they take refuge in the Buddha?", the two verses ask about the former distinct entities, which are divided into three parts;
this half-verse asks about the Jewel of the Buddha.
Regarding "attaining consolation," it is as explained in the previous section on the four marks.
Next is one line questioning the Dharma,
and three and a half lines questioning the Saṃgha.
Regarding "attaining supreme benefit through transformation": it is as previously described when Mahāprajāpatī made offerings to the Saṃgha and thereby attained the merit of the Buddha-dharma.
Since the Saṃgha are those who transmit the Dharma, it is said that they attain supreme benefit through transformation.
Third, from "How is it truly spoken? below, there are four and a half lines. Within this present single essence, there are further four [sections]:
first, one and a half lines explain it in terms of the Dharma.
From "If in the future it is not accomplished" onwards, the Three Jewels are hidden within one's own body; they shall be realized in the future and can be taken as a refuge.
If it were not established, could it serve as a basis?
It would not be like relying on distinct entities according to their sequence.
There is no prior cognition, nor is there a prior appointment of self-illumination; rather, the sequence is established in dependence upon others.
Next, the one line and three phrases beginning with "How is it that she has not yet conceived? are a metaphorical explanation of conceiving a child.
The metaphor for conceiving a child necessarily lasts ten months; these ten months are a metaphor for the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
If there is one who understands, then upon the fulfillment of the ten stages, they may attain Buddhahood;
if there is no understanding, then even ten thousand months spent in vain will not lead to Buddhahood.
3. The single phrase, "The karma of sentient beings is likewise," correlates with the analogy.

4. The following line, "As the Buddha has taught," and so forth, challenges the Buddha’s non-definitive teaching—whether it leads one to return to the present or to the future—thereby causing the ignorant to transmigrate and fall into suffering.
4. The two lines following "provisional name" (prajñapti) conclude the inquiry and request for an answer.
The first line clarifies that the speaker does not know [the answer] and thus requests it; the second line clarifies that because the Buddha knows [it], he is requested to provide the answer.
Second, from "Kāśyapa, you should know" onwards, the Buddha provides the answer, responding to the four questions in reverse order.
The first line grants permission to resolve doubts, answering his request as set forth in the text.
The next verse answers the question regarding their single essence.
The preceding discussion cited pregnancy as an analogy based on the inquiry concerning the "understanding cause" (*vidyā-hetu*).

The Buddha responds with the "Middle Way correct cause" (*madhyamā-pratītyasamutpāda-samyag-hetu*), clarifying that all Bodhisattvas are no different from the Buddha. How, then, can it be said that they lack the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as a fetal womb and thus cannot serve as a refuge?
Regarding the phrase "among all bodhisattvas," there have been three traditional explanations:

first, that the character *yu* (at) is equivalent to *ru* (and), meaning "you and all bodhisattvas" and so forth; however, this would render the seventh verse's text too cramped to accommodate the character *yu*.
Second, that one should change *yu* to *ru*.
The third point need not be revised: it clarifies that all bodhisattvas are identical to this Buddha.
In the Bhadrakalpa, he is the fourth; however, in the enumeration of the seven Buddhas, he is the seventh.
"Buddha" carries the meaning of "awakening"; because he is able to awaken to the Buddha-nature, his significance is the same as that of a Buddha, and so forth.
The three lines respond to the question concerning its distinct nature.
Because one turns away from heterodoxy and enters into the orthodox, it is necessary to take refuge.
Regarding "heterodoxy," the celestial deities are treated as the Buddha-jewel.
Regarding the ritual for killing by means of incantation: one says to the sheep, "Vāsudeva shall kill you so that you may attain rebirth in heaven.
This is the Dharma Jewel. The person capable of performing the killing is the Saṃgha Jewel.
Reversing these three perversions, one returns to the three corrects.
Question:
Previously, the three corrects were used to reverse the three perversions; why not use the correct self to reverse the perverse self?
If "non-self" is used to overturn false notions of self, why not use "non-triple-gem" to overturn false notions of the Triple Gem?
Answer: There are briefly two types of remedial methods. The first, employing the gate of existence as a remedy, establishes what is correct and refutes what is false.
Second, as for employing the gate of emptiness as an antidote: one uses non-self to destroy false notions of self, each having its own particular utility.
The Three Jewels are the objective realm; since there is a basis for taking refuge in them, it is appropriate to employ the gate of existence.
"Deceit is an internal affliction; one should [overcome it] with words that are not false," and so forth.
The second half of the fourth verse, "In this way," responds to the previous statement regarding ignorance.
Now, since it says one is "able to know" and has attained fearlessness, one ought not to be ignorant.
"Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha," and so forth, marks the second question and answer.
Regarding the intent of the initial question: [Kāśyapa] wishes to take refuge in all three types of Triple Gem together;
since all are spoken by the Buddha, what should be accepted and what should be rejected?
The first line intends to rely on the distinct substance of the past; since "distinct" is the opposite of "deviant," it is precisely the correct path.
The next two lines intend to rely on the single substance during the time of its own concealment.
The final line intends to rely on the single substance during the time of manifestation through others.
Having already transcended birth and death and attained perfect enlightenment, it is said that "all that exists does not exist.

Furthermore, regarding the interpretation of "existence" (*bhava*), there is the existence of those who have currently attained Buddhahood; regarding "non-existence," there is the non-existence of the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Second, from "At that time the Buddha told... onwards, the Buddha provides the answer.
Desiring to further analyze [the matter], he states that one must not rely on it recklessly.
The text is divided into three parts:

First, when the bodies are distinct, there is reliance and non-reliance; second, when manifested as a single body, there is reliance and non-reliance; third, when hidden as a single body, this very state is what is exhorted, and one must rely upon it exclusively.
Regarding the initial [distinction] between relying and not relying, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that one need not rely [on it] now; second, clarifying that one must have relied [on it] in the past.
The first part also has two sub-sections:
Since the distinct entities of the beginning served as conditions in the past, they need not be relied upon now;
whereas at the time of relying on them in the past, one was overturning delusion, so they had to be relied upon then.
From the phrase "Why is this? onwards, the text further explains the reason for not relying [on them].

Regarding the presence of the two treasures of Dharma and Saṃgha within the Buddha-nature: it is not merely that the already perfected Buddha possesses them; rather, the Buddha-nature itself inherently contains the Dharma and the Saṃgha.
Even when one is about to attain Buddhahood, one likewise possesses these two natures, namely, the Buddha and the Dharma.
The Dharma-Buddha is non-dual, which is itself the Sangha Jewel.

Since the body already possesses these three, why must one rely on a separate entity for the Three Jewels? Furthermore, there are two reasons why one must rely [on them]: 1. One must rely on them because they serve as the objects of refuge. 2. One must rely on them because they provide the basis for generating the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta).
The first section, beginning with "In order to transform and deliver," clarifies that one must rely [on the teacher] in the past.
The subsequent section, beginning with "If one wishes to accord with," further explains the reason why such reliance is necessary.
Xinghuang elucidated the four kinds of conditions: the condition of principle, the condition of approach, the condition of opposition, and the causal condition.
The former [the condition of opposition] was used to clarify the correct by opposing the heterodox; therefore, one must rely upon it.
If one relies on Nāgārjuna’s four *saṃvṛtis*, this refers to the meaning of "remedial intent" (*pratipakṣa-abhiprāya*), and so forth.
Next, from the passage beginning with "A bodhisattva should act," it clarifies that at one time they are of a single essence; furthermore, there are two aspects:
reliance and non-reliance.
Not relying on the literal text has two parts;
first, the explanation of not relying [on the literal].
The text says: "I now take refuge in the Buddha with this body of mine. This means taking refuge in the Buddha-jewel within one's own body; how could it mean venerating another Buddha?
Next, from "For what reason" onwards, the meaning of not relying [on others] is further explained.
However, since there is no difference between myself and other Buddhas, why should one need to take refuge in others?
Next, from "If one wishes to show respect" onwards, the meaning of having a basis for reliance is clarified.
Because they are to be mutually respected, one must rely upon them.
This further consists of two parts:
first, the formal clarification; second, the explanation.
Regarding the initial clarification: the Dharma-body is the fundamental ground, while the śarīra is the response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
My intention in wishing for sentient beings to revere me is to likewise transform them and cause them to give rise to wholesome roots.
The third section, beginning from "Also cause sentient beings," clarifies what is being exhorted now; during the period of concealment, one must invariably rely on this single essence.
This passage consists of three parts:
the principle, the analogy, and the application.
The first section on the Dharma is divided into five parts;
the first is the differentiation of the single essence,
which has three sub-sections:
This initial passage indicates that one’s own person possesses the Jewel of the Buddha.
The subsequent section, beginning with "All sentient beings rely upon," indicates that one’s own person possesses the Jewel of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, there is a refuge that is not true," refers below to the Saṃgha-treasure within one's own person.
Question:
It may be so that the Dharma and the Saṃgha exist within the person; however—
What constitutes the existence of a Buddha? Answer:

The Buddha-nature within the body; this Buddha-nature is the Buddha Jewel of the Dharma-body. That which can expound this Dharma is the Dharma Jewel, and those who can receive and uphold it are the Sangha Jewel.
"He has already taken refuge in my person as the Three Jewels; how could I now not take refuge in myself?
Question:
"If the convergence of the three vehicles into one vehicle is called the 'One Vehicle,' then the convergence of the three jewels into one jewel should likewise be called the 'One Jewel.'"

If one realizes that the three vehicles converge into the One Vehicle, there are no longer any distinctions between the three vehicles; likewise, if one realizes that the Three Jewels converge into the One Jewel, there are no longer any distinctions between the Three Jewels.
The masters of the Abhidharma and the Sāṃkhya school did not dare to cite this as a precedent, but the masters of the contemplative school did so.

The Three Jewels are unified into the One Jewel; yet, from the perspective of ultimate meaning, the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are explained as distinct. This is also like unifying the Three Vehicles into the One Vehicle, while explaining the Three Vehicles as distinct from the standpoint of conventional meaning.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says, "Truly they are śrāvakas; truly they are arhats," and so forth.
From the passage beginning with "If there is discrimination" onwards, he next establishes for others the Three Jewels as being of one essence.
The entire body is Buddha; "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*).
The entire body is Dharma; "Dharma" is non-awakening.
The entire body is Sangha; awakening and non-awakening do not contradict one another.
From the passage "Regarding those born blind" onwards, three points are established as distinct entities.
This analysis is made for the sake of ordinary persons who are like those born blind.
From the passage "Furthermore, for the sake of all... onwards, four points are established as a single entity.
For those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the state of a sage, it is taught that my body possesses the single essence of the Three Jewels.
The section beginning with "In this way, the bodhisattva" consists of five pairs, which summarize these two meanings.
To perform Buddha-work for sentient beings who commit evil, one binds the self-body and speaks of it as having distinct entities;
to perform Buddha-work for those who possess wisdom, one likewise binds the self-body and speaks of it as having a single entity.
Next, the explanation by way of analogy is threefold:
first, the great general; second, the crown prince; and third, the great minister.

The reason for citing these three analogies is that the great general represents the *vidyā-hetu* (the cause of realization), the crown prince represents the *samyak-hetu* (the true cause), and the great minister represents the *pratyaya-hetu* (the conditional cause).

This is also analogous to the Three Jewels: the crown prince represents the Jewel of the Dharma, the great general represents the Jewel of the Buddha, and the minister represents the Jewel of the Sangha.
The great general harbors three intentions:
first, to suppress the enemy when facing the battlefield; second, that he is the foremost; and third, that all the troops rely upon him.
