The various troops rely upon me as the analogy for the causal condition (*pratyaya*); their achieving victory is the analogy for the consummation (*pariniṣpanna*);

and the supreme analogy is the fundamental reality (*pariniṣpanna*). It is the same with the Crown Prince: his succession to the hegemonic enterprise is the analogy for the fundamental reality; his subduing of the princes is the analogy for the consummation; and the other princes rely upon him as the analogy for the causal condition.
As with the king and the former kings, this completes the preceding analogy.
Regarding "the prince and the great minister," the prince is analogous to that which belongs to the great minister.
The three bodhisattvas are likewise so.
The application of the analogy consists of two parts:
first, the formal application; second, the concluding exhortation.

Regarding the initial application: as for what are called the "three matters" and the "one essence," the three are spoken of separately while being identical to the one essence, and upon the basis of that one essence, the meaning is explained as the three.
Just as the three dots within the syllable *nirvāṇa* are in reality not distinct from one another, so it is here.
Following the section on the "Tathāgata," there is a concluding exhortation in two parts:
first, the exhortation to abandon the three [aspects] of a separate essence from the past; second, the exhortation to adopt the three [aspects] of a single essence in the present.
The initial section on renunciation further consists of two parts:
first, presenting the Three Jewels of the past; second, exhorting one to renounce them.
Within the description of their distinct entities in the past, the head is cited as a metaphor for the Buddha Jewel, for the head is the most supreme.
The limbs, joints, hands, and feet are metaphors for the Dharma and the Saṃgha; these are shown as a ladder to transform sentient beings.
Next, from "Therefore, you now... onwards, there is the exhortation to renounce [the Lesser Vehicle].
Next, from "Regarding the Mahāyāna... onwards, there is the concluding exhortation.

One should grasp the single entity within one's own body, just as a great general or a high minister forms a resolute intention regarding their own person, without grasping at any separate entity or that which has already been accomplished by another.
From "Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha" onwards is the third section, the Acceptance and Understanding (*anujñāna*).
The text is divided into four parts:
first, the acceptance and understanding; second, the Buddha’s exhortation to uphold [the teaching]; third, the praise; and fourth, the Buddha’s confirmation.
The first section [of the initial text] also has three parts:
first, revealing the origin; second, personal realization and understanding; and third, vowing to transform others—these may be sought therein.
From "Good son" onwards is the second part: the Buddha’s exhortation to uphold [the teaching].

It simply means that one first exhorts oneself to achieve liberation and then transforms others; "liberating oneself" is ascending to the sublime secret treasury, while "transforming others" is descending to deliver the ignorant and deluded, and so forth.
From the passage beginning with "Kāśyapa spoke again," the third section is the praise.
"Praising the Buddha-nature" refers to the single essence during the period of concealment, while "the marks and signs" and so forth refer to the single essence during the period of manifestation.
From the passage beginning "At that time the Buddha praised," the fourth section describes the fulfillment of the sequence.
The passage beginning with "I shall now further [explain] for you" below constitutes the third section, which clarifies the perfect contemplation of the Middle Way.
This text is divided into three parts:
first, the promise to speak; second, the actual exposition; and third, the praise of the teaching.
Regarding the statement at the beginning that "one enters the Tathāgatagarbha," this entry into the treasury occurs through contemplation; it is not entered without contemplation.
The section following "If I were to abide... constitutes the formal exposition.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the brief exposition; second, the detailed exposition.
The brief exposition is further divided into three sections:
First, the Middle Way is indicated; second, the delusions that deviate from the Middle are clarified; third, the contemplation that destroys such delusions is distinguished.
First, the indication of the Middle Way clarifies that it is neither existent nor non-existent.
If the self were to abide, it would be clear that it does not exist.

To say that the self dwells within the body is to claim it is a permanent phenomenon that is not separate from suffering; yet permanence is the self and the body is suffering—this is precisely existence, and such existence is not the Path.
If there were no self, it would not be the case that it is non-existent.

If it were definitively non-existent, then there would be no cultivation of causes to attain results, nor would there be parents or the wholesome dharmas of the world; such non-existence is not the Path.

Having already raised the two critiques regarding existence and non-existence, the fact that neither existence nor non-existence can be established means that they are not truly existent or non-existent;

this is called the teaching of the Middle Way. Next, the section beginning with "If one says that all dharmas... clarifies the delusions that deviate from the Middle Way, which is further divided into two parts:
first, the clarification of the delusions; second, the conclusion regarding the delusions.
The first section clarifying delusion (*moha*) contains six phrases, arranged in three pairs of opposites:
three phrases involve the calculation of permanence (*śāśvata*), and three phrases involve the calculation of annihilation (*uccheda*).
Within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one personally constructs these calculations, which obstruct the clarity of principle; therefore, they are termed "delusions."
If Kaishan says: "Birth and death are exclusively suffering and devoid of pleasure," while Guangzhai says: [birth and death contain both suffering and pleasure].
Within birth and death there is a fixed and real happiness.
Zhuangyan says:
Within birth and death there is a false happiness.
Delusive pleasure is oppressed by the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), and therefore it is not true pleasure.
However, the explanations of the three masters are all intended as a refutation of this [view].
Kaishan says that "birth and death are suffering" constitutes the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) within this context.
Guangzhai says that "exclusively blissful" refers to the eternalist view within this context.

Zhuangyan says that "delusive bliss" is further oppressed by the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), which corresponds to the view of being both eternal and annihilated within this context.
There should also be a fourth proposition, though it is not known who held it.
Next, from "cultivating the permanence of all phenomena" onwards, the delusions are summarized in three parts: namely, the dharma, the analogy, and the application.

In the initial section of the Dharma, following the statement "cultivating the permanence of all phenomena," there is a conclusion regarding those who fall into the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
There are two interpretations.
The first says:
Originally one clings to permanence, yet others challenge this with the difficulty of annihilationism;
when the meaning of permanence cannot be established, one then clings to annihilationism.
Originally one clings to annihilationism, yet others challenge this with the difficulty of permanence.
If the meaning of cessation is not established, one further clings to permanence.
The second [position] says:

since the two views are mutually dependent, when one sees the fault of abandoning through cultivation, one immediately cultivates permanence; when one sees the fault of cultivating permanence, one immediately cultivates abandonment.
The phrase "like a centipede" below is a simile.
The six-fascicle [version] calls it the "waist-bending insect.
The *I Ching* says: "The centipede contracts its body in order to seek extension."
At that time, the common saying was that it was a transformation of mulberry branches;
this was not necessarily entirely true. The same applies to the examples of mulberry roots becoming cicadas and decaying grass becoming fireflies.
This insect has its waist broken.
Regarding "cultivating both permanence and annihilation," this provides an analogy.
It clarifies that because the cause of annihilation arises from permanence, and the cause of permanence arises from annihilation, this analogy is employed.
From the phrase "For this reason" onwards, the third section clarifies the contemplation that destroys delusions; it also has two parts:

First, the explicit explanation; second, the concluding resolution. The first also consists of three pairs of six phrases. Although one should speak only of "self" in contrast to the prior "non-self," the fact that the Sūtra speaks of "permanence" has two interpretations: 1. It refers to the permanence of the *ālayavijñāna*. 2. It refers to the permanence of the *tathatā* (suchness). Regarding the first interpretation: although the *ālayavijñāna* is not permanent in the sense of being eternally unchanging, it is nonetheless called "permanent" because its continuity is uninterrupted throughout beginningless time. Furthermore, because it serves as the support for the various consciousnesses, it is called "permanent. Regarding the second interpretation: although *tathatā* is not permanent in the sense of being eternally unchanging, it is nonetheless called "permanent" because it is free from arising and ceasing. Furthermore, because it is the object of the wisdom of the noble ones, it is called "permanent. As for the concluding resolution: the term "self" is used because it is the support for the notion of self; the term "permanence" is used because it is free from arising and ceasing. This is because the *ālayavijñāna* is the support for the various consciousnesses, and *tathatā* is the object of the wisdom of the noble ones. Therefore, these two are called "self" and "permanence. As the verse says: "The *ālaya* is the support for the various consciousnesses; *Tathatā* is the object of the noble ones' wisdom. Because it is the support and the object, It is called 'self' and 'permanence. This concludes the section on the explicit explanation. Now follows the concluding resolution. First, the resolution regarding the explicit explanation; second, the resolution regarding the concluding resolution. Regarding the first: although the Sūtra speaks of "self" and "permanence," this does not contradict the principle of non-self, because it is taught according to the specific capacities of sentient beings. Regarding the second: although the Sūtra speaks of "self" and "permanence," this does not contradict the ultimate truth, because it is taught as a provisional designation based on the two types of supports and objects. Thus, the Sūtra’s teaching of "self" and "permanence" is established without contradiction. This concludes the section on the concluding resolution. This concludes the entire treatise.
The first view holds that this is an error;
the second view holds that "eternal" (*nitya*) is a general designation, whereas "we" (*asmākam*) is a specific one.
Regarding the ten thousand virtues of the Buddha-fruit, it is appropriately termed "eternal."
Regarding the phrase "other dharmas," everything outside of the Middle Way is termed "other dharmas.
"Permanence, bliss, self, and purity" refers specifically to the Tathāgata’s secret treasury: the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as true liberation and so forth.
One should know that the Middle Way is precisely the True Dharma, while the two extremes are "the rest.
The section beginning with "One should know thus" is the conclusion of the explanation.
It further consists of two parts:
The principle is presented first, followed by the analogy.
Regarding the statement in the initial section on the principle that "the fool has no doubt," there are two interpretations.
Doubt serves as the gateway to understanding; since the fool lacks understanding, he therefore has no doubt.
The second [teacher] says:
"The Middle Way is distinct, clear, and easy to understand; even a fool would not doubt it, let alone a wise person.
According to the text, the latter interpretation appears to be superior."
The passage beginning with "like a weak and sick person" is an analogy that returns to the previous two interpretations.
If one follows the meaning regarding afflictions (*kleśa*), it refers to how fools give rise to various views through discrimination, which is like taking ghee for its lightness and ease.

If one follows the latter interpretation, ghee is an excellent medicine; for a strong person who consumes it, it is inherently beneficial, and for a weak person who consumes it, it likewise brings lightness and ease.
This is analogous to the Dharma of the Middle Way, which even a fool can understand.
The sixth fascicle states, "Having taken it, he became dazed and confused," which refers to the meaning of being bewildered by what is not understood.
From the phrase "the dharmas of existence and non-existence" onwards, the second section extensively clarifies the Middle Way, which is further divided into two parts:
first, revealing the Middle Way by means of the existence and non-existence of all dharmas; second, revealing the Middle Way by means of the non-duality of all dharmas.

Regarding the initial passage: Now, as for existence and non-existence, they cannot be definitively grasped; that which is said to exist is explained as non-existent, and that which is said to be non-existent is explained as existent. Existence is non-existence, and non-existence is existence.
Regarding the unsurpassed, it is said that there is existence, yet this existence is not fixed as existence;
regarding that which is superior to existence, it is said that there is non-existence, yet this non-existence is not fixed as non-existence.
Neither existence nor non-existence is precisely the Middle Way.

Next, regarding "non-duality": there is no duality distinct from non-duality, nor is there non-duality distinct from duality; since neither duality nor non-duality can be apprehended, this is neither dual nor non-dual, and is called the Middle Way.
In the initial passage concerning existence and non-existence, there are both the principle (*dharma*) and the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The initial exposition of the principle is extremely concise, consisting of only this single sentence, which directly indicates that the nature of existence and non-existence is not fixed.
If another person clearly knows that the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) definitely do not exist and cannot be regarded as existing,
and that the three aggregates (triskandha) definitely exist and cannot be regarded as non-existent, this is not "indeterminate" and is not called the Middle Way.
“Just as the four great elements,” and so forth, next presents a simile, first the illustration and then the application.

Within the initial illustration, it is intended to clarify that existence and non-existence are not fixed; just as the Buddha responds to conditions, if someone clings to existence, he refutes existence to teach non-existence;
if someone clings to non-existence, he refutes non-existence to teach existence.

The four great elements are likewise: just as a skilled physician distinguishes various ailments, treating those with water-related illnesses using fire-based medicines, and those with fire-related illnesses using water-based medicines, so it is with earth and wind.
An unskilled physician does not distinguish the symptoms of a disease and rashly administers medicine.
From the section beginning with "Good son" (*kulaputra*) below, the analogy is applied: first, it is applied collectively; second, it is applied individually.
The first is visible.
Next, regarding the phrase "if one says," there are two distinct combinations:
first, citing existence and non-existence as the combination; second, citing permanence and impermanence as the illustrative combination.
The first section also has two parts:
first, the specific refutation of existence and non-existence; second, the summary conclusion as an admonition.
The initial passage consists of three sentences.
Regarding the first phrase, "Wisdom should not be stained," there are two interpretations. One says:
Wisdom, having heard the Buddha’s teaching that the Buddha-nature exists, should not become attached to it.
The fool then questions the locus where it manifests, whether within the six sense organs or throughout the entire body.
Second, if one hears that Buddha-nature exists, one should know that the Buddha’s intention is not fixed solely upon existence; for "existence" itself implies "non-existence."
"Non-existence is false speech" is the second phrase; it refutes non-existence.
It also has two meanings.
First, it says:
The principle is not non-existent; it certainly does not contradict reason, and thus [your claim] is false speech.
Second, [the opponent] says:
"Although Buddha-nature exists, its manifest function has not yet appeared; therefore, one says it is non-existent. You, being a person of wisdom, should not call this a falsehood."
If one says that it exists, this constitutes the third alternative.
Because there is a tendency to cling to the notion that sentient beings are numerous, this is further refuted.
"One should not remain silent" means that if Buddha-nature exists, it ought to be able to manifest auspicious signs.
"Why are you silent?
The second replied:
"If existence were definitely existent, why are you silent when subjected to your own investigation?"
Next, from "Furthermore, one should not... onwards, the conclusion is reached that debate is not permitted.
Whether one asserts existence or non-existence, or even the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), all are merely frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
From "If one speaks of suffering... onwards, the second section provides an analogy by applying the same principle to suffering, impermanence, and so forth.
Furthermore, there are five [aspects]:

first, concerning suffering; second, concerning impermanence; third, concerning self and non-self; fourth, concerning emptiness and quiescence; and fifth, concerning illusion and transformation. All of these resolve delusions and clarify understanding, as can be seen through their respective contrasts and explanations.

The text states: "Although there is coming and going, it is eternally abiding and unchanging. This refers to the identity of coming and going with neither-coming-nor-going, and the identity of movement with stillness.

From the passage beginning "If one says that ignorance... onwards, this is the second section, which clarifies the Middle Way by way of non-duality and non-difference; it also includes both the doctrinal exposition (dharma) and an analogy (dṛṣṭānta).
The Dharma is explained in three parts:

first, clarifying non-duality by way of causes and conditions; second, clarifying non-duality by way of contemplative practice; and third, summarizing to clarify non-duality. Causes and conditions refer to the object;
contemplation refers to the wisdom that illuminates; and the summary refers to both object and wisdom.
The initial section on the twelve links of dependent origination clarifies non-duality; it further consists of three parts:
first, ignorance is raised; second, formative action and consciousness are raised; third, good and evil are raised.
The traditional interpretation states:
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is delusion, while clarity (*vidyā*) is liberation.
Furthermore, it is said:
ignorance and formations (*saṃskāra*) belong to the past, while consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the subsequent factors belong to the present.
The differentiation of the three periods of time is not in accordance with this sutra.
The sutra rebukes it, saying: "To regard clarity and ignorance, as well as volitional formations, consciousness, and so forth, as distinct is the way of fools.
The wise thoroughly understand that their nature is non-dual."
"If one says it should be cultivated," and so forth, is the second section, which clarifies non-duality in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
This also has three parts: first, suffering; second, impermanence; and third, non-self.
Regarding "Self and Non-self," the third section concludes the non-duality in three parts:
first, the concluding praise; second, the concluding exhortation; and third, the concluding reconciliation.
The conclusion of the praise is twofold:

first, the conclusion of what the Buddha praised; second, the conclusion of having finished speaking. The conclusion of the exhortation is also twofold: [the first is the exhortation itself, and the second is the conclusion thereof].
First, he exhorts the upholding of the non-dual Dharma; second, he exhorts the upholding of the non-dual Sūtra.
From the words "As I... onwards, there is a third section that concludes the assembly and points forward to the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The old [commentary] says:
It quotes the analogy of the lamp wick from the "Profound Chapter" (*Gambhīra-parivarta*).
Alternatively, it says:
"The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* does not exhaust [the topic]; this passage must exist in the foreign edition of the sutra."
Some say: "Although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Dapin) is not definitive, its meaning of non-duality is without error.
Others further say:
The existence of duality is called "having attainment," while the absence of duality is called "non-attainment.
Furthermore, duality refers to the eye and consciousness: consciousness internally discerns, while the eye externally perceives forms; this constitutes duality.
Visual consciousness is non-dual; likewise, the wise thoroughly understand that all phenomena are also thus.
From the passage beginning with "Just as curd is produced from milk," the second analogy establishes the meaning of the non-duality of causes and conditions.

The way the five flavors arise from one another, lacking any nature of self or other, is precisely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); dependent origination is itself the Middle Way—this meaning is explicit.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, listing the five flavors; second, extensively refuting self and other; third, concluding with the principle of dependent origination.
First, the listing of the five flavors: the mutual generation of these five flavors is non-dual from the outset.
Next, from "In this way, the nature of curd" onwards, there is an extensive refutation of both self and other; first, the topical headings are established, and subsequently, they are explained.
In the first section, "curd arises from milk" serves as the primary thesis (*mukha*), followed by the analogy of the four flavors.
Within this first section, there are two parts:
first, "arising from milk to become curd" is the primary thesis; second, "arising from itself" and "arising from another" are both non-theses (*amukha*).

Next, following the passage "If [arising] were from another," the second section explains two thematic gateways: first, the explanation of the gateway of negation (*na-yukti*), and second, the explanation of the gateway of affirmation (*astu-yukti*).
Within the initial gateway of negation, there is first the explanation of non-arising from another, followed by the explanation of non-arising from self.

First, the refutation of arising from another can be seen. Within the refutation of arising from self, it says: "It is not logical that [a thing] should arise from itself through a similar continuity. This refers, for the time being, to what kind of similar continuity would there be? Yet we now observe that after milk, there is a continuity of flavor such as curd and so forth; therefore, we know it does not arise from itself.
If [taste) were produced spontaneously, the five flavors should occur simultaneously; yet since they follow one another in succession, how could they be simultaneous?
The section beginning with "Although not simultaneous" explains this topical heading.
After refuting the notions of self and other, it is provisionally designated through causes and conditions that curd arises from milk, being neither from itself nor from another.
To say that it existed beforehand is likewise a matter of causes and conditions.
Regarding the statement that "because the sweet flavor is predominant, it cannot transform itself," the flavor of milk is sweet and the flavor of curd is sour.
The subsequent section on the analysis of the meaning raises an objection to this.
From the words "This cow eats and chews" onwards is the third conclusion concerning causes and conditions; first there is the analogy, followed by the application.
In the first analogy, eating water and grass represents receiving the scriptural teachings; the transformation of blood into milk represents transforming evil into good.
Eating sweet grass is like receiving the Mahāyāna teachings, while eating bitter grass is like receiving the Hīnayāna teachings.

The Snowy Mountains are likened to this sutra; the fat and grease are likened to the Buddha-nature; the cow that eats them is likened to sentient beings; and the clarified butter (ghṛta) is likened to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Being able to rely on this sutra to practice and attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood—being devoid of colors such as blue, yellow, red, or white—is likened to practicing according to the teaching so as to obtain no fruits of śrāvakas or deva-humans, but purely the fruit of clarified butter, which is nirvāṇa.
Regarding these six stages, the text and meaning are perfectly clear, and so forth.

From the passage beginning "These sentient beings" onwards, within the second section on the application of the analogy, there is first the application [of the analogy] and subsequently the discussion of the meaning.
In the initial synthesis, first the duality is synthesized and subsequently non-duality is synthesized.
Regarding the statement in the section on non-duality that "ignorance transforms into clarity," another sutra further states: "The arising of clarity severs ignorance."
There are three traditional interpretations.
The first says:
"Cessation is itself transformation, and transformation is itself cessation; though the phrasing differs, the meaning is one."
The second says:
"Transformative language refers to the essence (*tǐ*); definitive language refers to function (*yòng*).

Within the essence of the one mind, there are two aspects—good and evil. It is simply that within one's own mind, good is transformed into evil and evil is transformed into good; the mind itself does not change."
Next, regarding its application: one must sever ignorance and attain only clarity; it cannot be attained without such severance.
This is the interpretation of Master Zhuangyan.

Kaishan criticized Zhuangyan’s explanation as being shallow and superficial, and thus explained it by applying it to the cultivation of the two conditions: the condition of the object (ālambana-pratyaya) and the condition of the cause (hetu-pratyaya).
From "Kāśyapa" onwards, the second section on the exposition of doctrine.
[The argument that] from the preceding milk, the nature of curd first arises.
This text is divided into two parts:
First the objection, then the response.
Within the objection there are two parts:
first the establishment of the premise, then the objection itself.
The refutations consist of two parts:
first, the refutation of its definite existence; second, the refutation of its definite non-existence.
The initial refutation of its definite existence is divided into three sections:
First, the correct refutation of the claim that there is curd within milk: if it already exists [within the milk], how can one say it is produced?
Now, as for the meaning of "production," it is defined as coming into being where there was previously nothing.
Next, from "If phenomena were originally non-existent" onwards, the difficulties are explained.
From "If one says that within milk... onwards, all three [points] are raised as objections.
For instance: if milk is the cause of curd, then grass would also be the cause of milk, and so forth.
Furthermore, these two positions are both inverted. If grass were the cause of milk, then milk should also be the effect of grass.
If grass is the cause of milk and milk exists within the grass, then since milk is the effect of grass, grass should likewise exist within the milk.
The causal relationship between milk and curd is also analogous to this; in the text, only one instance is cited.

Regarding the passage beginning with "If one says that within milk," the two difficulties concern the determination of non-existence: one should only challenge the existence [of the effect], rather than challenging its non-existence. Fearing that the Buddha might shift his position and fall into the extreme of non-existence, he preemptively obstructs this by challenging the notion of non-existence.
From "Good son" onwards, the two Buddhas provide the answer, which consists of three parts:
first, an examination of the analogy; second, a further application of the analogy; and third, a conclusion on the meaning of the analogy.
The first section also has three parts: first, the non-fixed adherence; second, the understanding through reasoning; and third, the conclusion regarding the non-fixed adherence.

Within the initial non-adherence, there are first three topical headings, followed by their sequential refutation: first, the gate of fixed existence; second, the gate of fixed non-existence; and third, arising from another.
To explain the three gates: first, explaining that it cannot be definitively established as existing [inherently], one says: "There is curd within milk. Why?
Milk is white and curd is yellow; milk is sweet and curd is sour. Since their color and taste differ, how can it be definitively established as existing?
Next, regarding the explanation that it cannot be definitively stated that there is no curd within milk, the text says: "If poison is placed in milk, the resulting curd will kill a person.

If one first places poison in the milk and later the milk transforms into curd, anyone who drinks this curd will still be killed by the poison; how, then, can it be said that there is definitely no curd in milk?
Below the phrase "This cow eats and chews," the second section provides an interpretation through understanding, which is further divided into two parts:
first, it clarifies that milk arises from grass, and thus is a conventional designation based on causes and conditions.
The subsequent clarification that curd arises from milk is likewise a provisional designation based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Each of these two passages contains two parts:
in the first pair, the former states that it exists "by virtue of conditions," while the latter concludes that it is "due to causes and conditions."
Regarding the power of the merit of sentient beings, there are three meanings:
first, the merit of the cow, whereby when she wishes to drink for her calf, her blood transforms into milk;
second, the merit of the calf, which causes the mother to have milk.
"The merit of milking a person" means that if a person lacks merit, they will not even have enough for their own children, let alone be able to satisfy others.
From the phrase "When this milk has ceased," there are two parts explaining how curd is produced from milk; these further consist of two sections:
first, explaining production through conditions, and second, concluding with the causal relationship.
*Máo* refers to stirring with an object; *wēn* refers to the heat of fire.

Some editions of the canon write this as the character "醋" (*cù*), but the current form, which attaches "liù" to the radical "jiǔ," does not mean stirring with an object, nor is it the name of a type of wine.
The name for "wine" (jiǔ) should have the radical for "dew" (yǒu); those who write it with the radical for "filial piety" (xiào) are in error.
The section beginning with "Therefore, one cannot speak of it as fixed" constitutes the third point, which concludes that there is no fixed dogmatic adherence.

"Good son, regarding 'knowledge and ignorance'... and so forth; this second section serves as a synthesis of the preceding parable. Within this, the meaning of the opening, turning, and severing is explained as previously stated, and so on.
From "By these causes and conditions" onwards is the third section, which concludes the meaning of the parable.
From "Good son, sentient beings have little merit" onwards is the third section, which praises the teaching and exhorts its upholding; this also has two parts:
first, praising the principle of Buddha-nature, and second, praising the teaching.
The praise of the principle is twofold:
first, the mention of the "grass of patience," and second, the restatement of the two similes.
Within this, first the two similes are restated, followed by the general synthesis of the two similes from the passage beginning with "all sentient beings."
Next, from the passage beginning "For example, like space" onwards, this is the praise of the teaching, which is further divided into two parts:
first, the praise of the sutra; second, the exhortation to believe.

In the initial section, there are both analogies and their applications: space represents the Dharmakāya; the thunder represents the preaching of the Dharma; the rising clouds represent compassion; the elephant tusks represent sentient beings; and the flowers represent the Buddha-nature.
There are three interpretations. One says:
there is a distinct plant called "elephant-tooth grass" (*dantakāṣṭha*), which produces flowers upon hearing thunder.
The second says:
"These are flowers produced from elephant tusks.
A sutra states: "When the thunder of the heavens is heard, flowers grow upon the tusks of the four types of elephants, such as the *utpala*."
The third [person] says:
"These elephant tusks do not produce flowers separately; rather, it is simply that there are patterns upon the tusks that resemble flowers.
From the phrase "the Buddha-nature of sentient beings" onwards, the analogy is applied; there are three stages of this application, which may be sought out.
The section beginning with "If there is a son of good family" is the second conclusion, intended to encourage faith.
From the section beginning with "Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha," this is the second part of the chapter, which answers the question regarding the nature that is difficult to see.
The text contains four sequences of question and answer:
the first two pairs distinguish the realization and vision of profound practice, while the latter two clarify the hearing and vision of shallow practice.
Hearing and vision respond to that which can be seen; realization and vision respond to that which is difficult to see.
Within the realization and vision, there are two sections in total:
the first section is directly observable;
the second section contains both questions and answers.
In the response, ten analogies are presented in general.
First, "a hundred blind men" serves as a comprehensive analogy for all sentient beings.
"A hundred" is a number representing totality; it is, for example, like referring to the many clans of the world as "the hundred surnames" (the common people).
Seeking to understand and realize the nature of seeing is like treating the eyes.
To seek out a skilled physician is for the faculties and conditions to respond to the Buddha.
At that time, the skilled physician is a metaphor for the Buddha’s compassionate manifestation.
Jin Yun’s fourfold interpretation:
first, he says that this finger in the sutra represents [the present teaching], while the three fingers represent the teachings of the three vehicles from the past.
It is also said:

"The golden shell is like the single finger of the Buddha’s skillful means and wisdom; the three fingers represent the faculties, conditions, and awakening to the Way; and the removal of the membrane represents the severing of ignorance and afflictions."
The second says:
"The three fingers represent the three types of wisdom.
The third says:
The initial teaching points with one finger; the Prajñāpāramitā through to the Lotus Sūtra point with two fingers; and the Nirvāṇa Sūtra points with three fingers.
The fourth [interpretation] states:
it is an analogy for the three patiences—patience through faith, patience through compliance, and the patience of non-arising.
The three types of patience (*kṣānti*) are explained as two.
One interpretation states:

the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) during the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*) during the thirty minds (*triṃśat-citta*), and the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*) during the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, it is said that from the first stage to the third stage there is the patience of faith (śraddhā-kṣānti), from the fourth stage to the sixth stage there is the conforming patience (anuloma-kṣānti), and from the seventh stage to the tenth stage there is the patience of non-arising (anutpāda-kṣānti).
Now, it will be shown that this is not so.
Since this scripture unifies with the Buddha-nature, how could it be interpreted otherwise?
To point this out directly: when the answer states that "it is not seen," it is analogous to not seeing the nature upon entering the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The inability to see with two fingers is a metaphor for not perceiving the nature of both the conventional and the ultimate truths.

When shown with three fingers, he replies that he sees a little; this is a metaphor for how the single truth and the three truths—namely emptiness, conventionality, and the middle—are called Buddha-nature.
At the first dwelling of the first stage, one is able to see [the truth] partially; therefore, it is said to be "slight.
From the words "Good son" onwards is the application of the analogy, which is further divided into two parts:
the first is the formal application, and this [section] illustrates the śrāvakas.

Regarding the first passage: if one examines the combined text, the golden ring is a metaphor for the teaching of *nirvāṇa*, while the three fingers are a metaphor for *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature), which is precisely the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and the three truths (*triratna*).
The text states: "The delusion of non-self" refers to a lack of understanding.
Because one was confused by the teaching of non-self in the former teachings, one did not perceive the nature;
now, through the teaching of the true self, one perceives the Buddha-nature.
The subsequent nine similes may be sought out [for their meaning].
From "Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha" onwards is the second section, which consists of two parts clarifying the hearing and seeing of those with shallow practice.
The first set of questions may be sought elsewhere.
The Buddha’s response consists of four parts:
first, an analogy; second, an application; third, an exhortation; and fourth, praise and censure.

Regarding the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception heaven" mentioned in the initial parable: it is the pinnacle of the four formless attainments within the realm of existence. Therein, there is no body yet consciousness remains; there is no perception yet perception exists. This matter is difficult to comprehend.
The Buddha-nature is likewise; it is not something realized by those of the Two Vehicles.
The three passages beginning with "the union of the two" can be seen [in the text].
From "Kāśyapa said to the Buddha: 'Neither noble ones nor ordinary people... onwards is the second round of question and answer.
Regarding the statement in the initial inquiry that "non-noble ones" refers to ordinary worldlings, these are none other than the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Although they claim for themselves to be noble (*ārya*), the Tathāgata strips them of that status; therefore, they are called "non-noble."
If an ordinary person within the principle [of the Dharma] is, in fact, a noble ordinary person,
then how can the two matters— the claim of "self" by both followers of the inner path and the outer paths—
be reconciled? The Buddha raised the analogy of two people, one poor and one wealthy.
There are three parts:
first, the analogy; second, the application; third, the conclusion.
The analogy consists of three sections:
First, the transformation through the giving of Bodhisattvas; second, the transformation through the giving of Śrāvakas; third, the transformation through the giving of Tathāgatas.
The first, the transformation of Bodhisattvas, is further divided into four:
first, the teaching of the doctrine; second, the reception thereof; third, the relinquishing of the response; and fourth, the arising of delusion.
"Those who act as close friends" refers to the mutual communication between the transformer and the transformed through the path of transformation; this is the meaning of "close friend.
Because the prince is rich in the wealth of the Dharma and the true self is manifested, he is said to "enrich sentient beings."
"Taking me as being within their own bodies and being fully possessed of various views," they are therefore called "poor people.
"Mutually coming and going" refers to the interrelation of response and stimulus.
From the phrase "At this time, the poor person" onwards is the second section on sentient beings receiving [the teaching].
Regarding the Prince receiving the sword, this was not a matter of direct perception; rather, it was because he had heard the Bodhisattva speak of the true self and Buddha-nature.
The fine sword serves as a metaphor for the Middle Way, the Buddha-nature, and the true self.
Those who harbor greed and attachment in their hearts love and delight in this teaching.
Regarding the passage "At a later time, the prince... and below, it concerns the third [aspect]: the Bodhisattva’s relinquishing of what should be abandoned.
Because he departs while maintaining his true self, it is said that he "carries a sword."
The response of the spiritual capacity is subtle and secret; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] "fled.
Because he further transformed others in other places, it is said that he was in "another country.
"The poor man afterwards" refers to the arising of delusion by the fourth type of ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
The Bodhisattva relinquishes his proper station, and as sentient beings transmigrate, they receive a body composed of the five aggregates; therefore, it is said that he "lodges.
Sleep is a time of darkness, which serves as a metaphor for the obscuration of ignorance.
Because they claim for themselves that there is a self, they are likened to delirious speech.
The ancient version reads "zhèn" (讇); as for the term "yè" (寱), it refers to snoring, while the *Diàngào* (典誥) uses the character "yè" (囈).
Following the phrase "others hear," the second section concerns the Śrāvakas receiving transformation through teaching.
One should fully discuss the four fruits; however, the text is abbreviated, omitting the third king.
The first king represents the first fruit.
My personal opinion is as follows:
As for the words of the other disciples, they may be taken two or three at a time.

"The old" refers to bystanders; using the analogy of a mechanical device, the device is like these people. Because they have been moved to realize the first fruit of the path, it is said that they are gathered in.

Xinghuang said: "The 'other person' represents the five provisional means (pañcopāya), which is a semblance of understanding; the 'King' represents the first fruit of realization (prathamaphala), which is true understanding.
While the former merely suppresses [delusion], the latter truly eradicates it by destroying the views of self and other; thus, one speaks of arriving at the King's abode."
Regarding the first fruit (srotāpanna), the meaning is that of "ruler and minister.
The "butcher" is a metaphor for analyzing the five aggregates to find the self, which cannot be found.
Because one has previously received this Dharma, it is said that they have long been close and intimate.
Since the transformer and the transformed are not of different paths, it is said that they are in one place.
Seeing with the eyes is analogous to the wisdom of hearing; touching with the hands is analogous to the wisdom of reflection; grasping is analogous to the wisdom of cultivation.
Furthermore, one must not contemplate or cultivate [such views]; hence it is said that one does not dare to touch them with the hand, much less intentionally grasp them.
"The horns of a sheep" refers to crooked and deviant conceptions of a self.
"Rejoicing and laughing" is a metaphor for grief and misery.
Not yet wishing to refute this erroneous calculation, he said, "Go as you please.
He then immediately established his other sons, who were transformed through the two fruits [of the stream-enterer and once-returner].
Subsequently, the four kings were the four fruits [of the arhat].
The section beginning with "In the future" refers to the third instance of the Tathāgata’s manifestation of transformation.
These are simply those bodhisattvas who previously fled; now they have returned to attain Buddhahood.
"Counting the time" merely means counting it.

The reason for clarifying only "no-self" (anātman) without mentioning a "true self" (ātman) is that, according to the subsequent section on the "Synthesis," there ought to be a teaching that speaks of the self.
As for the *utpala* flower, Brahmins reckon the spirit (*ātman*) to be white in color.
The ram's horn represents the Kṣatriya deity, who is yellow in color;
the mass of fire represents the Vaiśya deity, who is red;
and the black snake represents the Śūdra deity, who is black.
"Good son," [this phrase] combines the metaphors and returns to combine the three metaphors.
The metaphor says, "There is a fine sword," which corresponds to [the text] saying, "I explain the true nature.
The metaphor says, "Holding this pure sword, he flees to another country," which corresponds to [the text] saying, "Having finished explaining, he departs."
The section beginning with "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" combines with the preceding second [section], the transformation through bestowing the four fruits.
The section beginning with "In order to sever such... combines with the third.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s transformative bestowal is twofold:
The preceding clarification of the teaching on non-self precisely accords with what was mentioned before.
From the words "Good son" onwards is the second section, which further clarifies the teaching on the true self.
In the previous analogy, this was absent; it existed only as an underlying principle.
"Good son, if there are ordinary persons... and so forth: the third section concludes the intent of the answer, which can be seen in the text as stated above.

Compiled by Dharma Master Zhàngān Zhǐ of the Sui Dynasty; Revised by the Tiantai Śramaṇa Zhànrán of the Tang Dynasty. Chapter 13: On Words and Letters (12). This chapter has four intended meanings: 1. To clarify that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true body. 2. To reveal that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true teaching. 3. To demonstrate that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true land. 4. To show that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true liberation. Regarding the first meaning: All words and letters are the Buddha’s true body. Why? Because all words and letters are the Buddha’s true nature. Since the Buddha’s true nature is the Buddha’s true body, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true body. Furthermore, the Buddha’s true body is the Buddha’s true nature. Since the Buddha’s true nature is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true body. Moreover, the Buddha’s true body is the Buddha’s true teaching. Since the Buddha’s true teaching is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true body. Furthermore, the Buddha’s true body is the Buddha’s true land. Since the Buddha’s true land is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true body. Finally, the Buddha’s true body is the Buddha’s true liberation. Since the Buddha’s true liberation is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true body. Regarding the second meaning: All words and letters are the Buddha’s true teaching. Why? Because all words and letters are the Buddha’s true nature. Since the Buddha’s true nature is the Buddha’s true teaching, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true teaching. Furthermore, the Buddha’s true teaching is the Buddha’s true body. Since the Buddha’s true body is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true teaching. Moreover, the Buddha’s true teaching is the Buddha’s true land. Since the Buddha’s true land is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true teaching. Finally, the Buddha’s true teaching is the Buddha’s true liberation. Since the Buddha’s true liberation is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true teaching. Regarding the third meaning: All words and letters are the Buddha’s true land. Why? Because all words and letters are the Buddha’s true nature. Since the Buddha’s true nature is the Buddha’s true land, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true land. Furthermore, the Buddha’s true land is the Buddha’s true body. Since the Buddha’s true body is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true land. Moreover, the Buddha’s true land is the Buddha’s true teaching. Since the Buddha’s true teaching is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true land. Finally, the Buddha’s true land is the Buddha’s true liberation. Since the Buddha’s true liberation is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true land. Regarding the fourth meaning: All words and letters are the Buddha’s true liberation. Why? Because all words and letters are the Buddha’s true nature. Since the Buddha’s true nature is the Buddha’s true liberation, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true liberation. Furthermore, the Buddha’s true liberation is the Buddha’s true body. Since the Buddha’s true body is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true liberation. Moreover, the Buddha’s true liberation is the Buddha’s true teaching. Since the Buddha’s true teaching is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true liberation. Finally, the Buddha’s true liberation is the Buddha’s true land. Since the Buddha’s true land is all words and letters, it follows that all words and letters are the Buddha’s true liberation. Therefore, all words and letters are the Buddha’s true body, the Buddha’s true teaching, the Buddha’s true land, and the Buddha’s true liberation. They are not merely provisional names or conventional designations; they are the ultimate reality of the Dharma-nature. Thus, it is said: "All words and letters are the Buddha’s true body. This is the meaning of this chapter. (Note: The text provided in the prompt appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan* or related Tiantai works, specifically concerning the nature of words and letters as manifestations of the Buddha's reality.)

Regarding the sequential order: the preceding "Chapter on Nature" clarified the principle underlying the characters, while this chapter clarifies the characters that underlie the principle; it answers the prior question concerning how to understand the meaning of the full characters (*pūrṇākṣara*) and the half-characters (*ardhākṣara*).
In the previous inquiry regarding the merit of names, we were specifically discussing this sutra, which exclusively elucidates the supreme, world-transcending *maṃtra* (full-syllable) teachings;

in the present chapter, however, we discuss the various teachings in general, whether they be the partial (*ardha*) or full (*pūrṇa*), and the mundane, supramundane, superior, or most superior forms of written expression.
Regarding the "Opening of the Secret," another interpretation holds that impermanence is the "half" and permanence is the "full.
Xinghuang refuted this, saying:
It is like two slices of a *jambu* fruit; this is the fullness of a single half.
He further explains:
previously, when impermanence was taught alone, it was not called "full"; now, because the teaching fully expounds both permanence and impermanence, it is therefore called "full."
He further argued:
"If that which is permanent were sufficient to constitute the impermanent, then one piece of pear would suffice for half a piece of quince;
what ought to be a single fruit would instead be a complete whole."
Xinghuang’s Explanation:
The essence of *nirvāṇa* and *buddhadhātu* is neither permanent nor impermanent; because it is fully endowed with both permanence and impermanence, it is called "complete.
Here, I clarify that when that school critiques the old [teachings], they may regard them as being "one-sided" or "incomplete."

To say that it is neither impermanent nor permanent, yet that permanence and impermanence constitute the "full" (pūrṇa) character, is like taking four pieces of a *cāra*, *li*, *zhi*, and *li* fruit and joining them to form a single fruit.

Now, according to this chapter, all characters are opened up to be full characters. As the text says: "The Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is able to extinguish the 'half-words' (*ardha-akṣara*); therefore, you should now abandon the half-words and follow the full words, remaining unimpeded and unattached regarding all dharmas."
"The 'half' and the 'full' are mutually defined; since there is neither half nor full, one should know that characters are not characters. To be without characters is the 'full character.
As the text says: 'The half-character is the root of all sūtras, records, treatises, and literary compositions.'"
Furthermore, it is said: "The half-syllables (*ardhākṣara*) are the root of the discourse on afflictions.
It is also said: "The full-syllables (*pūrṇākṣara*) are the root of wholesome dharmas.
All discourse concerning wholesome dharmas, as well as all heterodox treatises, incantations, and scripts, are entirely the teachings of the Buddha and not the teachings of non-Buddhists."
One should know that all that the Buddha has spoken is the true Dharma of our own tradition; this is the "full letter" (paripūrṇākṣara) by virtue of being the true Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said: "If one understands written characters, one can cause the verbal karma of sentient beings to be purified."
The Buddha-nature is not like that; it does not depend upon written words to become pure, for the Buddha-nature is inherently pure.

One should know that all written characters are the Buddha-nature. The Buddha-nature is neither word nor non-word, yet it can manifest as both word and non-word; therefore, it is called the "full word" (pūrṇākṣara).
Although there are three meanings, do not form three separate interpretations.
