Some speak of the twelve links of dependent origination, some speak of the four conditions, and others speak of the four truths, the eight truths, and so forth, thereby causing confusion.
As for what the text calls the "three contemplations," there are many varieties:
one version states they are the contemplation of suffering, impermanence, and non-self.
One version says it is the contemplation of the aggregates, bases, and elements; another says it is the contemplation of the three poisons.
Regarding the "seven preparatory stages" (*saptaprayoga*), the Arithmeticians (*Sāṃkhyikas*) say they consist of:

the contemplation of impurity, the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), as well as Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).

The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* say: first, contemplating form as suffering; second, contemplating the origin of suffering; third, contemplating the cessation of suffering; fourth, contemplating the path to the cessation of suffering; fifth, contemplating the faults of suffering; sixth, contemplating the escape from suffering; and seventh, contemplating the entry into [the realization of] suffering. This applies to all phenomena in the same way.
From the passage beginning with "The World-Honored One [said], 'After the bhikṣu Ānanda saw these things... onwards, the second point clarifies that Ānanda was subjected to confusion.
Although Ānanda had attained the first fruit of the path and served as the Buddha’s personal attendant, he was now suddenly beset by the confusion of the various māras.
This has two meanings:
first, to manifest within the traces [of the teaching] that he receives [the transmission] here and now, demonstrating that the power and efficacy of the divine mantra can subdue Māra;

second, since Ānanda was not present in the assembly, it was intended to have the Tathāgata inquire after him, so that Mañjuśrī could engage in a dialogue with him regarding his virtues and deeds, establishing that he is worthy of being entrusted [with the Dharma].
Heji (河西) explains:
There are five reasons why Ānanda was troubled by Māra.
First, since Cunda (Cienru) was the one to respond to the Buddha’s exhortations and convert the various non-Buddhists, Ānanda did not come to sit in the assembly.
Second, it was because Māra had attained deliverance that [the Buddha] manifested his presence there;
third, it was to manifest the eight internal virtues of Ānanda;
fourth, it was to cause Ānanda to go and summon Subhadra.
Fifth, [the purpose is] to subdue Ānanda’s haughty mind.
From the passage "At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha" onwards, there is a second section discussing further doctrinal points to resolve doubts.
This is further divided into two parts:
First the question, then the answer.
Within the question there are two parts:
first, the question concerning the Bodhisattva’s own capacity to propagate [the teaching].
From the passage beginning with "For what reason and cause," this asks why Ānanda alone was granted such personal inquiry.
From the passage beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī," there are two responses, which are divided into three parts:
first, a detailed account of the original circumstances; second, a present-time eulogy; and third, the formal answer to the two questions.
This first section fully recounts the original causal conditions;
that is to say, the original causal conditions concerning how the Tathāgata, in the past, commanded the assembly to seek out an attendant, and so forth.
From the passage "Mañjuśrī and Ānanda" onwards is the second section, the manifest praise.
If Ānanda were present in the assembly, how could he have offered such praise?
Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, praising eight matters as inconceivable; second, praising them as rare.
Furthermore, regarding the name of Viśvabhū Buddha among the names of the seven Buddhas, it must certainly have been omitted [in some versions] as follows.
There are texts that read "Śābhū," which is incorrect.

From the passage beginning with "As you have said" onwards, the third section provides the formal response to the two questions, clarifying that although Bodhisattvas are capable of circulating the teachings, each has their own heavy responsibility for taming and guiding their own retinue; therefore, he did not entrust them with the mission.
Ānanda has attained the lower fruits of the path and personally serves as my attendant; he is the foremost among those of great learning, and for these reasons, I entrust [the teaching] to him.

At the beginning of the "Chapter on Longevity," it was clearly explained that śrāvakas are incapable while bodhisattvas are capable of receiving [this teaching]. Yet, here I entrust it to Ānanda and do not entrust it to the bodhisattvas. There are three meanings for this:
first, previously, because I censured those of literal practice, I said they were incapable; now, because I clarify that they are actually expedient means, I say they are capable.

Second, regarding the exalting of the Great Dharma and the proclaiming of its profound principles, he is incapable; yet, regarding the retention of the scriptural words and the sections of the teachings, he is capable.
As the subsequent text itself states: "If there is anything that Ānanda does not know, the Bodhisattva Hongguang shall himself proclaim it."
The profound meaning and correct principle are entrusted solely to the Bodhisattvas.

Third, regarding the Śrāvakas, they possess both the capacity to receive and the capacity to reject; because they reject [the profound], they are deemed incapable, yet because they receive [the conventional], they are said to be capable.

Regarding the statement in the text, "He is my younger brother," this refers to a nephew; however, because the author wished to speak of a close relationship, he did not mention "nephew" and simply said, "He is my brother.
As for the phrase, "That which has not yet been heard shall be propagated by the Bodhisattva Hongguang," there are three interpretations.
First, Yecheng said:

"Among the ten external numbers, he is ranked ninth; in reality, he is a bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha stated that the Bodhisattva Hongguang is naturally capable of disseminating [the teachings]."
Second, Zhaoti said:

"Within the Buddha-dharma, what is there that is not a Great Being? Yet you suddenly adopt names identical to those of non-Buddhists, claiming to be able to propagate the sutras. To speak of 'propagating extensively' does not depend on a single individual; rather, whoever can propagate, disseminate, teach, transform, and bring benefit is one who propagates extensively."
Therefore, in the compilation of the Dharma-piṭaka, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains these matters in detail:
when Kāśyapa confronted Ānanda, he brought forth the Sūtras and the Abhidharma; when he confronted Upāli, he brought forth the Vinaya, which is the Vinaya-piṭaka.
If Mañjuśrī and Maitreya, together with Ānanda, bring forth the Mahāyāna-piṭaka, then Mañjuśrī and Maitreya are themselves the Bodhisattvas of Vast Propagation.
The third interpretation:

This is neither a non-Buddhist teaching nor a general exposition; rather, there is a distinct Bodhisattva named Hongguang (Extensive Propagation), who belongs to the same class as those such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.
From the passage "Mañjuśrī, the bhikṣu Ānanda is currently elsewhere" onwards is the third [section], the Right Livelihood Ānanda.
Although the ancient commentaries explain three meanings, the text itself contains only the subduing of the celestial Māra.
There should have been an account of summoning Subhadra and the entrustment of the teaching, but the text is incomplete and does not include it.
Now, according to the extant text, there are five sections:

first, the Buddha’s command to Mañjuśrī; second, the Tathāgata’s recitation of the mantra; third, Mañjuśrī’s acceptance of the command; fourth, the King Māra’s arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment; and fifth, Ānanda’s expression of reverence.
First, the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to hold this mantra in order to liberate Ānanda.
As for the term "Great Dhāraṇī," the translations of its phonetics differ; it is also called "Total Holding" (Zǒngchí) and also called "Able to Hold" (Néngchí).
Because one can uphold the True Dharma without losing it and prevent false dharmas from arising, it is called "upholding" (*dhāraṇī*).
It is also translated as "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*), as this Sanskrit term carries both meanings.
Since it is correctly translated as "upholding," the text states: "Upon hearing this name, one upholds it."
Regarding the five matters that require the mantra-practitioner to observe, such as abstaining from pungent foods and so forth, all are exactly as stated in the text.
From the passage "At that time, the World-Honored One then spoke it" onwards, the two Tathāgatas recite the mantra.
The name and meaning of the mantra have already been explained as before.

However, regarding the term "juebi" (若竭裨) found within the mantra, there are different versions of the sūtra text: some read it as "yibian" (衣邊, edge of a garment), while others read it as "tubian" (土邊, edge of earth). For now, "yibian" is taken as the correct reading.

There are two pronunciations for this character: one is the slow and affectionate pronunciation, which is called the "base" (bēi) tone; nowadays it is read as bìlí (with the second character reversed).
Furthermore, when written with the radical for "earth" (tǔ), it also has two pronunciations.
It is also called *bālami*; the character is "wind under a mountain. This was originally the character for *xié* (携). If one pronounces it as *xié*, the character should be written as 󱊓.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is composed of the abbreviated form of *lán* (嵐) and the phonetic element *guī* (圭)."
Furthermore, the character 綈 (tí) may sometimes be pronounced as "dì," but it is now pronounced as "tí.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "It is thick silk.

However, in the new *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, in the chapter on the "Dhāraṇī for Purifying the Ground," the Buddha expounds ten sections of dhāraṇīs for Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). This particular dhāraṇī is precisely that which protects the tenth stage from the *sūtra*; this dhāraṇī specifically guards the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage.
If this is so, one should know that Ānanda’s stage of practice was already high; he was indeed a bodhisattva of the tenth bhūmi, whom the Tathāgata protected by bestowing this dhāraṇī.
That sūtra states: "One who obtains this dhāraṇī shall not fear venomous snakes, lions, tigers, wolves, and the like."

Since the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) permits one to transcend directly to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) within a single lifetime, the physical body cannot avoid such fears; therefore, it is protected by mantras.
However, even if Ānanda did not begin his realization in this life, how could his fundamental nature (*ben*) and his manifested trace (*ji*) differ?
The intent behind the protection of mantras can be seen by reflecting upon it.

If this were not the case, the Bodhisattva would have severed all afflictions and would no longer possess any fear; why, then, could it now be said that one must obtain a mantra before being able to escape fear?
Therefore, many have offered interpretations:
some say that the matter is indeed difficult to know and cannot be fathomed by those of shallow understanding.
Yet there is another perspective:
The essence of the Dharma-body is free from fear; however, speaking in terms of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), one must demonstrate what constitutes fear.
Even when the Tathāgata’s path has reached the realization of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), he still possesses the nine afflictions; how much more so, then, for a bodhisattva?
All [sections] follow the previous explanation.
From "At that time, Mañjuśrī received the mantra" onwards is the third section, Mañjuśrī’s reception of the command.
From "When the Māra King heard this" onwards is the fourth section, the awakening of the resolve of the various Māras.
From "Mañjuśrī together with Ānanda" onwards, the fifth section clarifies Ānanda’s prostration.
However, since ancient times, dhāraṇīs have not been translated [into Chinese], and there are five reasons for this:
first, names of the Triple Gem; second, names of the Four Noble Truths; third, names of the realm of emptiness; fourth, names of sublime practices; and fifth, names of spirits and deities.
Because it encompasses these five meanings, it is called "total" (zong).
Because it can maintain the good so that it is not lost and maintain the evil so that it does not arise, it is called "retaining" (chi).
Regarding the names of the Triple Gem, the *Sutra of the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara* says: "Namo buddhāya dharmāya saṃghāya."
"However, the names of the Three Jewels vary in their various forms; perhaps it was like this that the great makara fish closed its mouth upon hearing the names of the Three Jewels."
Regarding the names of the Four Truths: in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, a parrot was reborn in heaven upon hearing the names of the Four Truths.

Regarding the name of the principle of emptiness: the true realm is nameless, yet there is nothing that it cannot be named; therefore, by merely hearing this name of "emptiness," one immediately awakens to the Way, becomes a sage, and severs delusions.
Regarding the names of superior practices, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Prajñāpāramitā is the great mantra, the unsurpassed mantra.
Furthermore, the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-samantamukha-parivarta* clarifies the six-word phrase, which constitutes the six subtle gates:
first, counting; second, following; third, cessation; fourth, contemplation; fifth, returning; and sixth, purification.
Regarding the names of the spirits and deities: first are the names of the benevolent spirit-kings, and second are the names of the malevolent spirit-kings.
From the passage "The Buddha told Ānanda, 'Outside this Śāla grove... onwards, the fourth section concurrently converts Subhadra.
The text consists of three parts:
first, the introductory narrative (*nidāna*); second, the doctrinal discussion (*arthaviniścaya*); and third, the submission and conversion.
The initial introductory narrative further comprises three sections:
First, the address to Ānanda; second, Ānanda’s acceptance of the command; third, his following along.
Regarding the first section, Subhadra has two translations:
first, "One Who Cherishes the Virtuous," and second, "One Who Is Virtuous."
Regarding the statement that "although one has attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), one has not yet abandoned conceit (*māna*)," conceit is a defilement of the distracted mind.

Since one has already attained the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), one ought to have subdued the lower defilements; yet, as for the claim that conceit has not been abandoned, there are two interpretations according to the *Sāṃkhya*:
if following the *Sāṃkhya* doctrine, conceit arises from the back of the secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) of envy (*īrṣyā*).

Having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one immediately gives rise to pride (*māna*) by taking that very stage as an object; therefore, it is said that "conceit has not yet been abandoned.
According to the interpretation of the *Śāstra*:

pride is a defilement of the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*), which has indeed already been suppressed; however, pride still remains within the single stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, while one is inherently high-minded, yet attains a state of humility toward others, my mind remains particularly full of self-importance.
Because this sense of "I" exists, it is called not having abandoned arrogance.

To give rise to the thought of attaining omniscience and the thought of entering nirvana—this is Subhadra’s notion of permanence; that is to say, he gives rise to the thought of attaining omniscience and the thought of entering nirvana.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the person's habitual tendencies of affection have not yet been exhausted," there are two possible interpretations:
first, it refers to wholesome affection, namely the love between a father and son characterized by paternal kindness and filial piety.
This arises because there is still afflictive craving; thus, although this mind arises, it is merely categorized as mundane wholesome.
To say that it is "habitual" does not necessarily mean it is a latent predisposition (*vāsanā*), but simply clarifies that it arises frequently.
Because this wholesome [action] has been practiced repeatedly and without ceasing, it is therefore said that "the practice is not yet exhausted.
Second, this treatise discusses the habituation (*vāsanā*) of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the habituation of afflictions, there are two interpretations.
The old commentary says:
"One must first permanently subdue and sever [the afflictions] before beginning [the practice]; this is what is employed.
There are two interpretations:

Regarding the statement that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) arising in ordinary beings have not yet been exhausted: this is because, although they have attained the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the higher stages and thereby suppressed their heavy delusions, lighter remnants still remain; thus, it is said that the habits are "not yet exhausted."
From "At that time, Subhadra arrived and paid his respects" onwards, the second part concerns the discussion of doctrine.
This text is divided into two sections:
first, the discussion on karmic action; second, the discussion on liberation.

The practitioner at the initial stage refers to both mundane liberation and supramundane liberation; this fully accords with the Buddha’s discourse on the two matters of the mundane and the supramundane.
Regarding the preceding text, there are four parts:
first, the request to listen, which follows below.
“The Buddha said, ‘Now is indeed the right time’” refers to the second part, where the Buddha grants his permission.
“‘Gautama, you have various śramaṇas... and so forth” refers to the third part, where he formally questions the Buddha.
The four Tathāgatas respond as follows.
The first two answers are as stated in the text.

Regarding the third question addressed to the Buddha, he does not claim it to be his own doctrine, but merely states that there are various śramaṇas and others in the world who all make such assertions.
Why does he not put forward his own doctrinal position? There is a specific reason for this.

Having previously heard the Buddha refute the doctrines established by the various non-Buddhists, he now refrains from establishing a position of his own, fearing it might be refuted by the Buddha; instead, he directly cites the interpretations of others to question the Buddha, clarifying that all karmic retributions of good and evil arise solely from past karma, and that there is no arising of karma or present causes and conditions within the current lifetime.
The principle of karma is closely aligned with the correct teaching; however, if one lacks present causes and conditions, it becomes erroneous.

It is precisely because past karma can induce the two retributions of suffering and pleasure that, if one can now cultivate the path to sever these retributions of suffering and pleasure, one may attain nirvana in this very body through the cultivation of the path.

Therefore it is said that the karmic retributions of suffering and pleasure for all sentient beings do not arise from present karma; rather, the causes lie in the past while the fruits are experienced in the present.
There is no cause in the present, and thus there will be no fruit in the future.
From "If there be a śramaṇa" onwards is the fourth part, the Buddha’s response.
The text itself is divided into three sections:
first, refuting their false doctrines; second, rebuking their false teachers; and third, elucidating the correct principle.

Below this, the erroneous doctrines of the opponent are first challenged through four successive hypothetical arguments, each establishing a contrast between "the other" and "the self"; these passages are all clearly visible in the text.
From the words "I say, O virtuous one," onwards, the second section rebukes that false teacher.

The text states that he replied as if to Pūraṇa; however, Subhadra’s teacher was actually Udraka Rāmaputra. Therefore, the subsequent passage says: "Your teacher, Udraka Rāmaputra, possessed sharp faculties and was intelligent."
Now, the mention of "Pūraṇa" here is a figurative designation. Pūraṇa was the leader of the Six Heretics;
that man held false views, denying the reality of karma and its effects, asserting instead that even if one were the Fire-Master Pūraṇa, he too must be held accountable.

Regarding the statement, "If one experiences medium or superior suffering due to inferior causes and conditions," if one discusses cause and effect according to ultimate truth, an inferior cause indeed yields an inferior fruit; yet there are also instances where obstacles are transformed, such that the result is not fixed but varies according to conditions.
Therefore, it is said that when a lower cause results in a middle or upper suffering, or an upper cause results in a lower fruit, there can be a transformation of obstacles.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "it is possible for meritorious karma (*puṇyakarman*) to result in the experience of suffering," this means that while practicing good is meritorious karma, if one instead receives retribution in hell or experiences the fruit among humans, this is precisely the case of meritorious karma resulting in the experience of a pleasant fruit.

Regarding the case where one performs a painful karma yet receives a pleasant fruit: this refers to acting as a king’s executioner to eliminate bandits; although this is a painful karma, it results in wealth and nobility—this is a painful karma receiving a pleasant fruit.

Regarding the statement that "karma which is neither painful nor pleasant does not produce a result": this does not mean that karma which is unarisen is itself neither painful nor pleasant. Rather, it means that lower-grade wholesome karma serves as the cause for the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), and this is precisely what constitutes "karma that is neither painful nor pleasant."
Because [the karma] varies according to conditions, it does not receive a fixed retribution; thus it is said that "it does not receive a fruit.

Furthermore, as for the text stating, "Can it cause that which is without fixed retribution to become fixed retribution? this does not refer to a state of being entirely beyond retribution; rather, it asks whether a retribution that is itself indeterminate can be made into a fixed retribution.
"O Benevolent One, you should know that it definitely exists," and so forth, constitutes the third section: the Correct Meaning.
"O Benevolent One, if [you say] by the power of severing the causes and conditions of karma," and so forth, constitutes the second section: the Exposition of the Meaning of Liberation.
This consists of five sections; this is the first.
From "World-Honored One, I have already previously tamed my mind" onwards is the second section, wherein he recounts his own statement.
From "The Buddha said: 'How is it now? onwards is the third section, the repeated reprimand.

"From 'World-Honored One, I previously contemplated' onwards is the fourth section. The text says: 'I previously observed that desire is impermanent, without pleasure, and without purity. However, the contemplations practiced by non-Buddhists are mostly composed of six aspects, namely: suffering (*duḥkha*), coarseness (*audārika*), obstruction (*ādīnava*), cessation (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*)."

If a disciple of the Buddha practices the contemplation of eight aspects—namely, impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, being like an abscess, being like a wound, being like poison, and being like an arrow.

Now this Subhadra has also performed the eight contemplations; however, these are stated by way of general analogy. One should contemplate the desire realm as impermanent, without pleasure, without self, and without purity. Yet, in this case, he alone does not speak of "no-self" because, being an outsider, he practices dhyāna for the sake of a self and seeks liberation for that self, and thus lacks the contemplation of no-self.

However, this Subhadra sequentially severed the afflictions of the three realms and attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), taking it to be nirvāṇa; this was his prior conception of the mind.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddha asked, 'How do you [conceive it]?'", the fifth section represents the Tathāgata’s repeated refutation.
Although you speak of disciplining the mind, you still reckon the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to be nirvana.
Nirvana is signless; since you yourself have reckoned it thus, how can this be disciplining the mind?
Previously, you severed the afflictions of the three realms through contemplation; this was the elimination of coarse perceptions.
Yet, to still reckon that there is *nirvāṇa* is to preserve subtle perceptions.

Regarding this, it is said that your teacher Udraka Rāmaputra later regressed from the state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and took birth as a flying cat. The reason for this is that this non-Buddhist practitioner had originally attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception while possessing a body belonging to the desire realm. Being disturbed by flocks of birds, he then made a vow: [“May I become a flying cat.”]
He vowed to become a flying cat (*bi-li*) to prey upon fish and birds.
Later, when his concentration (*samādhi*) failed, he was reborn with this body.
Believing that his attainment of concentration constituted *nirvāṇa*, he gave rise to great false views; subsequently, falling into the Avīci Hell, he received this evil body.
"World-Honored One, how can one sever all modes of existence? Below this is the third section on taking refuge and submission.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the request to expound the Dharma of non-perception; second, the benefits obtained by the assembly at that time; and third, Subhadra’s realization of the Way.
I say: this text on awakening to the Way is too brief; it should be like the latter part.
Below this, the request to explain the dharma of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) is further divided into two sections:
First the request, then the response.
The response itself has two parts:
first, a brief summary; second, a detailed exposition.

Regarding this initial brief explanation of "true perception" (*satyasaṃjñā*): if named according to its object, it should be called "true characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*); if named according to the cognition, it is termed "true perception.
"Perception" (*saṃjñā*) is a name for cognition, while "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is a name for the object.
"Subhadra asked: 'How so? Below this, the second section further requests an extensive explanation.
Within this, there is first the request and then the Buddha’s response.
Regarding the statement in the response that "that which is the locus of cessation is called the perception of reality," there are two meanings:
First, because one eradicates all afflictions through true wisdom, it is said that "it follows the place where they are extinguished";
second, because one dispels conventional existence by means of this emptiness, it is said that "it follows what is extinguished."

Furthermore, as for the statement that "the ultimate truth" and "ultimate emptiness" are so named, these names also apply to the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, as was explained at the beginning of the "Lion's Roar" chapter.

In this present text, it is precisely clarified that true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*); because those of inferior wisdom contemplate it, they attain the bodhi of the śrāvaka, while those of middling wisdom attain the bodhi of the pratyekabuddha.
There have been ancient interpretations claiming that the three vehicles involve different modes of contemplation.

However, this present text clarifies that the three vehicles share the same contemplation of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); the distinction between the three vehicles arises solely from differences in the depth of their wisdom, just as, for example, three animals crossing a river perceive the water's depth differently according to their respective capacities.

The three vehicles equally contemplate the Middle Way; those with profound wisdom immediately attain unsurpassed bodhi, while those with shallow wisdom merely attain the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha or a śrāvaka.
"When this Dharma was spoken, ten thousand bodhisattvas... and so forth; this second section clarifies the benefits gained by the assembly at that time.

The text states that "attaining the true mark (*dharmatā*) in one lifetime and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in two lifetimes" means that a Bodhisattva in the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) is considered to be in one lifetime, while one in the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*) is considered to be in two lifetimes.
If one were to discuss this fully, it would be as explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the meaning of "diminishing birth.
Below the section on "Subhadra," the third part clarifies Subhadra’s realization of the Way.
There ought to have been a formal entrustment, yet the text has not come down in its entirety.
Kaishan said: "From this point onward, one can hardly help but feel sorrow."
Nevertheless, you have all already received the causal conditions for crossing over; thus, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who attain the Way will not be uniform.
Now that the teachings of the sutras are complete, it is only fitting that you exert yourselves; if you fail to do so and encounter [the Dharma] no more, how will you endure sinking into suffering?

The *Gṛhapati-āmantrita-bhikṣu-sūtra* states: "In the latter part of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, there are further the 'Chapter on Burning the Body,' the 'Chapter on Erecting Stūpas,' and the 'Chapter on Entrustment.'"
These three chapters do not appear in this text.
